en: This is the speech of Sūrya. He says: O Atri, let the deceiver, the asura, who is moved by desire for food (इरस्या (*irasyā*) here means by wish for food), not swallow me, who am in such a state and who belong to you, who am your own, with fearful darkness.

The sentence continues: let him not swallow me with the darkness that causes fear. And further: O Mitra, you are Mitra, for you become the one who saves from harm; you are also one whose wealth is truth. You and the royal Varuṇa, you two, protect me here. Or else, Atri himself is called Mitra, and Varuṇa is the other; you two protect me.
- तव संतं (*tava saṃtaṃ*)—who belong to you
- इमं मां (*imaṃ māṃ*)—me, who am covered by darkness
- इरस्या (*irasyā*)—who is moved by desire for food
- मा नि गारीत् (*mā ni gārīt*)—let him not swallow
- मित्रः असि (*mitraḥ asi*)—you are of the nature of Mitra

O Atri, let the deceiver, the asura, who is moved by desire for food, not swallow me, who belong to you and am covered by darkness, with fearful pitch darkness. You are of the nature of Mitra, whose wealth is truth. You together with Varuṇa, the lord, protect me in this situation. (This is the speech of Sūrya.)
[Surya speaks] : Let not the violator, Atri through hunger, swallow with fearful (darkness) me who am yours ; you are Mitra, whose wealth is truth : you and the royal Varuna both protect me.

Sāyaṇa explains that Atri, the Brahmin, saying "protect me here," engaged the pressing-stones for pressing, that is, pressed Soma for Indra; and with a hymn (कीर्यते विक्षिष्यत इति कीरि स्तोत्रं (*kīryate vikṣiṣyata iti kīri stotraṃ*), "what is scattered abroad is a kīri, a hymn") he worshipped the gods, with homage. By the means so stated he placed the eye of Sūrya, the impeller of all, that is, his disc, which pervades everything, in the sky: he made it free from darkness. He then makes this plain: the illusions of the asura named Svarbhānu are called illusion because they bewilder, by means of their own power, and so make others the same; it is such illusions that the fourth prayer drove away, as was said by "the fourth prayer". Thus Indra, with Atri's help, warded them off, that is, he held them back. Or else the third quarter may be explained thus: in the sky of Sūrya, where the light had before been covered, having removed that covering, he set his own eye; that is, he saw the removal of the obstruction and the mass of radiance. The covering of Sūrya by the illusion of Svarbhānu is recorded in the हारिद्रविके (*hāridravike*): the asura Svarbhānu pierced Sūrya with darkness; the gods sought an atonement for him; the first darkness that they struck away became Kṛṣṇāvi, the second became Phālgunī, the third became Valakṣmī, and what remained they cut away, and so on. ⟨NOTE:171⟩
notes: abbreviation ಬೃ. ಪೇ. printed

en: - युयुजानः (*yuyujānaḥ*)—joining together (and pressing Soma for Indra)
- नमसा (*namasā*)—with food in the form of an oblation
The Brahman-knowing Atri, pressing Soma for Indra with the pressing-stones, worshipping the gods with hymns, adorning them with food in the form of oblation, Sūrya's
disc-shaped eye (the radiance) in the sky; he removed the delusion-causing power of Svarbhānu.

Then the Brahman, 'Atri), applying the stones together, propitiating the gods with praise, and adoring them with reverence, placed the eye of Surya in the sky : he dispersed the delusions of Swarbhanu.

Sāyaṇa says that this Ṛk restates what Atri accomplished: यं वै सूर्यं (*yaṃ vai sūryaṃ*). Its explanation is already given. The Atris found that Sūrya afterwards: for Indra, in the Soma sacrifice, by praise of the deities and by homage, one after another, they resisted the thick darkness ⟨NOTE:172⟩ and obtained him. Others were not able; they did not obtain him.
notes: abbreviation ಬೃ. ಜೇ. printed

en: - यं वै सूर्यं (*yaṃ vai sūryaṃ*)—which Sūrya
- अत्रयः (*atrayaḥ*)—the sages born in the family of Atri
- नहि अशक्नु वन् (*nahi aśaknu van*)—were not able to do this work
The sages born in the family of Atri obtained that Sūrya whom Svarbhānu, the son of an asura, had covered and hidden with pitch darkness. No others were able to do this great deed.
The sun, whom the Asura Swarbhanu, had enveloped with darkness, the sons of Atri subsequently recovered : no others were able (to effect his release).

Sāyaṇa addresses the two deities Mitra and Varuṇa: which sacrificer, desiring the sacrifice (ऋतायन् (*ṛtāyan*)), could (so he supplies the missing verb) perform it for you? ⟨NOTE:194⟩ He then glosses दिवः सदसि (*divaḥ sadasi*) as "in the seat, the place belonging to the heaven-world", महो (*maho*) as "of the great", and takes पार्थिवस्य (*pārthivasya*) as the seat of the atmosphere, which gives rise to ṛta, the word being used of it because it is its cause. He explains त्रासीथां (*trāsīthāṃ*) as "protect": protect us in these three places; the word वा (*vā*) is used in the sense of ... ⟨NOTE:195⟩ Then the block goes on with "moreover" (किंच (*kiṃca*)).

The block continues the gloss: for the one who desires to sacrifice to you and for the giver of the oblation, and for me (यज्ञायते दे ना हनिर्दात्रे च मह्यं (*yajñāyate de nā hanirdātre ca mahyaṃ*)) ⟨NOTE:196⟩, give पशुषो न वाजान् (*paśuṣo na vājān*): the foods that dwell in animals, such as milk and curds. As you bestow them, so protect. Or else the word न (*na*) is in the sense of "and": give both animals and foods (पशुषः (*paśuṣaḥ*), वाजांश्च (*vājāṃśca*)).
notes: ಶ್ರಿತಃ printed; ತ್ರಿತಃ?
ಸಧ್ರ್ಯ ೧ ಜ್ಞಾಮ ಭದ್ರಂ: ಸಧ್ರ್ಯ ೧ ಜ್ಞಾಮ garbled in the first line
ಋ. ಸಂ. ೧೮-೩೨-೬ printed; no Maṇḍala 18 in the Saṃhitā; reference as supplied

en: - ऋतायन् (*ṛtāyan*)—to perform the sacrifice (is he able?)
- दिवः वा सदसि (*divaḥ vā sadasi*)—either from the place of the heaven-world
- पार्थिवस्य वा (*pārthivasya vā*)—or from the place of the earth
- ऋतस्य वा (*ṛtasya vā*)—or from the place of the atmosphere
- यज्ञायते (*yajñāyate*)—to one who wishes to worship (you) with sacrifice
- दे वा (*de vā*)—and to one who offers the oblation

O Mitra and Varuṇa, what sacrificer, with reference to you, is able to perform a sacrifice that is pleasing to you? Whether you are in the place of the heaven-world, in the great place of the earth, or in the region of the atmosphere, protect us from there. Provide animals and foods to the one who wishes to worship you through the sacrifice and to the one who offers the oblation.

Who, Mitra, and Varuna, desiring to sacrifice to you, (is able to do so) ? do you, whether (abiding) in the region of heaven, or of the vast earth, or of the firmament, protect us, and give to the donor (of the oblation), and to the sacrificer, cattle and food.

Those deities, Mitra and the others, are to accept our well-made hymn (सुवृक्तिं स्तोमं (*suvṛktiṃ stomaṃ*), a hymn of praise free from evil and the like) with praises or with oblations; जुषंत (*juṣaṃta*) means "let them enjoy". They are those who hold (दधते (*dadhate*)) the hymn so described. Deities are of two kinds, those who share in praise and those who share in oblations; here those who share in praise are meant. आयुः (*āyuḥ*), the ever-moving, is said to be Vāyu. Then the Maruts are separated off and specified. रुद्राय माळ्हुषे (*rudrāya māḷhuṣe*): the dative is used in the sense of the instrumental, so "together with Rudra, the showerer". सजोषाः (*sajoṣāḥ*) means "pleased together"; the idea is that they are his sons. Some say that "रुद्राय सजोषा (*rudrāya sajoṣā*)" is an epithet of all the deities, Mitra and the rest.
- दधते (*dadhate*)—those who accept and hold, they also (such sharers in praise); (or) ये (*ye*)—those who
- मीळ्हुषे (*mīḷhuṣe*)—the giver of what is desired
- सजोषाः (*sajoṣāḥ*)—those who with equal affection together receive the oblation (sharers in oblations); ते (*te*)—all those deities, that is,

Those deities who have accepted the well-made praises and are famed as sharers in praise, and those who, joined in equal affection with Rudra, the giver of what is desired, receive the oblation together and are renowned as sharers in oblations, that is, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Vāyu, Indra, Ṛbhukṣan and the Maruts, may all of them enjoy our praises and be satisfied.

May those divinities, Mitra, Varuna, Aryaman, Ayu, Indra, Ribhukshin, the Maruts who accept pious praise, be pleased by our adorations, partaking of the gratification afforded to Rudra, the showerer (of benefits).

By this verse the Aśvins and Rudra are addressed. O Aśvins, best controllers of desires: you, at the course of the wind (वातस्य पत्मन् (*vātasya patman*)), the possessor being taken by likeness of property, when a horse whose going equals the wind's is reached ⟨NOTE:197⟩, and for the nourishment of the chariot (रथ्यस्य रथस्य पुष्टौ (*rathyasya rathasya puṣṭau*)), I call (हुवध्यै (*huvadhyai*): I call; I am able to call). Or else: for the nourishing of your chariot, the means of swift going like the wind. उत वा (*uta vā*) means "and moreover". दिवः (*divaḥ*) means "to the shining one", the genitive being used in the sense of the dative; असुराय (*asurāya*), to Rudra, the taker of life. Or else: to the Asura belonging to the heaven-world, the giver of life, that is, to Sūrya or to Vāyu. यज्ञवे (*yajñave*): to the accomplisher of the sacrifice. O priests, bring forth (भरध्वं (*bharadhvaṃ*): provide) a hymn worthy of reflection (मन्म (*manma*)), and as foods (अंधांसीव (*aṃdhāṃsīva*)) the oblations; that is, both oblations and hymn.
notes: ಋ. ಸಂ. ೫.೧೦-೬ and ೫೧-೬ printed twice in a row; which is meant?

en: - पुष्पा (*puṣpā*)—for the increase of its speed
- असुराय (*asurāya*)—Rudra, the taker of life, with reference to whom
- अंधांसीव (*aṃdhāṃsīva*)—as one procures foods in the form of oblations

O Aśvin deities, restrainers of desire, we pray to you that your chariot, swift like the going of the wind, may attain increase of its speed towards our sacrifice. O priests, as you procure foods in the form of oblations to offer to Rudra, the shining, the accomplisher of the sacrifice and the taker of life, so procure (recite) a hymn worthy of reflection.
I invoke you, Aswins, the restrainers (of desire), for the acceleration
of your chariot with the swiftness of the wind: (priests) offer praise and
oblations to the celestial destroyer of life, to the accomplisher of the

The deities here are those named by their marks (liṅga). The construction is प्र जग्मुः (*pra jagmuḥ*), "they go forth". सक्षणः (*sakṣaṇaḥ*) is one who attends the sacrifice or one who overcomes enemies; दिव्यः (*divyaḥ*) is one born in heaven; कण्वहोता (*kaṇvahotā*): the Kaṇvas are seers, the wise,

who are the hotṛs, the callers, of that one; so he is described. त्रितः (*tritaḥ*) is the one spread out in the three places beginning with the earth; दिवः सजोषाः (*divaḥ sajoṣāḥ*), of the same course or the same pleasure with the sun (Sūrya); वातः (*vātaḥ*) is Vāyu as already characterised; Agni; Pūṣan, the nourisher of that name; and Bhaga. In this sacrifice, which has the bringing forward (प्रभृथे (*prabhṛthe*)), all the deities named, विश्वभोजाः (*viśvabhojāḥ*), protectors of all or devourers of all ⟨NOTE:198⟩, the best among those who possess horses of excellent going, go forth (प्र जग्मुः (*pra jagmuḥ*): proceed) as if to battle (आजिं न (*ājiṃ na*)).
notes: ಅಶ್ವಾ ನಾ ಸಂತಿ ತೈರಿತಿ — the last clause of the bhāṣya is damaged; sense uncertain

en: - सक्षणः (*sakṣaṇaḥ*)—the one who accepts the share of the sacrifice
- दिव्यः (*divyaḥ*)—the one born in the heaven-world
- कण्वहोता (*kaṇvahotā*)—the one who has the Kaṇva seers themselves as hotṛs
- विश्वभोजाः (*viśvabhojāḥ*)—all the deities who protect the universe
- आश्वश्वतमाः (*āśvaśvatamāḥ*)—the horses that are the best even among swift-going horses
- आजिं न (*ājiṃ na*)—as they run to the field of battle

The one who accepts the share of the sacrifice, who is born in the heaven-world, and who has the Kaṇva seers as his hotṛs, namely Trita; Vāyu, who has equal affection with the sun; Agni; the god Pūṣan; Bhaga; and all the deities who protect the universe: may they come quickly and graciously to this sacrifice, as the best of the swift-going horses run to the battle.
May the divine accepter of sacrifice, of whom the Kanwas are
the priests, Trita, Vayu, and Agni, concurring in satisfaction with (the
ruler of) heaven, or (Surya and) Pushan, and Bhaga, and they who are the
protectors of the universe, (come quickly) to the sacrifice, as the fleetest

The deities mentioned in the present mantra are all, Sāyaṇa has said in the introduction, deities indicated by marks (liṅgokta). Liṅga means the individual and unique quality of each deity. For example, what are the unique qualities of Agni, Indra, Vāyu and Sūrya? —

व्यवस्येन्मंत्रमाग्नेयं अंगैरग्नेशश्च लक्षितं । हविष्संक्ति प्रधान्यैश्च नामाह्वानैश्च केवलैः ॥ (*vyavasyenmaṃtramāgneyaṃ aṃgairagneśaśca lakṣitaṃ | haviṣsaṃkti pradhānyaiśca nāmāhvānaiśca kevalaiḥ ‖*)

By mantras that indicate the special qualities of Agni ⟨NOTE:199⟩, Agni is to be worshipped. One kind is that in which the havis-paṅkti is prominent, or the other kind is that which is to be recited in the form of an invocation. Thus the indication of the limbs of Agni is of two kinds. In the same way,
ऐंद्रस्तु मंत्रो वायवैर्लिंगैरैंद्रॆश्च लक्ष्यते । नामधेयैश्च वज्रस्य बलकृत्या बलेन च ॥ (*aiṃdrastu maṃtro vāyavairliṃgairaiṃdrèśca lakṣyate | nāmadheyaiśca vajrasya balakṛtyā balena ca ‖*)

Just as the mantras that indicate the special qualities of Indra describe the nature of Indra, they make known the natures of Vāyu in the same way. The nature of these two becomes known through the mention of the names of the thunderbolt weapon, through usages that suggest prowess, and through descriptions of prowess. And,

सौरस्तु लिंगैः सूरस्य गुणैः सर्वैश्च तैजसैः । नामधेयैश्च चंद्रस्य सूक्तं च भजतेऽत्र यैः ॥ (*saurastu liṃgaiḥ sūrasya guṇaiḥ sarvaiśca taijasaiḥ | nāmadheyaiśca caṃdrasya sūktaṃ ca bhajate 'tra yaiḥ ‖*)

The Sūrya mantras are to be recognised by the description of all the qualities of Sūrya and by the account of the divisions relating to his radiance. Thus the way of recognising the deities indicated by marks has been told. In the same manner, in the present mantra too, it takes no great effort to know the place of deities such as Agni and Pūṣan. But in "कण्वहोता त्रितः (*kaṇvahotā tritaḥ*)" it takes a little effort to understand the nature of Trita. Sāyaṇa has explained त्रिषु क्षित्यादिस्थानेषु तायमानः (सूरैण सह समानगतिः) वातः । वायुः (*triṣu kṣityādisthāneṣu tāyamānaḥ (sūraiṇa saha samānagatiḥ) vātaḥ | vāyuḥ*) as the Vāyu who is in the three worlds beginning with the earth and who has the same course as the sun. Therefore the two, दिवः सजोषाः (*divaḥ sajoṣāḥ*) and कण्वहोता (*kaṇvahotā*), become epithets of वातः (*vātaḥ*). In this view, what is the import of the epithet कण्वहोता (*kaṇvahotā*)? He has explained that too in this way: कण्वा ऋषयो मेधाविनो वा होतार आह्वातारो यस्य सः । (*kaṇvā ṛṣayo medhāvino vā hotāra āhvātāro yasya saḥ |*). The word kaṇva means a seer. This word is also used in the sense of "wise". Sāyaṇa, explaining the meaning of this word ⟨NOTE:201⟩,
कण्वशब्दार्थः । कणंति ध्वनंति स्तोत्रादिपाठेनेति कण्वा ऋत्विजः । (*kaṇvaśabdārthaḥ | kaṇaṃti dhvanaṃti stotrādipāṭheneti kaṇvā ṛtvijaḥ |*)

has said that priests are called Kaṇvas because they worship while making a sound in the form of praise. In the present mantra the import has been explained as Vāyu, who has as his hotṛs the seers endowed with intelligence. Besides, there is also the view that by the words दिवः सजोषाः त्रितः (*divaḥ sajoṣāḥ tritaḥ*) a special deity different from Vāyu is indicated, namely the god named Trita, who has equal affection with Āditya. Therefore, in this context, what precise meaning is possible from the epithet कण्वहोता (*kaṇvahotā*), and for which deity the epithet, if it is applied to him, makes the meaning natural here: these and similar points have to be examined at once.

Some have also given an import referring to Indra, by taking the words प्र सक्षणो दिव्यः (*pra sakṣaṇo divyaḥ*) to mean "the victor of the world of the gods". The scholar Griffith has translated it as "The heavenly victor, he whose priest is Kanva, Trita........." and has explained that "heavenly victor" means Indra. In this context one must understand what the word सक्षणः (*sakṣaṇaḥ*) means.

Sāyaṇa has given सक्षणः यज्ञं सेवमानः; शत्रूणां सोढा ना (*sakṣaṇaḥ yajñaṃ sevamānaḥ; śatrūṇāṃ soḍhā nā*), alternatively: one meaning, "one who attends the sacrifice", or another, "one who has the strength to defeat enemies". The word sakṣaṇa, formed from the root sac (sañj), gives the first meaning. It means "one who is joined together"; here the sense is "one who is joined with the sacrifice, that is, one who attends it". If this meaning is taken, then the epithet sakṣaṇa need not apply to Indra alone. This mark could apply to other deities such as Agni too. Therefore, in the present context, it is natural to take the second meaning. Then the word sakṣaṇa, formed from the root saha, gives the sense "one who has the power to face enemies".

The word sakṣaṇa is not used anywhere else in the whole Ṛk-saṃhitā except in this one place. But the word sakṣiṇi is used in other places. It can only be said that the meaning of the two words is the same. Although in one or two places the word sakṣiṇi is used in the first meaning, its use in the sense of enduring and in the sense of power is the more frequent. For example: सिंचंति हर्मस्य सक्षिणिं (*siṃcaṃti harmasya sakṣiṇiṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 9-71-4); परि वृत्राणि सक्षिणिः (*pari vṛtrāṇi sakṣiṇiḥ*) (9.110-1); पृतनासु सक्षिणिं (*pṛtanāsu sakṣiṇiṃ*) (1.111-3). In all such places the import is "one who has the power to win victory".

If, in the present mantra too, one takes the word sakṣaṇa to mean "victorious" and explains it as an epithet referring to Indra, an objection is possible even then. Trita too is famed as a renowned victor. The question why the word sakṣaṇa should not be an epithet of Trita as well is natural. Besides, the epithet कण्वहोता (*kaṇvahotā*) naturally states the quality of Trita.

It does not fit Indra very well. The epithet kaṇvahotā too is not used anywhere else in the Ṛk-saṃhitā except in this one place. Since there are usages such as कण्वसखि (*kaṇvasakhi*) and कण्वतम (*kaṇvatama*), one must examine what they mean in those contexts and the special quality of which deity they make known.

स इदग्निः कण्वतमः कण्वसखार्यः परस्यांतरस्य तरुषः । अग्निः पातु गृणतो अग्निः सूरीनग्निर्ददातु तेषामवो नः ॥ (*sa idagniḥ kaṇvatamaḥ kaṇvasakhāryaḥ parasyāṃtarasya taruṣaḥ | agniḥ pātu gṛṇato agniḥ sūrīnagnirdadātu teṣāmavo naḥ ‖*)

In this verse the word kaṇva means "praisers". The epithet कण्वतम (*kaṇvatama*) is used to show the sense that Agni is the best among praisers, and the epithet कण्वसखा (*kaṇvasakhā*) to show the sense that he has the praisers themselves as his friends. These two words make known special qualities of Agni. Besides,

नि यस्य ते ज्रयसानस्याजर धक्षोर्न वाताः परि संत्यच्युताः । आ रण्वासो युयुधयो न सत्वनं त्रितं नशंत प्र शिषंत इष्टये ॥ (*ni yasya te jrayasānasyājara dhakṣorna vātāḥ pari saṃtyacyutāḥ | ā raṇvāso yuyudhayo na satvanaṃ tritaṃ naśaṃta pra śiṣaṃta iṣṭaye ‖*)

in this verse there is a description of Trita, who has the quality of a warrior. It is a description of Agni. This same Agni, who is of the form of Trita, is described in the next mantra after the one quoted above with the epithets kaṇvatama and kaṇvasakhā. Thus, just as in many contexts there is a reference to Agni named Trita, it would not be wrong to say that in the present mantra too Agni is the one indicated. But here room remains for another kind of objection. Since the word Agni itself has been stated in the present mantra, some may also ask whether, when Agni is being indicated, the use of the word Trita again with reference to Agni is unnecessary. But there is no substance in that objection. If it were so, the reference to Pūṣan, who is a transformed form of Agni, being of the form of Sūrya, would also be out of place. Except for Vāta alone, all the other deities praised in the present mantra are deities whose nature is that of light. Among them, the epithet दिवः सजोषाः (*divaḥ sajoṣāḥ*) fits Trita naturally. Therefore, if it is said that it will not be wrong for Agni, who is of the form of light, to be denoted here by the word Trita, then, since the word Trita is used in other places to show the special qualities of Indra and others also, if one asks what the basis is for saying that in the present mantra Agni alone is precisely indicated, two kinds of answer can be given. First, another mantra contained in this same sūkta supports this view. How? Thus:

वृष्णो अस्तोषि भूम्यस्य गर्भं त्रितो नपातमपां सुवृक्ति । गृणीते अग्निरेतरी न शूषैः शोचिष्केशो नि रिणाति वना ॥ (*vṛṣṇo astoṣi bhūmyasya garbhaṃ trito napātamapāṃ suvṛkti | gṛṇīte agniretarī na śūṣaiḥ śociṣkeśo ni riṇāti vanā ‖*)

In this verse there is a description of the lightning-fire. This lightning-fire stands as the womb of the cloud. The word Trita is an epithet of this lightning-fire. Therefore it can be said that the word Trita here is an individual mark of Agni. Second, when Indra and others are indicated in other places, the import of this word is of a different kind. Therefore, to understand these contexts one must also notice for which of the remaining deities the word Trita is an epithet.

(1) Yāska, explaining this word in two contexts, has given two derivations of it. First, when giving the import of the mantra Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-105-8, he explained श्रितः तीर्णतमो मेधया बभूव (*śritaḥ tīrṇatamo medhayā babhūva*) ⟨NOTE:203⟩: Trita is the most excellent among the wise; because he crossed over ignorance exceedingly by his intelligence, he has this name. Here Trita is the name of a great seer, a disciple of Bṛhaspati. (The story of this seer and his greatness are explained in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, part 8, pp. 443-447. That explanation is not relevant here.) (Ni. 4.6)
(2) Second, when explaining the mantra Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-187-1, he has given the import त्रिस्थान इंद्रः (*tristhāna iṃdraḥ*), Indra who stands pervading all three worlds. (Ni. 9 25)

Sāyaṇa's derivation follows, more or less, the derivation of the author of the Nirukta. In about twenty mantras Trita is praised as a great seer. In all the other places he has explained him as pervading the three places, and has said that, according to the context, the word is an epithet of deities such as Vāyu, Varuṇa, Indra and Agni. As we said above, if it is to be stated precisely that the present mantra indicates only the lightning-fire, one must notice the use of this word in the other places. The word Trita is used in forty contexts in the Ṛk-saṃhitā. Among them, in most it is used either together with some deity of the atmosphere, or in identity with a deity. Besides, in some contexts he is described as a deity who has occupied a place beyond the range of sight. In this way the uses of the word Trita in these various contexts can roughly be divided into eight groups. All of them are descriptions of the power of Trita.
(1) Situations in which he is joined with Indra: 16. अनु त्रितस्य युध्यतः शुष्मं (*anu tritasya yudhyataḥ śuṣmaṃ*)
(2) Situation in which, not with Indra but alone, he is the slayer of Vṛtra: 1. (यस्य त्रितो व्योजसा वृत्रं विपर्वमर्दयत् (*yasya trito vyojasā vṛtraṃ viparvamardayat*)) (1-187-1)
(3) Described as having the form of a sacrificial horse: 1. असि त्रितो गुह्येन व्रतेन (*asi trito guhyena vratena*) (1-163-3)
(4) Situations in which he is joined with the Maruts: 4. त्रितं जराय जरतां (*tritaṃ jarāya jaratāṃ*) (2-34-10) and so on.
(5) Situations in which he is described as shown in identity with Agni: 7. यदीमह त्रितो दिवि (*yadīmaha trito divi*) (5-9-5) and so on.
(6) In identity with Varuṇa: 1. त्रितं जूती सपर्यत (*tritaṃ jūtī saparyata*) (8.41-6) and so on.
(7) Described together with Soma: 4. उप त्रितस्य (*upa tritasya*) (9-102-2) and so on.
(8) Described as one who has, in a place beyond the range of sight, an individual form that is beyond comprehension: 6. त्रिताय तद्विभावरी (*tritāya tadvibhāvarī*) (8-47-14) and so on.

Thus there are forty situations in all. Among these, Trita, when described together with Indra, is generally described as fighting with Indra against the demon Vṛtra, or as offering Soma to Indra. When he is connected with the Maruts, he is a helper in matters such as the shining of lightning. With Agni he has identity itself. As to who he is and what his nature is, it has been said that his place and nature are beyond the range of sight.

When one explains the subject of such an indescribable Trita, the opinions of the scholars cannot possibly be of one kind. Therefore some have explained by showing identity with Indra, some with Vāyu, and some with Agni. But the nature of each of the original deities cannot be described precisely. It cannot be said that, through the division called "deities indicated by marks", knowledge of the individual mark of each deity is possible. It is also possible that a single epithet makes known a quality common to many deities. For example, the epithet Trita alone describes the pervasion of the three worlds by deities such as Indra, Agni and Vāyu, and so in some contexts it is a means of stating the precise meaning. But in the present case, which deity's special quality Trita reflects most can be stated only as far as it is possible, on the basis of Vedic passages.

Although some scholars have shown identity between Trita and Indra, Trita and Indra are generally indicated together; so in all the contexts where he is described with Indra, he has to be regarded as a seer. (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1.52.5; 2-11-19, 20; 5-86-1; 8-13-16; 10.8-7; 10-99-6 and so on).

Identity with Vāyu cannot be stated. How? In places such as नि पस्त्यासु त्रितः स्तभूयन् (*ni pastyāsu tritaḥ stabhūyan*) (10.46-6) there is a description of Trita as the friend of the house. Vāyu is never described as the friend of the house; the friend of the house is none other than Agni.

It is described in many contexts that the atmosphere, which is the common abode of Agni, Vāyu and Indra, is the abode of Trita. Therefore it may be said that the view is sound that the lightning-fire, which has qualities common to all of them, is the one indicated by the name Trita. The identity shown, as stated above, between Trita and the horse of Varuṇa also supports this view. The association with the Maruts too becomes clear from this itself. This lightning-fire is one of the forms of the god Agni. Therefore it is the most natural view to show identity between Trita and Agni. Finally, the place beyond the range of sight also only suggests the nature of the lightning-fire.

There is no doubt that the derivation that Sāyaṇa has stated in the present mantra (5-41-4), त्रिषु क्षित्यादिस्थानेषु तायमानः (*triṣu kṣityādisthāneṣu tāyamānaḥ*), makes known these three forms: the earthly fire, the lightning-fire of the atmosphere, and the fire of the form of Āditya in the heaven-world. In the Ṛk-saṃhitā no other matter is described so much as these three conditions of Agni. (तिस्रो यह्वस्य समिधः (*tisro yahvasya samidhaḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-2-9).

अग्ने श्री ते वाजिना त्री षधस्था तिस्रस्ते जिह्वा ऋतजात पूर्विः । तिस्र उ ते तन्नो देववातास्ताभिर्नः पाहि गिरो अप्रयुच्छन् ॥ (*agne śrī te vājinā trī ṣadhasthā tisraste jihvā ṛtajāta pūrviḥ | tisra u te tanno devavātāstābhirnaḥ pāhi giro aprayucchan ‖*)

In this way, even when all kinds of powers of Agni, such as his origin, extent, nature and action, are described, this threefold character must invariably be described. (दिवस्परि प्रथमं जज्ञे (*divaspari prathamaṃ jajñe*) 10.45-1 and so on). Apart from the two forms that are well established, the earthly fire and Āditya, what remains is the third,
the lightning-fire. Therefore it appears that one may say freely that this lightning-fire itself is what the word Trita denotes.

In the present mantra too, if one takes the word Trita to mean Agni, and if one is to stress the point that the epithet kaṇvahotā indicates no deity other than Agni, one must again examine the qualities common to Trita and Agni. These qualities must be common only to Trita and Agni, and must not apply to other deities.
Therefore, just as above the details of the description of Trita were divided into eight kinds, the details of the descriptions of Agni too can be divided into the same eight parts.

(1) First, the association and relation of Agni with Indra. Apart from eleven sūktas that praise Agni and Indra together, addressed to both at once, in the other mantras contained in many more sūktas too these two deities are praised and extolled together.

चक्राथे हि सध्र्य १ ज्ञाम भद्रं सध्रीचीना वृत्रहणा उत स्थः । ताविंद्राग्नी सध्वंचा निषद्या वृष्टः सोमस्य वृषणा वृषेथां ॥ (*cakrāthe hi sadhrya 1 jñāma bhadraṃ sadhrīcīnā vṛtrahaṇā uta sthaḥ | tāviṃdrāgnī sadhvaṃcā niṣadyā vṛṣṭaḥ somasya vṛṣaṇā vṛṣethāṃ ‖*) ⟨NOTE:204⟩

O Indra and Agni, you have made your auspicious names known as always joined together. And you have been together even at the time of the slaying of Vṛtra, as slayers of the demon Vṛtra. Therefore, O Indra and Agni, bestowers of what is desired, you two, joined together and seated on the sacrificial altar, drink the flowing Soma juice of your share. In this way the constant association is praised in all the main activities such as the slaying of Vṛtra and the drinking of Soma. (This matter is described clearly in many mantras such as Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-108-5; 1-109-5; 1-109-8; 3-12-4.)

(2) Second, the very relation that has been shown above between Trita and the horse of Varuṇa is shown between Agni and the horse of Varuṇa. The horse called Dadhikrā, who is praised as being of the form of Āditya, is that same horse.

हंसः शुचिषद्वसुरंतरिक्षसद्दूता वेदिषदतिथिर्दुरोणसत् । नृपद्वरसदृतसद्योमसदब्बा गोजा ऋतजा अद्रिजा ऋतं ॥ (*haṃsaḥ śuciṣadvasuraṃtarikṣasaddūtā vediṣadatithirduroṇasat | nṛpadvarasadṛtasadyomasadabbā gojā ṛtajā adrijā ṛtaṃ ‖*)

This Agni, named Dadhikrā, is praised as being within the light in the form of a swan, in the atmosphere in the form of Vasu, on the sacrificial altar in the form of the hotṛ, in the house in the form of a guest, as born of the mountain, as born of ṛta, and with many other qualities. He is described in this way in दीदिवांसं नाग्निं (*dīdivāṃsaṃ nāgniṃ*) (4-39.2 ; ) and so on.

(3) In the way Trita is praised as the slayer of Vṛtra (alone, without Indra's company), Agni too is praised in the same way. तमु त्वा वृत्रहंतमं (*tamu tvā vṛtrahaṃtamaṃ*) (1-78-4); स वृत्रहा सनयो विश्ववेदाः (*sa vṛtrahā sanayo viśvavedāḥ*) (3-20-4); अग्निरगामि भारतो वृत्रहा पुरुचेतनः (*agniragāmi bhārato vṛtrahā purucetanaḥ*) (6-16-19): mantras such as these praise the act of Agni in slaying Vṛtra. In sixteen mantras in all Agni is praised as the slayer of Vṛtra. Among these, in seven the matter of his being joined with Indra is stated.

(4) The association between Trita and the Maruts, as it was described above, is established in the same way between Agni and the Maruts; epithets such as मरुद्वधः (*marudvadhaḥ*) (3-13-6) make known this point. It is also said that Agni is the tongue of the Maruts: अग्निजिह्वा (*agnijihvā*) (1-89-7). Here one more special point must be noticed. Just as the epithets kaṇvatama and kaṇvahotā and the like are used in the praises of Agni and Trita, in the same way, when Agni and the Maruts are praised together too, the praisers named Kaṇva are the ones addressed.
सहो षु णो वज्रहस्तैः कण्वासो अग्निं मरुद्भिः (*saho ṣu ṇo vajrahastaiḥ kaṇvāso agniṃ marudbhiḥ*)
In this verse the Kaṇvas are entreated to praise Agni joined with the Maruts. Sāyaṇa has said that here the word kaṇva means either praisers or the seers born in the Kaṇva lineage.

(5) Fifth, not only the direct relation between Trita and Agni, but the identity between Trita and Agni is the main point. In this context the question naturally arises whether any main quality that applies to no other deity is well known as showing a common property of Trita and Agni. In answer to this, one may say freely that such a common property is well known. The epithet आप्त्य (*āptya*) is used in the Ṛk-saṃhitā in ten contexts only with reference to Trita. Sāyaṇa, in the introduction to the sūkta Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-105, says that the derivation "Āptya, because he was manifested from the waters (water)" is stated in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa too:

त्रितस्य चापां पुत्रत्वं तैत्तीरियाः स्पष्टमामनंति । ततस्ति तोऽजायत । यदद्भ्योऽजायंत । तदास्यानामाप्यत्यं ॥ (*tritasya cāpāṃ putratvaṃ taittīriyāḥ spaṣṭamāmanaṃti | tatasti to 'jāyata | yadadbhyo 'jāyaṃta | tadāsyānāmāpyatyaṃ ‖*) (Tai. Brā. 3-2-8-11)

Sāyaṇa has cited just this Brāhmaṇa sentence. Because he was born from the waters, he became Āpya. But how does the derivation of the form Āptya arise? Sāyaṇa has given the answer elsewhere, that it is Vedic usage. Sentences such as त्रितस्तद्वेदात् (*tritastadvedāt*) and so on are the illustrations (1-105-9 etc.). That Agni too has manifested from the waters is well known, with accounts in many places. O Agni, you are kindled in the firmament, the abode of the waters (अग्ने अपां समिध्यसे दुरोणे (*agne apāṃ samidhyase duroṇe*)). (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-25-5) When Agni, held by the waters, occupies them, then the streams of water, in the dwelling-place of Āditya, their place of origin, are pervaded by his rays and receive a new refinement. Afterwards Agni, who is in the form of lightning, unites and joins with the waters. (अपामुपस्थे विभृतः (*apāmupasthe vibhṛtaḥ*) Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-144-2).

The hotṛ who knows the sky is stationed in the lap of the waters in the form of lightning (10-46-1). The Bhṛgu seers realised Agni, who stands in the midst of the waters, and established him among men. (10-46-2; 2-4-2). निधीयमानपमगूळ्मप्पु प्र मे देवानां व्रतपा उवाच ॥ (*nidhīyamānapamagūḷmappu pra me devānāṃ vratapā uvāca ‖*) The great seer who knew the secret of the gods told me that Agni is within the waters. (18-32-6)⟨NOTE:205⟩

Thus the account that Agni too is born of the waters, and the account that Trita, being born of the waters, is Āptya, both tell in the same way of an origin from the waters of the firmament; so there is no doubt that both accounts convey the very nature of the lightning-fire.

In the same way the epithet Apāṃ Napāt too conveys the nature of the lightning-fire. How? अपां नपादा ह्यस्थादुपस्थं जिह्मानामूर्ध्वो विद्युत्व वसानः । तस्य ज्येष्ठं महिमानं वहंतीर्हिरण्यवर्णाः परि यंति यह्वीः ॥ (*apāṃ napādā hyasthādupasthaṃ jihmānāmūrdhvo vidyutva vasānaḥ | tasya jyeṣṭhaṃ mahimānaṃ vahaṃtīrhiraṇyavarṇāḥ pari yaṃti yahvīḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-35-9)

Clothed in a garment of lightning, the son of the waters stands within the shining waters. In his own form he is golden-hued and exceedingly attractive. The sentences quoted above show the identity of Trita Āptya with the fire named Apāṃnapāt. Both epithets are descriptions of the nature of the lightning-fire that dwells in the firmament. As has been said above, it can be stated with certainty that Trita, the Kaṇva hotṛ indicated in the mantra under discussion, is none other than this lightning-fire.

6) Just as the identity of Trita and Varuṇa has been shown, there are also many sentences showing the identity of Agni and Varuṇa. For example: I have known the face of Agni to be the face of Varuṇa. (अनीकं वरुणस्य मंसि (*anīkaṃ varuṇasya maṃsi*) Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-88-2).
7) युवमेतानि दिवि रोचनान्यग्निश्च सोम सक्रतू अधत्तं । (*yuvametāni divi rocanānyagniśca soma sakratū adhattaṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1.93-5)

O Agni and Soma, you two are of like action. These shining star-systems, visible to our eyes, you two together have lifted up in the heaven. In sentences such as these, the relation between Agni and Soma is stated in the same way as the relation between Trita and Soma was shown above.

8) Lastly, just as Trita is described as hidden in a place beyond sight, so Agni too is praised. त्वामग्ने अंगिरसो गुहा हितमन्वदिंदञ्छायाणं वनेवने । (*tvāmagne aṃgiraso guhā hitamanvadiṃdañchāyāṇaṃ vanevane |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5.10-6) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 51-6)⟨NOTE:206⟩
O Agni, the Aṅgirases found you hidden in a secret place.

बृहंत इद्वानवो भाय्जीकमग्निं सचंत विद्युतो न शुक्राः । गुहेव वृद्धं सदसि स्वे अंतरपार ऊर्वे अमृतं दुहानाः ॥ (*bṛhaṃta idvānavo bhāyjīkamagniṃ sacaṃta vidyuto na śukrāḥ | guheva vṛddhaṃ sadasi sve aṃtarapāra ūrve amṛtaṃ duhānāḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-1-14)
Great lights, like the gleams of lightning, served Agni who stood in a secret place. And so on: this is a description of Agni as hidden in a place beyond sight.

Thus, having set out the common qualities of Trita and Agni, it has been shown that the sentences of the Ṛk-saṃhitā themselves are clear proofs for establishing that Trita is none other than the lightning-fire. Other sentences of the Brāhmaṇas and the like, which help to confirm this very point, have also been quoted above.

en: Maruts, you bring wealth that is yoked with horses, that is, wealth accompanied by horses, or a son fit for horses: provide it. The riches, that is, wealth in the form of cattle, horses and the like, have been obtained. अव (*ava*) is a name for food; so for food, or for the protection of the wealth that has been obtained, the praiser holds, that is, offers, his praise. And may the hotṛ Atri, of Auśija Kakṣīvat, be well happy (शेवमिति सुखनाम (*śevamiti sukhanāma*), "śeva" is a name for happiness), through the objects of desire that are means of going, or through horses. Maruts, who are swift, he says, the desires or horses of you swift ones are the means.⟨NOTE:207⟩
notes: the number of this Ṛk is not printed in the Saṃhitā or Pada block; 15 follows from the sequence of 14 and 16

en: - युक्ताश्वं (*yuktāśvaṃ*)—so that it is accompanied by horses
- ये एवाः (*ye evāḥ*)—whatever swift-moving horses there are

O Maruts, procure for us wealth accompanied by horses. Both for obtaining new riches and for preserving what we have, the praiser composes and recites praise that extols you. O Maruts, may the hotṛ Atri, of Kakṣīvat, obtain excellent happiness together with the horses that belong to you, the swift-going, and that move swiftly.

Maruts, you bring wealth comprising horses: to acquire and preserve riches the wise man offers you praise: may the ministrant priest, (Atri), of the son of Ushij (Kakshivat), be made happy by those swift-going (horses) which are the swift.going (horses), Maruts, of you who are rapid in motion.

The sixth Ṛk is the yājyā for the oblation in the animal sacrifice to Vāyu; it is prescribed by the sūtra प्र वो वायुं रथयुजं कृणुद्धमुत त्वामदिते महि (*pra vo vāyuṃ rathayujaṃ kṛṇuddhamuta tvāmadite mahi*) (Ā. 3-8). O priests who are mine, make Vāyu, the god, yoked to the chariot for going to the sacrifice. Praise with hymns, that is, with the mantras that are means of worship, the shining one, the vipra, who is the special fulfiller of desires or is worshipful like a vipra, the one who is to be praised, or the giver of fruit. Moreover, the goers, those who touch the sacrifice, the women of fair form, or the excellent, praiseworthy wives, the wives of the gods,
in this sacrifice, for our rite, to accomplish it,⟨NOTE:208⟩ may come: so he says, आगतवत्यः (*āgatavatyaḥ*), "they who have come".

en: - रथयुजं (*rathayujaṃ*)—so that he makes ready his chariot (for going to the sacrifice)
- विप्रं (*vipraṃ*)—the special fulfiller of desired ends
- ऋतसापः (*ṛtasāpaḥ*)—those who accept the sacrificial rite
- धिये (*dhiye*)—for the sake of the rite

O priests, cause Vāyu to make ready his chariot for going to the sacrifice. Praise with hymns Vāyu, the shining one, the special fulfiller of desired ends, the praiseworthy. May the goers, the acceptors of the sacrifice, the wives of the gods, of woman's form and praiseworthy, come to this sacrifice for the sake of our rite.

Prevail, (priests), by your prayers, on Vayu, the divine, the fulfiller of desires, the adorable, to harness his chariot: may the light-moving accepters of sacrifice, the lovely and excellent wives (of the gods), come hither to our rite.

This Ṛk, प्र वो वायुं (*pra vo vāyuṃ*), is to be recited as the yājyā mantra when the oblation is offered in the animal sacrifice made for the deity Vāyu; it is prescribed by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, प्र वो वायुं रथयुजं कृणुध्वमुत त्वामदिते महि (*pra vo vāyuṃ rathayujaṃ kṛṇudhvamuta tvāmadite mahi*) (Ā. 3-8).

O Uṣāsānaktā, deities presiding over day and night, you who are great: together with the other gods who are worthy of salutation, from the sky, that is, the firmament, from every region without exception, I bring to you the oblation, together with mantras that give comfort and make known. O deities so named, as though knowing all that is to be done, the two carry the sacrifice to the mortal, the sacrificer; they bring it face to face. The word ह (*ha*) is a filler. Or else: some say that शूषैः (*śūṣaiḥ*) and the other words in the instrumental plural are epithets of वंद्येभिः (*vaṃdyebhiḥ*).
- उषासानक्ता (*uṣāsānaktā*)—O deities of day and night
- नंद्येभिः (*naṃdyebhiḥ*)—together with the other gods who are worthy of worship
- उप प्र एषे (*upa pra eṣe*)—I offer (the oblations, O gods)
- विदुषी इव (*viduṣī iva*)—like wise and learned women
- विश्वं (*viśvaṃ*)—all matters of the rite (you being knowers of them)
- यज्ञं (*yajñaṃ*)—so that it becomes the means of his sacrifice

O deities of day and night, of great nature: together with the other gods who dwell in the firmament and are worthy of worship, I offer to you oblations accompanied by comfort-giving and knowledge-filled mantras. O gods, like wise and learned women, knowing all matters of the rite, bring to the human sacrificer that knowledge, so that it becomes the means of his sacrifice.

Mighty Day and night, to you, along with the adorable (deities) of heaven, I present (the oblation) with prayers delighting and explicit knowing, like two sages, all (that is required), you bring (it) to the worshipper for his sacrifice.

I worship, that is, I praise, you, who have many to nourish, the leaders of food and rites.⟨NOTE:209⟩ Who are you? He says: Vāstoṣpati and Tvaṣṭṛ, whom I, delighting with praises and the like, or giving oblations, worship; the giver of wealth, who goes together with the other gods and gratifies them, the Dhiṣaṇā, that is Speech, the goddess of speech.⟨NOTE:210⟩ These words, standing in the first case, are used in the sense of the second case. The construction is: I worship, together with salutations, the speech so described, the lords of the forest and the herbs. For what purpose? To obtain riches, that is, to attain wealth.
notes: ಪುಂ ಸಂ. printed; abbreviation not in the list, perhaps ಋ. ಸಂ.
ಸಾ. ಭಾ. printed; abbreviation not in the list, read as Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya

en: - रराणः (*rarāṇaḥ*)—I who recite praise and the like
- नृन् (*nṛn*)—and who carry out rites such as sacrifices
- सजोषाः (*sajoṣāḥ*)—who has equal affection with the other gods
- वनस्पतीन् (*vanaspatīn*)—the deities presiding over trees, or the trees
- ओषधीः (*oṣadhīḥ*)—the herbs, such as trees and creepers,
or the deities that preside over them
- रायः एषे (*rāyaḥ eṣe*)—for the obtaining of wealth

I who recite praises worship you, who nourish people and lead rites such as sacrifices: that is, the deity named Vāstoṣpati; the goddess of speech, the giver of wealth, who is affectionate together with the other gods; and the trees, the creepers and the climbers, or the deities who preside over them, with recitation of praises, salutations and the like, for the obtaining of wealth.

I glorify you, leaders (of rites), cherishers (of many), gratifying (with oblations, you) Twashtri the lord of foundations, and the goddess of speech, bestower of opulence, and sharer in the satisfaction (of the other divinities); also the lords of the forest, and the herbs, that I may obtain riches.

The पर्वताः (*parvatāḥ*) are those having joints, that is, full ones: the clouds. तने (*tane*) means extended; तुजे (*tuje*) means in giving. Or else: तने (*tane*) is a name for son, and the fourth case stands in the sense of the sixth: the meaning is in the giving of a son. Or again: may they be of good going, in our तुजे (*tuje*), our son, and in तने (*tane*), his son. What are they like?

They are the Vasus, who make the world dwell, like heroes. Moreover, the Āditya, praised, to be obtained by all, adorable, beneficial to men, may always increase our praise, that is, make it grow, when there is longing or approach on every side.
- वसवः (*vasavaḥ*)—such as give the world its dwelling

May those clouds which, like heroes, give the world its dwelling, move excellently so as to give us water in great abundance. May the Āditya, praised by all, easily attained by all, worthy of worship, beneficial to all men, increase our praise while he pervades all around.

May the Parvatas be (bountiful) to us in liberal donations; may they be favourable (to us) who are the establishers (of the world) like heroes; may the adored and adorable (deity), who is accessible (to all), who is friendly to man, ever grant us increase, being propitiated by our praise.

भूम्यस्य (*bhūmyasya*): भूमि (*bhūmi*) is the firmament; भूम्यस्य (*bhūmyasya*) means worthy of it. Of such a rain-giving Parjanya, or: भूम्यो (*bhūmyo*) means worthy of the earth alone, because he gives rain fitting to it. Of such a cloud, the embryo, that stands in the place of the womb, the protector of the waters, the lightning-fire, सुवृक्ति (*suvṛkti*), a word of praise: with praise that has avoided sin and the like, I have praised him. That Trita, who has crossed over most, who is preserved in the three places, the others having become threefold,⟨NOTE:211⟩ Agni, does not गृणीते (*gṛṇīte*), that is, does not roar, with comfort-giving rays, at me, who go to him: that is, he does not become angry. But, with blazing rays as his hair, he नि रिणाति (*ni riṇāti*) the forests, that is, harms them: the meaning is that he burns them.
notes: ನಿರ್ಯತಿ printed (also on pp. 393-394) where ನಿರ್ಋತಿ is meant; kept as printed

en: - भूम्यस्य (*bhūmyasya*)—of him who dwells in the firmament
- वृष्णः (*vṛṣṇaḥ*)—and who causes rain, to Parjanya
- अपां नपातं (*apāṃ napātaṃ*)—the protector of the waters, the lightning-fire
- त्रितः (*tritaḥ*)—who is in the three places, the earth and the rest
- एतरि (*etari*)—upon me, who go near him
- न गृणीते (*na gṛṇīte*)—does not show anger (but)

I have praised, with well-composed praise, the lightning-fire, who dwells in the firmament, is as an embryo to the rain-giving Parjanya and is the protector of the waters. Agni, who is in the three places, the earth and the rest, does not show anger with his comfort-giving rays at me, who approach him with devotion. But, with blazing rays as his hair, he burns all the forests.
I glorify with unqualified praise the embryo of the earth-fertilizing rain, the grandson of the waters, Agni, who is threefold, who rages (upon
me) not, when travelling, with (his) withering rays, but, bright-haired. consumes the forests.

We, the Atris: in what manner shall we speak praises to the great रुद्रियाय (*rudriyāya*), the son of Rudra, the host of the Maruts? And what praise shall we speak, for the gaining of wealth, to the all-knowing deity named Bhaga? Moreover, may the waters, the herbs, Dyu the deity of heaven, the woods, and the mountains whose tresses are trees, that is, those whose hair is the trees themselves, these deities named, protect us.
- राये (*rāye*)—so that wealth may come to us
- रुद्रियाय (*rudriyāya*)—to the host of the Maruts, the sons of Rudra
- द्यौः (*dyauḥ*)—the deity presiding over the heaven
In what manner shall we offer praise to the worshipful host of the Maruts, the sons of Rudra, so that wealth may come to us? What praise shall we recite to the all-knowing Bhaga? And
the deities of the waters, the herbs, the deity presiding over the heaven, and the mountains and woods that have trees for hair, may they protect us.

How can we offer (fit praise) to the mighty posterity of Rudra, or to the all-knowing Bhaga, for (the sake of obtaining) riches? may the waters, may the plants, protect us, and the heaven, the woods, and the mountains, whose tresses are trees.

May the lord of strengths, Vāyu, hear our praises. Or else: the lord of ऊर्जामन्नानां (*ūrjāmannānāṃ*), of foods. That Vāyu, under the limitation of breath, is the eater of all is well known,⟨NOTE:212⟩ and there is the Śruti: प्राणस्यान्नमिदं सर्वं प्रजापतिरकल्पयत् (*prāṇasyānnamidaṃ sarvaṃ prajāpatirakalpayat*) (Ma. Smṛ. 5-28). He moves in the sky, is तरीयान् (*tarīyān*), to be crossed over, इषिरः (*iṣiraḥ*), given to motion, परिज्मा (*parijmā*), one who goes all round. Moreover, may the waters hear the praises. What are they like? Bright, shining like cities, flowing all round, of the growing mountain or cloud.
notes: ಮೂರಿಮತ್ತಾಗಿ printed; read as ಮೂರ್ತಿಮತ್ತಾಗಿ "as embodied"?
ಶ. ಭಾ. printed; abbreviation not in the list; the next line gives ಶ. ಬ್ರಾ.

en: May Vāyu, who moves in the firmament, is always in motion, pervades all around and is lord of all powers, hear our praises. May the waters also, which flow around the exceedingly lofty mountain and shine like cities, hear our praises.
May the lord of vigour, (Vayu), hear our prayers; he who traverses the firmament, the circumambient: may the waters hear, bright as cities, flowing round the towering mountains.

notes: ಶ. ಪ್ರಾ. printed; abbreviation not in the list, perhaps ಶ. ಬ್ರಾ.

en: O great Maruts, quickly विद (*vida*), know, understand our praise. O beautiful ones, worthy of sight, we who approach you, serving you, desirable

oblation, holding it, offering it, speak praise. Or else: ये वो (*ye vo*) means you who are, in your own right, the ones who come to our sacrifice; you know it, the word चित् (*cit*) being a filler. Moreover, these Maruts, who are goers, सुभ्वः (*subhvaḥ*), well-being, greatly grown, come, go, towards us. What do they do? Warding off with weapons, with arms, the mortal, the enemy who is subject to death, who has come against them, accompanied by agitation, they come.
- वयश्चन (*vayaścana*)—the Maruts who are coming towards us
- क्षुभा (*kṣubhā*)—who is accompanied by an agitated mind
- वधस्नैः (*vadhasnaiḥ*)—striking and driving away with weapons

O great Maruts of attractive form, holding the oblation that is dear to you, we approach you and recite your praise. Know the nature of our praise. The Maruts who are coming towards us come to us, being gracious to us, and striking and driving away with their weapons the man who opposes them with an agitated mind.

Mighty Maruts, of goodly aspect, quickly hear (the praises) that we who repair to you repeat, offering acceptable (oblations): (the Maruts) coming hither, well-disposed, come down to us, (destroying) with their weapons the mortals opposed to them, (overcome) by agitation.

दैव्यानि (*daivyāni*) are things related to the gods, and पार्थिवानि (*pārthivāni*) are things related to the earth: births and waters.⟨NOTE:215⟩ To obtain them I speak to the Maruts, the host of the good sacrifice. May the praises grow: they are shining, making known the meaning that they set forth, with a delightful gold at their head, and being such, may they grow. And may the rivers, cherished by the Maruts, grow with water, that is, be full.
notes: no Ṛk number printed after this Saṃhitā block; number 19 taken from the sequence

en: - सुमखाय (*sumakhāya*)—to the host of the Maruts, worthy of the excellent sacrifice

For the gaining of waters, whether born of heaven or born of earth, I offer praise to the host of the Maruts, who are worthy of the excellent sacrifice. May the praises, which are shining and have a delightful forepart, grow. May the rivers, cherished by the Maruts, be filled with water (may they flow full).

I offer adoration to the company of the Maruts deserving of sacred sacrifice, to obtain the waters, whether born of heaven or earth : may my praises prosper : may the joy-bestowing heavens (flourish): may the rivers cherished (by the Maruts) be filled with water.

notes: Pada-pāṭha number ೨೮ printed where ೨೦ is expected

en: My praise is placed, that is, laid down, offered, on the ground at every step, at each time. And that praise, being powerful, with its protections, becomes the warder-off of troubles that come upon us; the word वा (*vā*) is in the sense of "and". May the mother, the maker of all, great, worthy of worship, the essence, the Earth, attend our praise; or else, being praised, may she attend to us. The word स्मत् (*smat*) expresses praise: by reason of the praises of the wise praisers, that is, pleased by acquaintance with them, may she be straight-handed, that is, with a hand favourable to us, and a giver of good gifts.
- पदे पदे (*pade pade*)—from time to time
- सूरिभिः (*sūribhiḥ*)—pleased with the praises of the praisers
- ऋजुहस्ता (*ṛjuhastā*)—having a hand favourable to us

From time to time our praise is offered. That same praise, being powerful, becomes with its protections the remover of troubles. May the Earth, the maker of all, great and full of essence, attend to our praise (hear it). Pleased by the praises of the praisers, may she be of a hand favourable to us and of a beneficial gift.

My praise has been continually proffered as a protectress, powerful with (the means of) preservation: may the maternal and venerable earth accept our (praises), and, (pleased) with her pious (worshippers) be (to us) straight-handed, and the giver of good.

In what manner shall we serve, that is, wait upon, with praise or with food, the Maruts of good gifts? In the manner thus being carried out, with a speech addressed to them as the occasion, how shall we serve those Maruts? The sense is that they are hard to propitiate. How are they possessors of excellent food, in me whose praise is an utterance that goes towards them? Or else: when there is praise from me, who have excellent food, in what manner shall we serve the Maruts? The repetition is for respect. May the god Ahirbudhnya not set us to the harmful one, that is, not establish us there; may that god be ours, the slayer of enemies.
- अच्चोक्तौ (*accoktau*)—when there is excellent praise addressed to them
- प्रश्रवसः (*praśravasaḥ*)—can excellent oblation be offered to them? (in what manner)
- अच्चोक्तौ (*accoktau*)—I being ready with excellent praise
- मरुतः (*marutaḥ*)—the Maruts (in what manner shall I worship them?)
- मा धात् (*mā dhāt*)—may he not give up

With what praise shall I worship the Maruts, who are exceedingly generous? Or: when I am ready with the most excellent praise, in what manner shall I make them recipients of the excellent oblation? May the god Ahirbudhnya not give us up to the harmful enemy. May he be the slayer of our enemies.

How may be (duly) worship the liberal (Maruts) with praise, how adore the Maruts with present praise in a fitting manner, the glorious Maruts with present praise? may Ahirbudhnya contrive not for our harm ; may he be the destroyer (of our enemies).

The Nirukta-writers regard the deity named Ahirbudhnya as a deity of the middle region (antarikṣa). The word *ahi* ordinarily means a serpent; it is read among the names of the cloud and also among the names of water (Ni. 2-21; 2-24). But when the nature of the deity Ahirbudhnya is to be stated, what connection is there between the cloud and water? And what is the reason that this deity bears this name? These questions must be examined.

For the word *ahi* alone, the Nirukta-writers give the derivation अहिः अयनात् एति अंतरिक्षे (*ahiḥ ayanāt eti aṃtarikṣe*), that is, because it moves about in the middle region, the cloud is the meaning of *ahi*; and then अयमपीतरोऽहिरेतस्मादेव निर्ह्रसित उपसर्ग आहंतीति । (*ayamapītaro 'hiretasmādeva nirhrasita upasarga āhaṃtīti |*): in the sense of a serpent too the derivation is the same. But the meaning "one that strikes with its hood" is also possible; (आहंत्यसौ भोगेन इत्यादिः (*āhaṃtyasau bhogena ityādiḥ*), Durga), so they have explained another meaning as well. In the same context they cite the mantra
दासपत्नीरहिगोपा अतिष्ठन्निरुद्धा आपः पणिनेव गावः (*dāsapatnīrahigopā atiṣṭhanniruddhā āpaḥ paṇineva gāvaḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-32.11)

and explain the word अहिगोपाः (*ahigopāḥ*) there as "those who guard the clouds". That is, here the word *ahi* means Vṛtra. But the word *ahi* is also used in the sense of a particular deity. For example—

उत नोऽहिर्बुध्न्यो ३ मयस्कः शिशुं न पिप्युषीव वेति सिंधुः । येन नपातमपां जुनाम मनोजुवो वृषणो यं वहंति ॥ (*uta no 'hirbudhnyo 3 mayaskaḥ śiśuṃ na pipyuṣīva veti siṃdhuḥ | yena napātamapāṃ junāma manojuvo vṛṣaṇo yaṃ vahaṃti ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-186-5)

Here Sāyaṇa has explained the word *ahi* as meaning a particular deity, and has shown the derivation अहिः अंतरिक्षगामी अहंता ना अहीनो वा अहन्यमानो ना एतन्नामको देवः (*ahiḥ aṃtarikṣagāmī ahaṃtā nā ahīno vā ahanyamāno nā etannāmako devaḥ*). The nature of this derivation was explained earlier, when the purport of this cited Ṛk was set out. And the word बुध्नः (*budhnaḥ*) here is to indicate the place of this deity: बुध्नं अंतरिक्षं तदर्हतीति बुध्नः अंतरिक्षचारी एतन्नामको देवः । (*budhnaṃ aṃtarikṣaṃ tadarhatīti budhnaḥ aṃtarikṣacārī etannāmako devaḥ |*). The purport is: the deity of this name who moves in the middle region. What the individual nature of this deity who moves in the middle region is, is the chief matter to be examined. The Nirukta-writers have stated the derivation of this word thus:
अहिर्बुध्न्यः । योऽहिः स बुध्यो बुध्नमंतरिक्षं । तन्निवासात् । (*ahirbudhnyaḥ | yo 'hiḥ sa budhyo budhnamaṃtarikṣaṃ | tannivāsāt |*) (Ni. 10-44)

*Budhna* means the middle region. How so? बुद्धमंतरिक्षं बद्धा अस्मिन् ; धृता आप इति ना । इदमपीतरद्बुध्नमेतस्मादेव । बद्धा अस्मिन् धृताः प्राणा इति । (*buddhamaṃtarikṣaṃ baddhā asmin ; dhṛtā āpa iti nā | idamapītaradbudhnametasmādeva | baddhā asmin dhṛtāḥ prāṇā iti |*).⟨NOTE:217⟩ Because it holds the waters, the middle region is called *budhna*. In the present context, the Nirukta-writers have shown only the deity's place of abode, namely that this deity is called Ahirbudhnya because he dwells in the middle region; they have not stated the individual nature of this deity. But first it must be examined whether any particulars on this matter are found in the passages of the Ṛk-saṃhitā.

अब्बा मुक्कैरहिं गृणीषे बुद्धे नदीनां रर्जसु षीदन् । मा नोऽहिर्बुध्यो रिषे धान्मा यज्ञो अस्य स्रिधदृतायोः ॥ (*abbā mukkairahiṃ gṛṇīṣe buddhe nadīnāṃ rarjasu ṣīdan | mā no 'hirbudhyo riṣe dhānmā yajño asya sridhadṛtāyoḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-34-16, 17)

In these mantras there is a prayer to the god Ahirbudhnya. In the first of them the nature of this god is described to some extent: the poet resolves, "I praise the *ahi*, who is born in the waters and abides in the middle region." Sāyaṇa has explained the purport here as अहिश्चासौ बुध्न्यश्चेत्यहिर्बुध्न्योऽग्निः (*ahiścāsau budhnyaścetyahirbudhnyo 'gniḥ*), that is, the *ahi*-nature contained in Budhnya is a quality of the god Agni. The epithet *ahi* is applied to Vṛtra just as it is to Agni. In many contexts the word *ahi* means Vṛtra. But in
हिरण्यकेशो रजसो विसारेऽहिर्धुनिर्नात इव ध्रूजीमान् । (*hiraṇyakeśo rajaso visāre 'hirdhunirnāta iva dhrūjīmān |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-79-1)

and similar places the word *ahi* has been explained as "the striker". Agni is described as the one who makes the clouds tremble (*dhuniḥ*) and the one who splits the clouds asunder. In this way the word *ahi* shows the qualities of Agni as it shows the qualities of Vṛtra. But the purport of another word that shows a special quality of Agni must also be chiefly noted.

स जायत प्रथमः पस्त्यासु महो बुद्धे रजसो अस्य योन् । अपादशीर्षा गुहमानो अंतायो युवानो वृषभस्य नीळे ॥ (*sa jāyata prathamaḥ pastyāsu maho buddhe rajaso asya yon | apādaśīrṣā guhamāno aṃtāyo yuvāno vṛṣabhasya nīḷe ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-1-11)

Agni, who is without feet and without head, lies hidden in the *budhna* of the middle region, that is, in the corner beyond the range of sight. Such descriptions occur only as synonyms of Agni. From these examples it is also understood that the epithets *ahi*, Vṛtra and Apāṃ Napāt are common to both Agni and Vṛtra.

Moreover, this deity Ahirbudhnya is described as ordinarily associated with the deities अज एकपात् (*aja ekapāt*), अपां नपात् (*apāṃ napāt*) and Savitṛ. There are also contexts in which he is praised separately. It is clear that all these deities are variant forms of Agni or of Sūrya. One may also say that they are deities of the middle region. That अपां नपात् (*apāṃ napāt*) is used as an epithet of the deity Ahirbudhnya is likewise stated in the mantra Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-34-16 cited above. There the word अब्ब (*abba*) also shows the special nature of this deity. It would not be wrong to give one and the same meaning to both अपां नपात् (*apāṃ napāt*) and अब्ब (*abba*). (That Agni is "born of water" because he is produced from the lotus leaf will be stated later, in the special topics of the mantra 6-16-13.) In the manner in which the word *ahirbudhnya* shows the special quality of Agni, that is, of the Agni of the middle region, in that same manner it also shows the special quality of Vṛtra, the chief of the Asuras; so the question is how one epithet can describe the special qualities of the opposite forms, gods and non-gods (Devas and Asuras). It may be examined that there are a few more such examples, like this one.

In the mantra cited above, हिरण्यकेशो रजसः (*hiraṇyakeśo rajasaḥ*) (1-79-1), the epithet धुनिः (*dhuniḥ*) which describes the nature of Agni also shows a quality of an Asura. Moreover, this word is itself the name of an Asura. For example,

त्वं नृभिर्नृमणो देववीत् भूरीणि वृत्रा हरश्व हंसि । त्वं नि दस्युं चुमुरिं धुनिं चास्वापयो दभीतये सुहंतु ॥ (*tvaṃ nṛbhirnṛmaṇo devavīt bhūrīṇi vṛtrā haraśva haṃsi | tvaṃ ni dasyuṃ cumuriṃ dhuniṃ cāsvāpayo dabhītaye suhaṃtu ‖*) (Puṃ. Saṃ. 7-19-4)⟨NOTE:218⟩

In this mantra *dhuni* stands as the name of an Asura. The same point is shown by the mantra इंद्रो धुनिं च चुमुरिं च दंभयन् (*iṃdro dhuniṃ ca cumuriṃ ca daṃbhayan*) (10-113.9). In 1.174-9 धुनिः (*dhuniḥ*) is an epithet of Indra himself. Thus it cannot be improper that one and the same word, according to the context, should be an epithet describing the nature of persons of two groups, the gods and the Asuras. In the present case, if the word Ahirbudhnya is an epithet of a deity, then it must be examined which deity's individual nature it describes. In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa the nature of this deity is described thus—

तासु ना अहिना बुद्ध्येन परोक्षात्तेजोऽदधादेष ह वा अहिबुध्यो यदग्नि गार्हपत्योऽग्निनैवासु तद्गार्हपत्येन परोक्षात्तेजो दधाति । (*tāsu nā ahinā buddhyena parokṣāttejo 'dadhādeṣa ha vā ahibudhyo yadagni gārhapatyo 'gninaivāsu tadgārhapatyena parokṣāttejo dadhāti |*) (Ai. Brā. 3-36)
In this sentence *ahirbudhnya* is explained as the Gārhapatya fire. Explaining the same view further, Sāyaṇa has said in his commentary:

अहिना बुध्येन अहिशब्दबुध्यशब्दद्वयनामकाग्नि विशेषेण परोक्षात् परोक्षरूपेण तेजोऽदधात् । यो गार्हपत्योऽग्निरस्ति एष एवाहिशब्देन बुध्यशब्देनाभिहितः ॥ (*ahinā budhyena ahiśabdabudhyaśabdadvayanāmakāgni viśeṣeṇa parokṣāt parokṣarūpeṇa tejo 'dadhāt | yo gārhapatyo 'gnirasti eṣa evāhiśabdena budhyaśabdenābhihitaḥ ‖*) (Sā. Bhā.)⟨NOTE:219⟩

The two words *ahi* and *budhya* are both names of Agni. By the help of this Agni, brilliance is spread among the people. The very Gārhapatya fire that exists is denoted by the word *ahi* and by the word *budhya*. Moreover, the invisibility of this god is also indicated; the word *budhya* shows this invisibility. This invisibility is shown by the sentence cited above (4-1-11), अपादशीर्षा गुहमानो अंता (*apādaśīrṣā guhamāno aṃtā*). Though he is invisible, he is praised as spreading visible radiance among the people. Because Agni is footless, headless and hiding, it would not be wrong to say that he is denoted by the word *budhya*. This same invisibility and *budhya*-nature of Agni are described in many places. In all such contexts it is understood that the description is of Agni in the form of Sūrya. For example—

द्विमाता होता विधथेषु सम्राळन्वग्रं चरति क्षेति बुद्धः । प्र रण्यानि रण्यवाचो भरंते महद्देवानामसुरत्वमेकं ॥ (*dvimātā hotā vidhatheṣu samrāḷanvagraṃ carati kṣeti buddhaḥ | pra raṇyāni raṇyavāco bharaṃte mahaddevānāmasuratvamekaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-55-7)

Here there is a description of Agni. But in explaining the sentence बुद्ध्यः चरति (*buddhyaḥ carati*), क्षेति (*kṣeti*), Sāyaṇa has said सूरभूतः तत्र वर्तते (*sūrabhūtaḥ tatra vartate*): having become Sūrya, he moves in the middle region; in the form of Agni he dwells on the earth. When this same Sūrya is hidden in a cave, he also becomes denoted by the word *ahi*.

सूर‍्यं न दस्रा तमसि क्षियंतं (*sūryaṃ na dasrā tamasi kṣiyaṃtaṃ*) (1-117-5); गूळ्हं सूर‍्यं तमसापव्रतेन (*gūḷhaṃ sūryaṃ tamasāpavratena*) (5-40-6). These sentences state the invisibility of Sūrya. This same Sūrya, who is hidden in the cave, may also be denoted by the word *ahi*.

गुहा हितं गुह्यं गूळ्मप्पपीवृतं मायिनं क्षियंतं । उतो अपो द्यां तस्तभ्वांसमहन्नहिं शूर वीर्येण ॥ (*guhā hitaṃ guhyaṃ gūḷmappapīvṛtaṃ māyinaṃ kṣiyaṃtaṃ | uto apo dyāṃ tastabhvāṃsamahannahiṃ śūra vīryeṇa ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-11-5)

Here the manner in which Indra slew the *ahi* hidden in the cave is described. Here all the epithets गुहाहितं (*guhāhitaṃ*), गुह्यं (*guhyaṃ*), गूळं (*gūḷaṃ*) and the rest are just like the description of Sūrya given in the mantra 5 40-6, गूळं सूर्‍यं (*gūḷaṃ sūryaṃ*) and so on. Here the epithets अपीवृतं (*apīvṛtaṃ*), अपव्रतेन (*apavratena*) and so on indicate the Vṛtra-nature of Sūrya or Agni, who is hidden in the cave or is *budhya*. The description of Agni in the mantra 4-1-11 cited above, गुहमानो अंता (*guhamāno aṃtā*), also shows the same point. That is, if the word Ahirbudhnya is explained as Sūrya or Agni hidden in the cave, then one may say that the *ahi*-nature and the Vṛtra-nature are attributed to him. If it is asked what Vedic authority there is for explaining it in this way, the answer is that Vedic sentences themselves can be shown as the proof.
अहन्वत्रमृचीषम और्णवाभमहीशुवं । हिमेनाविध्यदर्बुदं ॥ (*ahanvatramṛcīṣama aurṇavābhamahīśuvaṃ | himenāvidhyadarbudaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-22-26)
आदीं शवस्यब्रवीदौर्णनाभमहीशुवं । ते पुत्र संतु निष्टुरः ॥ (*ādīṃ śavasyabravīdaurṇanābhamahīśuvaṃ | te putra saṃtu niṣṭuraḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-77-2)

In these and similar sentences Vṛtra has the epithet और्णवाभ (*aurṇavābha*). In explaining the meaning of this same epithet in the mantra Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-11-18, Sāyaṇa has stated the purport: और्णः ऊर्णनाभिः । तदाभं तत्सदृशमित्यर्थः । ततः तमोरूपस्य हननात् । (*aurṇaḥ ūrṇanābhiḥ | tadābhaṃ tatsadṛśamityarthaḥ | tataḥ tamorūpasya hananāt |*), that is, "like a weaver-insect (spider)", that is, "of the nature of darkness". In the Brāhmaṇas and other works, Ūrṇāyu is a Gandharva. (Sūrya too is praised as a Gandharva in the Saṃhitās and other works.) Moreover,

अग्ने विश्वेभिः स्वनीक देवैरूर्णावंतं प्रथमः सीद योनिं । कुलायिनं धृतवंतं सवित्रे यज्ञं नय यजमानाय साधु ॥ (*agne viśvebhiḥ svanīka devairūrṇāvaṃtaṃ prathamaḥ sīda yoniṃ | kulāyinaṃ dhṛtavaṃtaṃ savitre yajñaṃ naya yajamānāya sādhu ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-15-16)

Here the altar, the womb of Agni, is praised with the epithet ऊर्णवंतं (*ūrṇavaṃtaṃ*). One may say that there is no difference in purport between ऊर्णवंतं (*ūrṇavaṃtaṃ*) here and the epithet और्णवाभं (*aurṇavābhaṃ*). Such epithets also show the spiritual nature of Sūrya or Agni who is hidden in the cave. How? Thus:
अमी ये सप्त रश्मयस्तत्रा मे नाभिरातता । (*amī ye sapta raśmayastatrā me nābhirātatā |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-105-9)
The description that "my navel grew spread out in these seven rays of the sun, which are in the form of the seven vital breaths"—this description

स यथोर्णनाभिस्तंतुनोच्चरेद्यथाग्नेः क्षुद्रा विस्फुलिंगा व्युच्चरंति एवमेवास्मादात्मनः सर्वे प्राणाः सर्वे लोकाः सर्वे देवाः सर्वाणि भूतानि व्युच्चरंति........प्राणा वै सत्यं तेषामेष सत्यं ॥ (*sa yathorṇanābhistaṃtunoccaredyathāgneḥ kṣudrā visphuliṃgā vyuccaraṃti evamevāsmādātmanaḥ sarve prāṇāḥ sarve lokāḥ sarve devāḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni vyuccaraṃti........prāṇā vai satyaṃ teṣāmeṣa satyaṃ ‖*) (Bṛ. U. 2-1-20)

If it is compared with this description, that as small sparks go forth from fire and as threads go forth from the spider, so from this Self all the vital breaths come into being, then a likeness may be stated between the navel of Sūrya (or of Agni) and the navel of the Self. The extension of the seven threads of Sūrya in Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164.5 was explained at length earlier. In the Kauṣītakī Brāhmaṇa Sūrya is compared to a spider (19.3). Therefore the purport is: when Sūrya, or Agni in the form of Sūrya, does not shine forth his rays but lies dormant, he is marked with the name Vṛtra; when he makes his rays shine, he is called a god. The same view is stated in the Śatapatha and other Brāhmaṇas by such sentences as
तदसानादित्य इमांल्लोकान्सूत्रे समापयते तद्यत्तूत्रं (*tadasānāditya imāṃllokānsūtre samāpayate tadyattūtraṃ*) (Śa. Brā. 8-7-3-10)
This same Sūrya, or Agni in the form of Sūrya, has two states: one the awakened state, the other the state of deep sleep. How so? Thus:
अतृप्नवंतं वियतमबुध्यमानं सुषुपाणमिंद्र । (*atṛpnavaṃtaṃ viyatamabudhyamānaṃ suṣupāṇamiṃdra |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-19-3)

Here the epithets अबुध्यं (*abudhyaṃ*) and सुषुपाणं (*suṣupāṇaṃ*) are noteworthy. In a time without awareness, that is, without light, these epithets show the nature of the *ahi*. For Sūrya as for Agni, the two states, the time of sleep and the time of waking, are well known in the Saṃhitās and other works.
तदिंद्र प्रेव वीर्यं चकर्थ यत्ससंतं वज्रेणाबोधयोऽहिं । (*tadiṃdra preva vīryaṃ cakartha yatsasaṃtaṃ vajreṇābodhayo 'hiṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-183-7)

"O Indra, you struck the intoxicated Vṛtra with the thunderbolt and woke him by your valour"; such sentences show the sleeping state and the waking state of Sūrya. In the same way, sentences such as उषर्बुधः (*uṣarbudhaḥ*) and अबोध्यग्निः (*abodhyagniḥ*) (5-1.1; 4-23-7) show the sleeping state and the waking state of Agni. Therefore, in the sleeping state, either for Sūrya or for Agni, there is the *ahi*-nature or Vṛtra-nature; in the awakened state, godhood. In the same way,
अपादहस्तो अपृतन्यदिंद्रमास्य वज्रमधि सानौ जघान । (*apādahasto apṛtanyadiṃdramāsya vajramadhi sānau jaghāna |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-32-7)
सहदानुं पुरुहूत क्षियंतमहस्त मिंद्र सं पिणक्कुणारुं । (*sahadānuṃ puruhūta kṣiyaṃtamahasta miṃdra saṃ piṇakkuṇāruṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-30-8)

In these and similar sentences, the epithets आपात् (*āpāt*), अहस्त (*ahasta*) and the like, which are well known as describing particular Asuras such as Vṛtra and Ahivṛtra, are without doubt also descriptions of Sūrya.

गुहा शिरो निहितमृधगक्षी असिन्वन्नत्ति जिह्वया वनानि । अत्राण्यस्मै पड्भिः सं भरंत्युत्तानहस्ता नमसाधि विक्षु ॥ (*guhā śiro nihitamṛdhagakṣī asinvannatti jihvayā vanāni | atrāṇyasmai paḍbhiḥ saṃ bharaṃtyuttānahastā namasādhi vikṣu ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-79-2)
In these and similar sentences the descriptions गुहा शिरो निहितं (*guhā śiro nihitaṃ*) are the same as the descriptions बुद्धे रजसः (*buddhe rajasaḥ*).

The authorities cited above explain the nature of Ahirbudhnya. The purport is that Agni acquires the state of Ahirbudhnya at the time when he lies asleep in a hidden region of the middle region. The purport of the sentence in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, which describes the Gārhapatya fire that possesses invisibility as the god Ahirbudhnya, is the same.
