en: May the Aśvin gods, Bhaga and the goddess Aditi bring about welfare for us. May Pūṣan, who is unobstructed and a destroyer of enemies, and Heaven and Earth, endowed with excellent understanding, be makers of good fortune for us.

May the Ashwins contribute to our prosperity : may Bhaga, and the divine Aditi (contribute) to (our) prosperity : may the irresistible Vishnu, the scatterer (of foes), bestow upon us prosperity : may the conscious Heaven and Earth (bestow upon us) prosperity. ⟨NOTE:393⟩
notes: ನಿರ್ವಚನದ ಅರ್ಥವು: the sentence breaks off at the end of p. 598; p. 599 begins a new subject

en: It is the custom to recite the next five Ṛks, beginning स्वस्ति नो मित्रावरुणा (*svasti no mitrāvaruṇā*), to express the wish that welfare (auspiciousness) may be ours.

On the sixth day of the sacrifice called Pṛṣṭha, when the mantras of the Vaiśvadeva-śastra are recited, the three Ṛks beginning स्वस्ति नः (*svasti naḥ*) are to be recited; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta-sūtra, स्वस्ति नो मिमीतामश्विना भग इति तृच इति वैश्वदेवं (*svasti no mimītāmaśvinā bhaga iti tṛca iti vaiśvadevaṃ*) (Ā. Ā. 1) ⟨NOTE:394⟩. And in the sacrifice called Bṛhaspatisava too these three Ṛks are to be inserted among the mantras of the Vaiśvadeva-śastra and recited as nivid-dhāna mantras; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta-sūtra, स्वस्ति नो मिमीतामाश्विना भग इति वैश्वदेवं (*svasti no mimītāmāśvinā bhaga iti vaiśvadevaṃ*) (Ā. 9.5).
notes: ಅರವತ್ತರ ಮೂವತ್ತರಷ್ಟು: the sense of the expression is not clear

en: For welfare, that is, for safety, we address Vāyu, and we address Soma, who is the lord and protector of the world, since the life of all the worlds depends on Soma. Likewise, for welfare we praise Bṛhaspati, the protector of great ritual and of the mantra, together with the whole company of the gods. May the Ādityas, the sons of Aditi, that is, all the gods, or else the twelve beginning with Aruṇa, be for our welfare.
- सर्वगणं (*sarvagaṇaṃ*)—accompanied by the whole company of the gods

For the gain of welfare for us we praise Vāyu and Soma, the protector of the worlds. In the same way we praise Bṛhaspati, accompanied by the whole company of the gods. May the Ādityas, the sons of Aditi, be gracious so that welfare may come to us.

We glorify Vayu for prosperity, Soma for prosperity, he who is the protector of the world : (we praise) Brihaspati (attended by) all the compa-nies (of the deities), for prosperity, and for our prosperity may the Adityas be ours.

When the sacrificer who has taken the consecration falls ill in the middle of a sattra, this tṛca serves as the nivid-dhāna in the Vaiśvadeva-śastra of that day. The sūtra is cited: स्वस्त्यात्रेये निविदं दध्यात् (*svastyātreye nividaṃ dadhyāt*) (Ā. 6-9); the explanation there is that by the word स्वस्त्यात्रेय (*svastyātreya*) this tṛca is meant. Likewise, in the case of रूपादिके (*rūpādike*) ⟨NOTE:395⟩ this tṛca is to be muttered. Sāyaṇa explains: may all the gods help us today, on this day of the sacrifice, for welfare, that is, for safety. Vaiśvānara: विश्व एनं नरा नयंतीति वैश्वानरः (*viśva enaṃ narā nayaṃtīti vaiśvānaraḥ*), all men lead him, therefore he is Vaiśvānara. Vasu: the god Agni, who gives dwelling to everyone.

This very Agni is Vaiśvānara, says Śākapūṇi, as Yāska reports: अयमेवाग्निर्वैश्वानर इति शाकपूणिः (*ayamevāgnirvaiśvānara iti śākapūṇiḥ*) (Ni. 7-23). May he too protect us for welfare. May the divine Ṛbhus also help us for welfare. Rudra, the god who makes one run away from sorrow, may protect us from sin for welfare.
notes: abbreviation ಅ. ವೇ. printed, here and below

en: - अद्य (*adya*)—on this day of the sacrifice
- स्वस्तये (*svastaye*)—for the gain of welfare for us (may they protect)
- स्वस्तये (*svastaye*)—may he be a maker of good fortune for us

May all the gods too protect us on this day of the sacrifice for the gain of our welfare. May Agni, the guide of all and giver of dwelling, be a maker of good fortune for us. May the divine Ṛbhus protect us for our welfare. May the god Rudra protect us from sin for our welfare.

May all the gods be with us to-day for our prosperity : may Agni, the benefactor of all men, and giver of dwellings, (be with us) for (our) prosperity : may the divine Ribhus protect us for ( our ) prosperity : may Rudra preserve us from iniquity for (our) prosperity.

If, in the middle of the sacrificial rites, the sacrificer who has taken the sacrificial consecration becomes afflicted by disease, then on that day the tṛca, that is, the three Ṛks, beginning विश्वे देवा नः (*viśve devā naḥ*), is to be inserted among the mantras of the Vaiśvadeva-śastra as nivid-dhāna mantras and recited; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta-sūtra, स्वस्तात्रेये निविदं दध्यात् (*svastātreye nividaṃ dadhyāt*) (Ā. 6-9) ⟨NOTE:396⟩. The sense of the word स्वस्तात्रेय (*svastātreya*) in the sūtra is explained as the tṛca, that is, the three Ṛks, beginning with this Ṛk. Likewise it is said that when calamities such as fear arrive, muttering these three Ṛks brings relief from fear.
notes: (೧೧-೭೭-೨): mandala 11 printed

en: O Mitra and Varuṇa, the deities presiding over day and night, bring about welfare for us. O Pathyā: the path is the way through the atmosphere, and the goddess who presides over the paths and is beneficial there is Pathyā. O such Revatī, O wealthy goddess, bring about welfare. Indra and Agni, each of them, bring about welfare for us. O goddess Aditi, bring about welfare for us. The verb "do" is to be supplied throughout.
- स्वस्ति (*svasti*)—may there be welfare for us
- स्वस्ति (*svasti*)—may there be well-being for us

O Mitra and Varuṇa, may there be welfare for us. O path of the atmosphere, endowed with wealth, may there be well-being for us. May Indra and Agni bring about welfare for us. O Aditi, bring about welfare for us.
Mitra, and Varuna, grant us prosperity : Path (of the firmament), and Goddess of riches, ( grant us ) prosperity: may Indra and Agni (grant us) prosperity ; Aditi, bestow prosperity upon us.

May we travel along the path in welfare, that is, in safety, like the sun and the moon: just as those two travel on a supportless course, unharmed by rākṣasas and the like, so may we. Further, we who are living abroad: पुनर्ददता (*punardadatā*) means one who gives back what is desired; अघ्नता (*aghnatā*) means one who does not harm through anger at our long delay; जानता (*jānatā*) means one who does not forget, who does not doubt "who is this who has been gone for a long time?" but understands "this one is mine". May we meet such kinsfolk, as described. Or else: the first half is the speech of those who live abroad, the second half that of the kinsfolk. We, the kinsfolk, may meet the one who lives abroad, who gives what he has earned and desired, who does not harm through anger at his departure, who knows us and approaches us with affection.
- सूर‍्याचंद्रमसौ इव (*sūryācaṃdramasau iva*)—as the moon and the sun follow their own paths eternally
- पंथां (*paṃthāṃ*)—our path of conducting the sacrifice
- पुनर्ददता (*punardadatā*)—who return a benefit for our benefit
- जानता (*jānatā*)—who know well our kinship; with such kinsfolk
- सं गमेमहि (*saṃ gamemahi*)—may we be united

As the moon and the sun follow their own paths eternally, so may we too follow our path of conducting the sacrifice without obstacle. May we be united with kinsfolk who return a benefit for our benefit and who know well our kinship.
May we ever follow prosperously our path, like the sun and the moon: may we be associated with a requiting, grateful, and recognisant (kinsman).

In addition to the meaning stated above, the commentator says that the phrase पथां स्वस्ति अनुचरेम (*pathāṃ svasti anucarema*) may also be given the meaning: may we travel without obstacle and in safety together with the travellers whom we may meet in the middle of the road at the time of the journey.

O Śyāvāśva, seer of this name, being bold, worship the Maruts, who are to be praised by ऋक्वभिः (*ṛkvabhiḥ*); the instrumental stands in the sense of the accusative. Thus he sends himself forth. Or else: the sacrificer says it to the Hotṛ Śyāvāśva. Or else: worship, that is, praise, along with the Maruts, along with praisers like the Maruts, who are ऋक्वभिः (*ṛkvabhiḥ*), or with hymns. The Maruts who are worthy of sacrifice, अनुष्पधं (*anuṣpadhaṃ*) daily (स्वधा (*svadhā*) is the giving of food in the form of an oblation; or अनु (*anu*) means afterwards), having obtained harmless food, rejoice.
- धृष्णुया (*dhṛṣṇuyā*)—you who are tolerant of hair ⟨NOTE:412⟩
notes: the Kannada gloss takes ಪ್ರ ಯುಜತ as "strive", while Sāyaṇa takes it as "yoke" with the dappled mares as object

en: O Śyāvāśva, you who are tolerant of hair ⟨NOTE:413⟩, worship exceedingly those praiseworthy Maruts who, being worthy of sacrifice, rejoice every day in harmless food.
notes: ಯಭ್ವಸಂ printed here and in the Pada; Sāyaṇa has ಋಭ್ವಸಂ

en: Offer worship with perseverance, Shyavaswa, to the praise-deserving Maruts: they who are adorable and delight in the daily offered and inoffensive sacrificial food.

In this Ṛk the seer of the sūkta, Śyāvāśva, addresses himself, saying "worship the Marut deities". Or else it may be said that the sacrificer who performs the sacrifice addresses in this Ṛk the seer Śyāvāśva, who is carrying out the sacrifice taking the part of the priest called Hotṛ.

ऋक्वभिः मरुद्भिः प्र अर्च (*ṛkvabhiḥ marudbhiḥ pra arca*)—स्तुत्यान् मरुतः पूजय (*stutyān marutaḥ pūjaya*): worship the praiseworthy Maruts. In this sentence, although the words ऋक्वभिः (*ṛkvabhiḥ*) and मरुद्भिः (*marudbhiḥ*) are words ending in the instrumental plural, the commentator has said that for these words, द्वितीयार्थे तृतिया (*dvitīyārthe tṛtiyā*), the instrumental case is used to indicate the sense of the accusative. That is, instead of the natural sense "by the Marut deities worthy of worship", it must be understood as "the Marut deities who are worthy of praise or of worship". Or for this sentence, मरुद्धिर्मरुत्सदृशैर्युक्वभिः स्तोत्रैर्वा अर्च स्तुहीत्यर्थः । (*maruddhirmarutsadṛśairyukvabhiḥ stotrairvā arca stuhītyarthaḥ |*), the meaning "praise with priests who chant hymns and are equal to the Marut deities, or with hymns" can also be given; thus Sāyaṇa has made two kinds of explanation of the meaning.

अनुष्टदं (*anuṣṭadaṃ*)—प्रत्यहं (*pratyahaṃ*): the meaning is "every day". For the indeclinable word अनु (*anu*) Yāska has given the derivation अन्विति शादृश्यापरभावं (*anviti śādṛśyāparabhāvaṃ*) (Ni. 1-3). अनु (*anu*) means likeness: when pointing to one thing that is like another, the word अनु (*anu*) is used in stating likeness or comparison, "like that". Or the word अनु (*anu*) is used also when the meaning "one after another" is stated. In the present Ṛk, for the word अनुस्वधं (*anusvadhaṃ*) the meaning given is "the next day after one day", that is, every day.

They indeed are the friends of steady, unwavering strength (शवसः (*śavasaḥ*)); they are to me bold ones (धृष्णया (*dhṛṣṇayā*) means bold). And they, even on the march (आ (*ā*) is in the sense of "and"), being daring, by themselves, out of favour alone, without regard to any service from us, always protect us, who are many, with our sons, servants and the rest.
- यामन् (*yāman*)—even at the time of going about
- शश्वतः (*śaśvataḥ*)—our numerous sons, servants and the rest
notes: ಪರುಷ್ಟೀನದಿಯಲ್ಲಿ / ಪರುಷ್ಲೀನದಿಯಲ್ಲಿ printed in the Kannada gloss and Bhāvārtha for the river's name

en: Those very gods who, even at the time of going about, having the power to confront enemies, protect by their own impulse our numerous sons, servants and the rest, those same gods, possessed of the power of boldness, are dear men to eternal strength.
They are the firm friends of steady vigour, who, proceeding resolute on their way, willingly protect (our) numerous (descendants).

ते स्थिरस्य शवसः सखायः संति (*te sthirasya śavasaḥ sakhāyaḥ saṃti*)—those Marut deities are friends of steady strength; that is, there is always a mutual relation between them and strength; they are always powerful. The meaning is that their strength and power are great and never fail.

The form of the word त्मना (*tmanā*)-आत्मना (*ātmanā*) has lost its initial letter according to the Vedic usage, and only त्मना (*tmanā*) remains. Even so, the word त्मना (*tmanā*) has the very meaning of the word आत्मना (*ātmanā*). This kind of usage is particularly common in the Ṛgveda.
Yāska has said that the indeclinable आ (*ā*) has many meanings and has made them clear by examples.
From here onward, or all around, is the meaning. In आ पर्वतात् (*ā parvatāt*) the meaning is the regions beyond the mountain, or the regions around the mountain.
एतस्मिन्नेवार्थे (समुच्चयार्थे) देवेभ्यश्च पितृभ्य एत्याकारः ॥ (*etasminnevārthe (samuccayārthe) devebhyaśca pitṛbhya etyākāraḥ ‖*) (Ni. 1.4)

The meaning "and" (samuccaya: showing the connection between two words) also belongs to the word आ (*ā*). In the sentence देवेभ्यश्च पितृभ्य आ (*devebhyaśca pitṛbhya ā*) the word आ (*ā*) has just the meaning "and" that the word च (*ca*) has. That is, the sentence means "to the gods and to the fathers".

Nine words beginning with हिकं (*hikaṃ*) are included in the list called सर्वपदसमाम्नाय (*sarvapadasamāmnāya*). Among these words the word अ (*a*) also occurs. That is, the word आ (*ā*) is used merely to fill out a sentence, without any particular meaning.

अथाप्युपमार्थे दृश्यते । जार आ भगं । (ऋ. सं. १०-११-६) जार इव भगं । आदित्योऽत्र जार उच्यते । रात्रेजरयिता । स एव भासां ॥ (*athāpyupamārthe dṛśyate | jāra ā bhagaṃ | (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-11-6) jāra iva bhagaṃ | ādityo 'tra jāra ucyate | rātrejarayitā | sa eva bhāsāṃ ‖*) (Si, Pi.-13) ⟨NOTE:415⟩

The word आ (*ā*) is also used in the sense of comparison (likeness); that is, the word आ (*ā*) has the meaning of the word इव (*iva*). The sentence जार आ भगं (*jāra ā bhagaṃ*) means जार इव भगं (*jāra iva bhagaṃ*): the deity Bhaga, who is like the Sun (Āditya).

आ । आ इत्याकार उपसर्गः पुरस्तादेव व्याख्यातः । अथाप्यध्यर्थे दृश्यते । अभ्र आ अपः । अभ्रे आ अपो sपोऽभ्रेऽधीति ॥ (*ā | ā ityākāra upasargaḥ purastādeva vyākhyātaḥ | athāpyadhyarthe dṛśyate | abhra ā apaḥ | abhre ā apo spo 'bhre 'dhīti ‖*) (Ni. 5-2)

The word आ (*ā*) is a preposition (upasarga). Some of its meanings have been stated above. Besides these meanings, this word also has the meaning "above, over" (अधि (*adhi*)). For example, in अभ्र आ आपः (*abhra ā āpaḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-48.1) the meaning is the water that is above the cloud; and in तोदस्येव आ महस्य (*todasyeva ā mahasya*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-150-1) also, the word आ (*ā*) has the meaning "above" (अधि (*adhi*)).
notes: the Pada block ends with the number ೧೮, the verse is ೧೦

en: Those Maruts are flowing, that is, of a flowing nature, and sprinklers of water. The word न (*na*) is used in the sense of "and". ⟨NOTE:416⟩ The शर्वरीः (*śarvarīḥ*) are the nights, that is, the divisions of time. They go beyond these, pass over them: the meaning is that they are everlasting. Since they are of such a kind, we now praise the might (tejas) of the Maruts, which abides in the heaven-world above and on the earth below.
notes: ವಿಸ್ವಜ್ಮಾರ್ಗಾ damaged

en: - स्यंद्रासः (*syaṃdrāsaḥ*)—who make (the world) wet with drizzles
- अति स्कंदंति (*ati skaṃdaṃti*)—move on, transgressing (being free of the regulations of time) (therefore)
- महः (*mahaḥ*)—the might, which is spread out

The Maruts move about with their powers, making the world wet with drizzles and sprinkling water, and transgressing the regulations of time such as the nights. Therefore we now praise the might of the Maruts, which is spread out in the heaven-world and on the earth.
Gliding along, and shedding moisture, they pass through the nights: therefore we now celebrate the might of the Maruts, manifested in both heaven nad earth. ⟨NOTE:417⟩
notes: ಚಂದ್ರೋಭಿಃ printed, probably for ಛಂದೋಭಿಃ

en: Because the movement of the Maruts is especially marked while rain is falling, that is, because the wind blows with great force, the Maruts are described here as sprinklers of water.

Addressing the Adhvaryus, Hotṛs and others: "you" offer to the Maruts, who are assailants, that is, to the Maruts among the assailants. The first person दधीमहि (*dadhīmahi*) stands, by an interchange of person, for the imperative second person धत्त (*dhatta*), "offer". What is offered? Praise (stoma, hymn) and the sacrifice (यज्ञं (*yajñaṃ*)): that by which one sacrifices, namely the oblation. Why are both given? Because the Maruts, all the human ages, that is, at all times, protect the mortal sacrificer, one subject to death, from the harmful one who injures.
- मानुषा युगा (*mānuṣā yugā*)—throughout the life-spans of man
notes: abbreviation ಋಗ್ವೇ printed; reference as printed
ನೃ ನಯ ಇತ್ಯಸ್ಯ ವಾ ನರ್ತತೀರ್ವಾ ವಿಕ್ಷೇಪಮಾತ್ರಾರ್ಥಸ್ಯೇದಂ — the block is cut off here

en: O Adhvaryus, offer praise and oblation to those Maruts who assail enemies, and who through all the life-spans of man protect the human sacrificer from the injuring enemy.
We enjoin you, (priests), to offer earnestly praise and sacrifice to the Maruts, who through all human ages, protect the mortal worshipper from harm.

मानुषा युगा (*mānuṣā yugā*)—मानुषाणि युगानि । सर्वेषु कालेष्टित्यर्थः । (*mānuṣāṇi yugāni | sarveṣu kāleṣṭityarthaḥ |*) In the time that a man lives; the intention is, in the time that the sacrificer lives.

Addressed to the Hotṛ, or to oneself (आत्मन् (*ātman*)): the Maruts who are worthy of worship, bountiful in giving, leaders of rites, and of no small strength: to those Maruts, worthy of the sacrifice and shining, offer the sacrifice. Case-endings and number are interchanged here; or else the genitive stands in the sense of the object. "The shining sacrifice" is the oblation, the means of the sacrifice: प्रार्च (*prārca*) means present, offer. Or else the connection is "to those come from the heaven, that is, from the atmosphere".
- सुदानवः (*sudānavaḥ*)—who have an excellent disposition to give
- असामिशवसः (*asāmiśavasaḥ*)—who have exceedingly great strength; to such
- यज्ञियेभ्यः (*yajñiyebhyaḥ*)—to those worthy of the sacrifice

O Hotṛ, offer the oblation with devotion to those Maruts who are worthy of the sacrifice and shining, who are worthy of worship, have an excellent disposition to give, are leaders of rites, and have exceedingly great strength.
Offer sacrifice to the adorable Maruts, who (have come) from heaven who are worthy of worship, munificent leaders (of rites), and possessors of unequalled strength.
असामिशवसः (*asāmiśavasaḥ*)—अनल्पबलाः (*analpabalāḥ*). Not small, that is, having abundant strength, is the meaning. Yāska has given the etymology of the word असामि (*asāmi*) in this way:

असामि । बृहस्पतिं वर्धय नव्यमर्कैरर्चनीयैः स्तोमैरसामि सामि प्रतिषिद्धं । सामि स्यतेः । असाम्योजो बिभृथा सुदानवः । अनुसमाप्तं बलं बिभृत कल्याणदानाः ॥ (*asāmi | bṛhaspatiṃ vardhaya navyamarkairarcanīyaiḥ stomairasāmi sāmi pratiṣiddhaṃ | sāmi syateḥ | asāmyojo bibhṛthā sudānavaḥ | anusamāptaṃ balaṃ bibhṛta kalyāṇadānāḥ ‖*) (Ni. 6-23)

The word सामि (*sāmi*), formed from the root स्यति (*syati*) ("kill"), means that which brings to an end, that which is small. When the negative prefix अ (*a*) joins this word, असामि (*asāmi*) results. Therefore the word असामि (*asāmi*) has the meaning opposed to that of the word सामि (*sāmi*), which has the meaning "small". So for the word असामि (*asāmi*) one may give the meaning "not small", that is, "very great". In the illustrative sentences given here by the author of the Nirukta, बृहस्पतिं वर्धय नव्यमर्कैरसामि (*bṛhaspatiṃ vardhaya navyamarkairasāmi*) and असाम्योजो बिभृथा सुदानवः (*asāmyojo bibhṛthā sudānavaḥ*), the meaning of the word असामि (*asāmi*) is "great, abundant".

The Maruts, leaders of the rain, mighty, shine with brilliant ornaments of various kinds; "they shine" is the word to be supplied, because the preposition आ (*ā*) is heard (the verb is understood from the preposition). Likewise they shine with a weapon, an instrument of striking. These Maruts hurl the spears, a special kind of weapon, to split the cloud. Their lightnings also follow them, like noisy waters. The Nirukta says: जझुतीरापो भवंति शब्दकारिण्यः (*jajhutīrāpo bhavaṃti śabdakāriṇyaḥ*) (Ni-6-16) ⟨NOTE:420⟩. The lightnings follow the shining host of Maruts; the radiance of the host came forth of itself.
notes: ಕೇಚಿತ್ವಿಷೇ ಶರೀರದೀಪ್ತೈಶ್ಚಿ ಬಲಾಯ ವಾಸನ್ — damaged; sense of the sentence not settled

en: - युधा (*yudhā*)—with a weapon, an instrument of striking
- जज्ञतीरिव (*jajñatīriva*)—like streams of water flowing with a noise
- दिवः (*divaḥ*)—of the shining host of Maruts

The Maruts, leaders and great-souled, shine with their golden ornaments and with their weapons of striking. They hurl their spears at their enemies. These lightnings follow the Maruts constantly, like waters flowing with a noise. The radiance of the shining host of Maruts is self-luminous.
Leaders (of the rains), the mighty Maruts shine with brilliant ornaments and weapons, and hurl javelin (at their foes, the clouds): the
lightnings, like roaring (torrents), daily follow the Maruts: the radiance of the resplendent (cohort) spontaneously breaks forth,

Those Maruts who, being connected with the earth, increase; and those who increase also in the vast atmosphere. The word आ (*ā*) is used in the sense of "and" (आ इति चार्थे (*ā iti cārthe*)). They increase also in the strength (बले (*bale*)) of the rivers, that is, of the resounding ones; and in the common abode (सहस्थाने (*sahasthāne*)) of the great heaven-world. In both places the word वा (*vā*) is used in the sense of "and". Thus the Maruts, growing everywhere, hurl their spears for the sake of rain: this is the connection with the preceding verse.
- पार्थिवाः (*pārthivāḥ*)—those who dwell on the earth
- नदीनां (*nadīnāṃ*)—of the rivers, which are of the nature of floods
- वृजने वा (*vṛjane vā*)—in the speed, whoever are there, they too
- सधस्थे (*sadhasthe*)—in the abode, whichever Maruts there are, all of them too gain increase

The Maruts who dwell on the earth, those who dwell in the atmosphere, those who produce the speed of the rivers that are of the nature of floods, and whichever Maruts dwell in the great heaven-world: all of them gain increase.
The Maruts, who are of the earth are augmented, so are those in the vast firmament; they increase in the force of the rivers, and in the aggregate of the spacious heaven.

O praiser, praise the might (शर्धः (*śardhaḥ*), strength) of the host of Maruts, excellently (उत् (*ut*)). Of what kind is that might? Of true speed, and great, exceedingly grown. Moreover those Maruts, the leaders of the rain, for the sake of water, yoke, that is, harness forth by their own will, with the thought of protecting the world, the moving ones, that is, the dappled mares: this is the meaning. ⟨NOTE:421⟩
notes: ಶಿಕ್ಷವಃ printed; the verse has ಶಿಕ್ವಸಃ

en: - सत्यशवसं (*satyaśavasaṃ*)—(O praiser) possessing strength of the nature of truth
- मारुतं शर्धः (*mārutaṃ śardhaḥ*)—the might of the host of Maruts
notes: ಋ. ಸಂ. ೫೩ ೫೯-೫೩ printed; the reference does not fit the usual form of mandala-sūkta-Ṛk

en: O praiser, the Maruts, the leaders, being of a moving nature, strive of their own impulse for our welfare. Therefore praise excellently the might of the host of Maruts, which possesses strength of the nature of truth and is great.
Glorify the truth-invigorated and infinite strength of the Maruts, for they, the leaders (of the rains), gliding along, are labouring voluntarily for (our) good.

Moreover those Maruts abide in the river of that name, the Parushni. The radiance (दीप्तिः (*dīptiḥ*)) of those purifiers they put on, that is, they cover themselves with it. And with the felloe (नेम्या (*nemyā*)) of their own chariot wheels and with their strength they split the mountain (अद्रिं (*adriṃ*)), that is, they tear apart the cloud or the mountain.
- परुष्णां (*paruṣṇāṃ*)—(they abide) in the river Parushni ⟨NOTE:423⟩
- पव्या (*pavyā*)—of the form of a felloe
notes: ನಾ printed; ವಾ expected?

en: The Maruts abide in the river Parushni. They are clothed with a splendour that is radiant and purified. And with the strength of the felloes of their chariots they split the cloud.
Whether they (abide) on the Parushni (river), or, purifying (all), they clothe themselves with light, or whether they break through the clouds with strength by the wheels of their chariots.

notes: ಪೃಶ್ನಿಯೆಂದರೆ ಸ್ವರ್ಗವು, ಅಂತರಿಕ್ಷ ಪುತ್ರರು: words seem missing between ಅಂತರಿಕ್ಷ and ಪುತ್ರರು

en: आपथयः (*āpathayaḥ*): those Maruts whose paths lead towards us. विपथयः (*vipathayaḥ*): those whose paths are of various kinds ⟨NOTE:425⟩. अंतस्पथा (*aṃtaspathā*): those whose paths are caves, hollows and the like. अनुपथा (*anupathā*): those whose paths are favourable. With these four kinds of names, that is, forms, those Maruts, being spread out, bear the sacrifice for me, for my sake. Or else: with these names, that is, with waters, they bear the sacrifice.
notes: reference printed as సి. ೩-೧೫ (first letter is not Kannada); the same passage was cited above as Ni. 2-13

en: - आपथयः (*āpathayaḥ*)—let them follow the path that faces us (or)
- विपथयः (*vipathayaḥ*)—let them follow various different paths (or)
- अंतस्पथाः (*aṃtaspathāḥ*)—let them resort to paths such as mountain caves (or)
- अनुपथाः (*anupathāḥ*)—let them have a favourable path
- एतेभिः (*etebhiḥ*)—even though they are of these four kinds
Whether the Maruts follow the path that faces us, or follow various different paths, or resort to paths such as mountain caves, or have a favourable path, even though they are of these four
kinds, they bear the sacrifice for me, extending and increasing it, each in their respective forms.

(Whether), following the paths that lead (to us), or that spread diversely, or those that sink into the hollows (of the mountain), or those that extend smoothly, they, (however) scattered, accept the sacrifice for my benefit, (when invoked by these appellations).

Now the leaders, the bringers of the desired rain and the like, carry the world down, that is, bear it constantly. Now the नियुतः (*niyutaḥ*), themselves mixing (all things together), bear. Now the पारावताः (*pārāvatāḥ*): परावद्दूरदेशः (*parāvaddūradeśaḥ*); those belonging to it, that is, those who in the distant regions such as the atmosphere are the upholders of planets, stars, clouds and the like, bear: this is the meaning. In the manner thus stated their forms are manifold, of many kinds, or worthy of being gathered, and दर्श्या (*darśyā*), that is, to be seen through their own activities: may they be so; this is what is to be supplied.
- न्यूहते (*nyūhate*)—bear the burden of the world
- ओहते (*ohate*)—bear the burden of conducting the sacrifice
- पारावताः (*pārāvatāḥ*)—being situated in very distant regions, they bear the burden of planets, stars and the like

The Maruts in one way, as leaders of the rain and the like, bear the burden of protecting the world. In another way, all gathering together, they bear the burden of conducting the sacrifice. In another way, being situated in very distant regions, they bear the burden of planets, stars and the like. In this way they are of manifold forms and of an attractive nature.
Now, leaders (of the rains), they support (the world): now, blending together, they bear (the oblation): now, situated remote, (they uphold distant objects): so may their manifold forms be manifest.

छंदःस्तुभः (*chaṃdaḥstubhaḥ*): praisers with metres (चंद्रोभिः (*caṃdrobhiḥ*) ⟨NOTE:426⟩). कुभन्यवः (*kubhanyavaḥ*): those desiring water. कीरिणः (*kīriṇaḥ*): praisers. Having regard to the well, for the thirsty Gotama, the Maruts whom (the praisers) set going all around, or led, with praise. Or else: those who are to be praised with metres; the root स्तोभतिः (*stobhatiḥ*) means the act of praising. कुभन्यवः (*kubhanyavaḥ*) are the sprinklers of the rain-water; कुभि (*kubhi*) means the act of wetting. कीरिणः (*kīriṇaḥ*): of the praiser Gotama, for the sake of drinking, the Maruts brought the well. For it is said: असिंचन्नुत्सं गोतमाय तृष्णजे । (*asiṃcannutsaṃ gotamāya tṛṣṇaje |*) (Ṛgve-1-85.11) ⟨NOTE:427⟩. ⟨NOTE:428⟩

Those Maruts, "some of them", for me, are the "thieves" (तायवो (*tāyavo*)): they stood like thieves, never visible, as ऊमा (*ūmā*), protectors. Others came into view, into sight. Some, with the radiance of their bodies, for strength ⟨NOTE:429⟩, were in the form of the life-breath: this is the idea.
notes: reference printed as సి. ೨-೧೪ (first letter is not Kannada)
ಸಂಸ್ಪಷ್ಟಾ printed here, ಸಂಸ್ಪೃಷ್ಟಾ above
ಪೃಶ್ಚಿಮಾತರಃ printed; ಪೃಶ್ನಿಮಾತರಃ intended
ಪ್ರಯಚ್ಛಂತೃತಿ ನಾಶೀಃ: the Sanskrit is damaged here; sense taken as a benediction, "let them give"

en: - छंदस्तुभः (*chaṃdastubhaḥ*)—those who are praised with metres
- कुभन्यवः (*kubhanyavaḥ*)—and who pour down the water of the rain: the Maruts
- आ नृतुः (*ā nṛtuḥ*)—made to come into being
- तायवो न (*tāyavo na*)—staying hidden like thieves
- त्विषे (*tviṣe*)—through the power of their splendour
- दृशि आसन् (*dṛśi āsan*)—have come into view

The Maruts, who are praised with metres and who pour down the water of the rain, caused a well to come into being for the thirsty Gotama, the praiser. Some of those Maruts, staying hidden like thieves, are my protectors. The others, through the power of their splendour, are visible right before me, and are protectors.

The reciters of sacred metres, desirous of water, and celebrating (the Maruts), have drawn them to (provide) a well (for Gotama): some of them, (invisible) as thieves, have been my defenders: some have been (obvious) to view through the light (of life).

The Maruts who are ऋष्वा (*ṛṣvā*), worthy to be seen, shining with their weapons (ऋष्टिविद्युत (*ṛṣṭividyuta*)), wise (कवयः (*kavayaḥ*)), intelligent, वेधसः (*vedhasaḥ*), the creators of everything: the host of those Maruts, with a pleasing (रमणीयया (*ramaṇīyayā*)) praise, O sage Śyāvāśva, venerate, serve, praise.
- ऋष्वाः (*ṛṣvāḥ*)—who are worthy to be seen
O sage Śyāvāśva, worship with a pleasing praise the host of those Maruts who are worthy to be seen, who shine with their weapons, and who are wise and creators.
Glorify, Rishi, with grateful praise, the company of the Maruts, who are manifest, bright with lightning lances, who are wise, and the creators (of all things).

O sage, approach the host of Maruts, like Mitra, that is, like Āditya, with the gift of the oblation and with praise (योषणा (*yoṣaṇā*), which is explained as praise); the verb "approach" is to be supplied. The latter half of the verse is the sage's direct address: with strength, O bold Maruts, assailers, from the heaven-world, or, because the word ना (*nā*) is heard, from the other two worlds, praised by our hymns, come to the sacrifice.
- मारुतं गणं (*mārutaṃ gaṇaṃ*)—the host of Maruts
- मित्रं न (*mitraṃ na*)—as one approaches a friend
- दिवो वा (*divo vā*)—whether from the heaven-world or from any other region

O sage, approach the host of Maruts, as one approaches a friend, with the gift of the oblation and with praise. O Maruts of enduring strength, praised by our hymns, graciously come to our sacrifice with your strength, whether from the heaven-world or from any other region.
Approach, Rishi, with offerings and with praise, the company of the Maruts like a friend: come, sustaining (Maruts), with your strength, from heaven or (any other region), glorified by our hymns.

Quickly, praising these Maruts, he does not intend, as a means of conveying (them), to approach deities other than the Maruts. The praiser, with the wise ones, famed for their swift going (यामश्रुतेभिः (*yāmaśrutebhiḥ*)), the Maruts, who are the revealers of the fruit (अंजिभिः (*aṃjibhiḥ*)): all the instrumentals here are in the sense of the ablative. From the Maruts of the said characteristics he joins (सचेत (*saceta*)) the desired gifts, that is, he receives them.
- अंजिभिः (*aṃjibhiḥ*)—by the Maruts, the revealers of the fruit (by their favour)

The sacrificer, praising these Maruts duly, does not approach deities other than them, to invoke them. By the favour of the Maruts, who are wise, renowned for their swift going and revealers of the fruit, he receives the desired gifts.

Glorifying them promptly, desiring not to bring (other) deities to (his) presence, let (the worshipper) associate his gifts with those wise (divinites) renowned for their velocity, and distributors (of rewards).

The Maruts who, for me, in the seeking of their own kinsmen, being impellers (सूरयः (*sūrayaḥ*)), uttered गां (*gāṃ*), that is, the speech of the middle region, or the cow deity. The sage repeats the speech of the Maruts. They called Pṛśni, the deity of the sky, or the cow of dappled colour, their mother: for it is said, पृश्नियै वै पयसो मरुतो जाता इति श्रुतेः (*pṛśniyai vai payaso maruto jātā iti śruteḥ*). Then they, being capable, called their own father the moving, food-possessing Rudra. The adoption of Rudra as father of the Maruts has been established many times.
- गां (*gāṃ*)—in the form of the speech of the middle region
notes: abbreviation ಋಗ್ವೇ- printed; the Kannada commentary gives this passage as ಋ. ಸಂ. ೧-೧೮-೩

en: When the Maruts, impellers of the world, were asked about their kinsmen, they gave me a reply in the form of the speech of the middle region. The capable Maruts said that Pṛśni was their mother and that Rudra, endowed with food, was their father.

To me, inquiring of their kindred, the sage (Maruts) have uttered a reply; they have declared Prishni (to be their) mother; the mighty ones have declared the food-bestowing Rudra (to be their) father.

गां (*gāṃ*)—for this word two kinds of meaning are given: the speech of the middle region, or the cow deity. The speech of the middle region means the goddess of speech. Because this deity is one who dwells in the atmosphere, the middle region, she is called the deity of the middle region, or the speech of the middle region. The word for "cow" here means the cow in the form of Pṛśni, the mother of the Maruts. It is explained that while the sage was considering what relation the Maruts had with the cow called Pṛśni, the Maruts spoke to him in reply to the sage's question in this way. What the Maruts said in reply, the sage has explained in his own sentences in this way:

पृश्निं मातरं वोचंत अध इष्मिणं रुद्रं पितरु वोचंत (*pṛśniṃ mātaraṃ vocaṃta adha iṣmiṇaṃ rudraṃ pitaru vocaṃta*)—the sage explains here that the Maruts told him that Pṛśni was their mother and Rudra their father. How Pṛśni is mother to the Maruts and how Rudra is their father, we have explained on pages 594-596 of this part.

पृश्निं (*pṛśniṃ*)—the Maruts are described in many Ṛks of the Ṛgveda as पृश्निमातरः (*pṛśnimātaraḥ*), those who have Pṛśni for their mother. It is therefore necessary to give here an explanation of the words पृश्नि (*pṛśni*) and पृश्निमातरः (*pṛśnimātaraḥ*):
मरुन्माता नानावर्णा । तामेवांतरिक्षदेवतां केचिदाहुः। (*marunmātā nānāvarṇā | tāmevāṃtarikṣadevatāṃ kecidāhuḥ|*)

The word पृश्नि (*pṛśni*) is stated among the common names of the atmosphere (स्वः नाकः (*svaḥ nākaḥ*)) and of the Ādityas (Ni. 2-13), and: पृश्निरादित्यो भवति प्राश्नुत एनं वर्ण इति नैरुक्ताः (*pṛśnirādityo bhavati prāśnuta enaṃ varṇa iti nairuktāḥ*) (Ni. 2-14). Yāska has explained that, because abundant colour pervades him in an excessive manner, Āditya is called Pṛśni. The goddess Pṛśni is the mother of the Maruts, and she is of many colours: having explained one kind of meaning in this way, of those who say that she herself is the deity presiding over the atmosphere, and say

the opinion of some. And on the point that Pṛśni is the mother of the Maruts, they have quoted the sentence of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā प्रश्नियै वै पयसो मरुतो जाताः (*praśniyai vai payaso maruto jātāḥ*) (Tai. Saṃ. 2-2-11-4), and the sentence of the Ṛk-saṃhitā प्रश्नेः पुत्राः उपमासः (*praśneḥ putrāḥ upamāsaḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-58-5). The meaning is explained thus: सा देवी त्वेषं अयासं मरुतामनीकं असूत (*sā devī tveṣaṃ ayāsaṃ marutāmanīkaṃ asūta*): the goddess Pṛśni has brought forth the host of the Maruts, radiant and ever moving, forty-nine in number (having forty-nine persons).
पृश्निमातरः (*pṛśnimātaraḥ*): for this word the commentator has given the meaning "the sons of the earth, endowed with various colours". And as an example he has given the Ṛk
पृश्नेः पुत्रा उपमासो रभिष्ठाः स्वय्या मत्या मरुतः सं मिमिक्षुः ॥ (*pṛśneḥ putrā upamāso rabhiṣṭhāḥ svayyā matyā marutaḥ saṃ mimikṣuḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 53 59-53)⟨NOTE:431⟩

and, in explaining that Ṛk, he has explained the words पृश्नेः पुत्राः (*pṛśneḥ putrāḥ*) as गोरूपाया अंतरिक्षस्य ना पुत्रस्थानीयाः (*gorūpāyā aṃtarikṣasya nā putrasthānīyāḥ*)⟨NOTE:432⟩, that is, the sons of the earth in the form of a cow, or of the deity of the atmosphere. Skandasvāmin has said: पृश्निरिति द्युनाम । द्यौर्माता येषां मरुतां ते पृश्निमातरः । दिवः पुत्रा इत्यर्थः ॥ (*pṛśniriti dyunāma | dyaurmātā yeṣāṃ marutāṃ te pṛśnimātaraḥ | divaḥ putrā ityarthaḥ ‖*). Pṛśni means heaven; the atmosphere ... sons, he has said.⟨NOTE:433⟩ Since the movement of the Maruts is in the atmosphere itself, it is proper to say that they are born from it. Yāska has explained this word in the following way:

स्वः । पृश्निः । नाकः । गौः : विष्टं । नभ इति षट् साधारणानि ॥ साधारणान्युत्तराणि दिवश्चादित्यस्य ॥ (*svaḥ | pṛśniḥ | nākaḥ | gauḥ : viṣṭaṃ | nabha iti ṣaṭ sādhāraṇāni ‖ sādhāraṇānyuttarāṇi divaścādityasya ‖*) (Ni. 3-15)⟨NOTE:434⟩
That is, the six words स्वः (*svaḥ*), पृश्निः (*pṛśniḥ*), नाकः (*nākaḥ*), गौः (*gauḥ*), विष्टं (*viṣṭaṃ*) and नभः (*nabhaḥ*) are common words denoting heaven (दिवः (*divaḥ*)) and the Ādityas. And:

पृश्निरादित्यो भवति । प्राश्नुत एनं वर्ण इति नैरुक्ताः । संस्पृष्टा रसान् ! संस्पृष्टा भासं ज्योतिषां ॥ संस्पृष्टो भासेति वा ॥ अथ द्यौः संसृष्टा ज्योतिभिः पुण्यकृद्भिस् ॥ (*pṛśnirādityo bhavati | prāśnuta enaṃ varṇa iti nairuktāḥ | saṃspṛṣṭā rasān ! saṃspṛṣṭā bhāsaṃ jyotiṣāṃ ‖ saṃspṛṣṭo bhāseti vā ‖ atha dyauḥ saṃsṛṣṭā jyotibhiḥ puṇyakṛdbhis ‖*) (Ni. 2-14)⟨NOTE:435⟩

Pṛśni means Āditya. Because excellent radiance pervades him all around, the Nairuktas (the authors of the Nirukta) say that Pṛśni means Āditya. संस्पष्टा रसान् (*saṃspaṣṭā rasān*)⟨NOTE:436⟩ means स हि नित्यकालमेव रसानां संस्पष्टाभवति । अथास्यकर्म रसादानं । (*sa hi nityakālameva rasānāṃ saṃspaṣṭābhavati | athāsyakarma rasādānaṃ |*). Rasa means water; since he is the cause of

pouring it down as rain, Āditya has the name Pṛśni. Or संस्पृष्टा भासं ज्योतिषां (*saṃspṛṣṭā bhāsaṃ jyotiṣāṃ*): the light of the planets, stars, moon and the rest becomes dim through the excess of the sun's light; or संस्पृष्टो भासेति वा (*saṃspṛṣṭo bhāseti vā*): because he pervades everywhere with his own radiance, Pṛśni means Āditya.

Further, Pṛśni also means द्यौः (*dyauḥ*). For संस्पृष्टा ज्योतिर्भिः पुण्यकृद्भिश्च (*saṃspṛṣṭā jyotirbhiḥ puṇyakṛdbhiśca*): because it is attained by light and by the virtuous, Pṛśni means द्यौः (*dyauḥ*) (heaven). This is the explanation of Yāska. Therefore it is proper to accept for Pṛśni the meaning द्यौः (*dyauḥ*), heaven, the atmosphere, and to say that the word पृश्निमातरः (*pṛśnimātaraḥ*) means दिवस्पुत्राः (*divasputrāḥ*), those born in the atmosphere.
यद्यूयं पृश्निमातरो मर्ताः स्यातन (*yadyūyaṃ pṛśnimātaro martāḥ syātana*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-38-4)

he has explained the word पृश्निमातरः (*pṛśnimātaraḥ*) as पृश्निनामकधेनुपुत्रा (*pṛśnināmakadhenuputrā*), the Maruts, sons of the cow named Pṛśni. In many contexts where the Maruts are praised the use of the word पृश्निमातरः (*pṛśnimātaraḥ*) is seen in particular. One may therefore say freely that a definite meaning was current for this word. The Ṛks of the Ṛgveda in which this word is used are given below.
यद्यूयं पृश्निमातरो मर्तासः स्यातन (*yadyūyaṃ pṛśnimātaro martāsaḥ syātana*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-38-4)
अर्चंतो अर्कं जनयंत इंद्रियमधि श्रियो दधिरे प्रश्नॆमातरः ॥ (*arcaṃto arkaṃ janayaṃta iṃdriyamadhi śriyo dadhire praśnèmātaraḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-85-2)
पृषदश्वा मरुतः पृश्निमातरः शुभंयावानो विधथेषु जग्मयः ॥ (*pṛṣadaśvā marutaḥ pṛśnimātaraḥ śubhaṃyāvāno vidhatheṣu jagmayaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-89-7)
सुजातासो जनुषा पृश्निमातरो दिवो मर्या आ नो अच्छा जिगातन (*sujātāso januṣā pṛśnimātaro divo maryā ā no acchā jigātana*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-59-6)
उदीरयंत वायुभिर्वाश्रासः पृश्निमातरः (*udīrayaṃta vāyubhirvāśrāsaḥ pṛśnimātaraḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-7-3)
उदु स्वानेभिरीरत उद्रथैरुदु वायुभिः । उत्सॊम्मैः पृश्निमातरः ॥ (*udu svānebhirīrata udrathairudu vāyubhiḥ | utsòmmaiḥ pṛśnimātaraḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-7-17)
अभीमृतस्य विष्टपं दुहते पृश्निमातरः (*abhīmṛtasya viṣṭapaṃ duhate pṛśnimātaraḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 9-34-5)
स्वश्वाः स्थ सुरथाः पृश्चिमातरः स्वायुधा मरुतो याथना शुभं ॥ (*svaśvāḥ stha surathāḥ pṛścimātaraḥ svāyudhā maruto yāthanā śubhaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-57-2)⟨NOTE:437⟩
कोपयथ पृथिवीं पृश्निमातरः शुभे यदुग्राः पृषतीरयुग्ध्वं ॥ (*kopayatha pṛthivīṃ pṛśnimātaraḥ śubhe yadugrāḥ pṛṣatīrayugdhvaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-57-3)

All the Ṛks in which the word पृश्निमातरः (*pṛśnimātaraḥ*) is used have been given above. Since in these Ṛks the word पृश्निमातरः (*pṛśnimātaraḥ*) is explained as meaning the Maruts, one may say freely that this word is used in a definite sense in respect of these deities alone.

ಖಾದಿಸು printed; ಖಾದಿಷು in the Ṛk

en: "Seven" means groups of seven in number; the Maruts are indeed in seven troops, according to the Veda: सप्तगणा वै मरुतः (*saptagaṇā vai marutaḥ*) (Tai. Saṃ. 2-2-11-1). It is well known in the Purāṇas that Indra entered the wind dwelling in the womb of Aditi, split it into seven, and then split each part again into seven, and so they became the forty-nine troops of the Maruts. These seven troops are able to do everything. Each single troop gave, or let it give, to me hundreds, that is, hundreds of herds of cattle and horses⟨NOTE:438⟩. What was given by them stands on the river Yamunā. There I rub up (उन्मार्जयामि (*unmārjayāmi*)) the renowned wealth connected with cattle, consisting of a mass of cows. In the same way I rub off (निमार्ज्मि (*nimārjmi*)) the wealth given by them, consisting of horses, a mass of horses or connected with them.
notes: ವಿನೋಕ್ಷಯಂತಿ printed; the word looks damaged

en: - सप्त (*sapta*)—the seven troops of the Maruts
- शता (*śatā*)—cows and the like, hundreds in number
- यमुनायां अधि (*yamunāyāṃ adhi*)—on the bank of the river Yamunā

May the Maruts, seven in number in each of the troops of seven, all-capable, give me, each single troop, hundreds of cows and the like. May we obtain the renowned wealth in the form of cows on the bank of the river Yamunā. And may we obtain also wealth in the form of horses.

May the seven times seven all-potent (Maruts, aggregated as) a single troop, bestow upon me hundreds (of cattle): may I possess wealth of cows, renowned upon the (banks of) the Yamuna: may I possess wealth of horses.

The word एषां (*eṣāṃ*) means "of these Maruts": since the Maruts were the subject of the previous sūkta and are here referred to again, the word has no accent. Who knows their origin, their birth? What man knows it? Or who, even in former times, was a sharer in the pleasures of these Maruts? When these spotted deer were harnessed to the chariot, who knows their state, their marks of strength and their pleasures? Such is the meaning: since in every matter of speed the wind is the standard of comparison, the Maruts are beyond reckoning.
- सुम्नेषु (*sumneṣu*)—as a sharer in the pleasures
- को वा आस (*ko vā āsa*)—who indeed was?
Who has known the origin of these Maruts? When these Maruts harnessed their spotted deer to the chariot, who, formerly, was a sharer in the pleasures of these Maruts?
Who knows the birth of these (Maruts)? who has formerly been (participant) of the enjoyments of the Maruts (by whom) the spotted deer are harnessed (to their chariots)?
किलास्यः (*kilāsyaḥ*): किलासीः पृषती इत्यर्थः (*kilāsīḥ pṛṣatī ityarthaḥ*). It is said that the vehicle of the Maruts is the deer with white spots. On this matter Yāska:

हरी इंद्रस्य । रोहितोऽग्नेः । हरित आदित्यस्य । रासभावश्विनोः । अजाः पूष्टः । पृषत्यो मरुतां । अरुण्यो गाव उषसः । श्यावाः सवितुः । विश्वरूपा बृहस्पतेः । नियुतो वायोः । (*harī iṃdrasya | rohito 'gneḥ | harita ādityasya | rāsabhāvaśvinoḥ | ajāḥ pūṣṭaḥ | pṛṣatyo marutāṃ | aruṇyo gāva uṣasaḥ | śyāvāḥ savituḥ | viśvarūpā bṛhaspateḥ | niyuto vāyoḥ |*) (Ni. 9-28)

thus he has explained the vehicles of various deities. That is: for Indra the vehicles are two horses named Hari; for Agni, horses of a slightly red colour; for Āditya or Sūrya, (seven) horses of green or yellow colour; for the Aśvins, two asses; for the deity called Pūṣan, goats; for the Maruts, spotted deer; for the deity Uṣas, cows of aruṇa (red) colour; for the deity Savitṛ, horses of dusky colour; for Bṛhaspati, horses of various colours; for the deity Vāyu, swift-running horses named नियुत् (*niyut*). Thus he has given the explanation. In the present Ṛk the vehicles of the Maruts, the पृषतीः (*pṛṣatīḥ*), the spotted deer, are indicated by the word किलास्यः (*kilāsyaḥ*).

Who has made it heard (शुश्राव (*śuśrāva*); the sense is "would make hear") of these Maruts standing in their chariots? Or else: who could hear their shouting and the sound of their chariots? And how they go, who knows that too? Or else: how could other gods and the rest follow them? For what good giver (सुदासे (*sudāse*)) do the rains, kinsmen-like and pervading, come pouring down together with manifold foods, one after another?
- इळाभिः सह (*iḷābhiḥ saha*)—together with manifold foods
- कस्यै सुदासे (*kasyai sudāse*)—for the benefit of what sacrificer who offers excellent oblations
- अनु सस्सुः (*anu sassuḥ*)—do they pour down together

While the Maruts are seated in their chariots, who can hear their divine sound and the sound of their chariots? Who knows how they travel? For the benefit of what sacrificer who offers excellent oblations do the rains, agreeable like kinsmen, pour down together with manifold foods?
Who has heard them, when standing in their cars, (declare) whither they go? Upon what liberal worshipper do their kindred rains descend together with manifold food ?
In this Ṛk and in the previous Ṛk the seer has explained, by way of questions, that nobody knows well the majesty, the power and the capacity of the Marut deities.

The seer, seeing the Maruts who have appeared, speaks with this and the next Ṛk, in order to announce the appearance of the Maruts. The Maruts said to me, who thus lament: those who came to me. By what means? With shining (द्युभिः (*dyubhiḥ*)), that is, gleaming, going horses (विभिः (*vibhiḥ*)). For what purpose? For exhilaration (मदे (*made*)) produced by drinking Soma. What did they say? That he now declares: they are leaders (नरः (*naraḥ*)), beneficial to men (मर्याः (*maryāḥ*)), without stain (अरेपसः (*arepasaḥ*)). "O seer, looking with your eyes at us who stand thus, praise us," they said. Or else: "seeing us thus, praise."
- मदे (*made*)—for the joy of the drinking of Soma

When the Maruts came to me with their resplendent horses, for the joy of the drinking of Soma, they said: "O seer, praise us as soon as you see us, who are leaders, benefactors of men and free from stain."

To me have they spoken ; they who came to me with radiant steeds to (drink) the exhilarating beverage : to me (they have said), when beholding them, who are the formless leaders (of rites), and friends of man, repeat our praise.

By this Ṛk he describes the form of the Maruts. O Maruts, those well-known self-radiances (स्वभानवः (*svabhānavaḥ*)) of yours are a support (श्रायाः (*śrāyāḥ*)) in your ornaments (अंजिषु (*aṃjiṣu*)); those that are in your weapons (वाशीषु (*vāśīṣu*)); those in your garlands (स्रक्षु (*srakṣu*)); those in your breast ornaments (रुक्मेषु (*rukmeṣu*)); and those in the bracelets (खादिषु (*khādiṣu*)) that stand on hands and feet. For two Vedic texts say: हस्तेषु खादिश्च कृतिश्च (*hasteṣu khādiśca kṛtiśca*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1.168.3)⟨NOTE:439⟩ and पत्सु खादयः (*patsu khādayaḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5.54.11). And those self-radiances that are a support in your chariots and bows. And there is the Vedic passage सुधन्वान इषुमंतः सुरथाः पृश्निमातरः (*sudhanvāna iṣumaṃtaḥ surathāḥ pṛśnimātaraḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8.57.2)⟨NOTE:440⟩. "All these we praise" is to be supplied. Or else: the Maruts whose radiance is their own say, "We shall be a support on the occasion of ornaments; and those on the occasion of weapons"; so it is to be applied everywhere; the connection with the earlier part is "praise, seeing such as these". This is the saying of those same Maruts.

en: - श्रायाः (*śrāyāḥ*)—have taken refuge (praise such Maruts as soon as you see them)
Praise the Maruts as soon as you see them, in whose ornaments, weapons, garlands, bracelets and bows that well-known self-radiance has taken refuge.
(The praise of them) who are all self-irradiating, splendid in ornaments, in arms, in garlands, in breast-plates, in bracelets, in chariots, in bows.

In this Ṛk there is a description of the form of the Marut deities, and a description of their ornaments and weapons. स्वभानवः—स्वयं दीप्तयः (*svabhānavaḥ—svayaṃ dīptayaḥ*). Self-radiance means the light that is natural. The light that has the nature of shining of itself, without the help of other things, is called self-radiance or स्वभानु (*svabhānu*). This word स्वभानवः (*svabhānavaḥ*) is used especially for describing the Marut deities.

In regard to ornaments, some words are used in this Ṛk. The words स्रक्षु (*srakṣu*), रुक्मेषु (*rukmeṣu*), खादिसु (*khādisu*)⟨NOTE:441⟩ indicate the names of various ornaments. All these words are in the locative plural. स्रक्षु (*srakṣu*) means garlands, necklaces, necklaces made of gold and jewels, or else flower garlands. रुक्मेषु (*rukmeṣu*) means certain special ornaments worn on the breast. Their shape, form and so on may have been like some of the ornaments used at that time; now it is not possible to describe their form. Moreover, the adornment with these ornaments is spoken of only in respect of the Marut deities; the description of the ornaments of the other deities is of a different kind. The commentator has explained खादिषु (*khādiṣu*) as the bracelets (bangles) worn on the hands and feet. The description of the ornaments of the Maruts occurs in the Ṛk
विषामंसेषु रंभिणीव रारभे हस्तेषु खादिश्च कृतिश्च सं दधे । (*viṣāmaṃseṣu raṃbhiṇīva rārabhe hasteṣu khādiśca kṛtiśca saṃ dadhe |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-18-3)
Here it is described that they wear arm-bands on the upper arms, and bracelets or bangles on the hands.
अंसेषु न ऋष्टयः पत्सु खादयो वक्षस्सु रुक्मा मरुतो रथे शुभः । (*aṃseṣu na ṛṣṭayaḥ patsu khādayo vakṣassu rukmā maruto rathe śubhaḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-54-11)

Here it is described that they wear arm ornaments on the shoulders, bracelets called खादि (*khādi*) on the feet, and on the breast the golden ornament called रुक्म (*rukma*). In regard to the weapons of the Maruts also, the present Ṛk mentions the chariot and the bow.
स्वश्वाः स्थ सुरथाः पृश्चिमातरः स्वायुधा मरुतो यथना शुभं । (*svaśvāḥ stha surathāḥ pṛścimātaraḥ svāyudhā maruto yathanā śubhaṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-57-2)⟨NOTE:442⟩
In this Ṛk it is said that the Marut deities have good chariots, furnished with excellent horses, and good weapons.
