en: O quick givers (जीरदानवः (*jīradānavaḥ*)), O Maruts, with reference to your chariots I hold (दधे (*dadhe*)) them for joy, that is, I make (praises); सामर्थ्य्यात्सुतीरिति (*sāmarthyyātsutīriti*): the word understood by the sense is a plural feminine object⟨NOTE:443⟩. स्म (*sma*) is a filler. The connection is: the chariots that are seen as वृष्टी (*vṛṣṭī*) (वृष्टा (*vṛṣṭā*)), moving (यतीः (*yatīḥ*)) everywhere, like lights (द्यावः (*dyāvaḥ*)).
notes: ತ್ವೇಸಂ and ನೃಸ್ಟಯಃ printed in the Pada text; read ತ್ವೇಷಂ and ವೃಷ್ಟಯಃ as in the Saṃhitā

en: - जीरदानवः (*jīradānavaḥ*)—O you who give most generously
- द्यावः इव (*dyāvaḥ iva*)—shining like the light of lightning
notes: ಸೌಮೀತ್ಯರ್ಥಃ printed; read "I praise" (stomi)?

en: O generous givers⟨NOTE:445⟩, O Maruts, I contemplate with delight your chariots, shining like the light of lightning accompanied by rain.
notes: ಗಣ್ಯಗಣಂ printed in the Pada text; read ಗಣಂಗಣಂ as in the Saṃhitā

en: I contemplate your chariots, munificent Maruts, with delight, like wandering lights in the rains.

In this Ṛk the chariot of the Marut deities is praised. जीरदानवः—शीघ्रदानाः (*jīradānavaḥ—śīghradānāḥ*): the meaning is those who quickly give what the sacrificers desire. In some places the epithet सुदानवः (*sudānavaḥ*), those who give good gifts of what is desired, is used in regard to the Marut deities.

In the Kārīrī (कारीर्यां (*kārīryāṃ*)) three balls (पिंड्यो (*piṃḍyo*)) are to be offered. Among them, for the second, आ यं नर (*ā yaṃ nara*) is the anuvākyā. And it is laid down in the sūtra: आ यं नरः सुदानवो ददाशुषे विद्युन्महसो नरो अश्वदिद्यवः । (*ā yaṃ naraḥ sudānavo dadāśuṣe vidyunmahaso naro aśvadidyavaḥ |*) (A-2-13)⟨NOTE:446⟩. The leaders (नरः (*naraḥ*)), the Maruts of good gifts (सुदानवः (*sudānavaḥ*)), cause to fall (आच्यावयंति (*ācyāvayaṃti*)) from heaven, from the atmosphere, for the sacrificer who has offered the oblation (ददाशुषे (*dadāśuṣe*)), the cloud (कोशं (*kośaṃ*), a name of the cloud), which holds the waters like a store; the cloud (पर्जन्यं (*parjanyaṃ*)) they release; following heaven and earth (रोदसी (*rodasī*))
They release (वि सृजंति (*vi sṛjaṃti*); विनोक्षयंति (*vinokṣayaṃti*)⟨NOTE:447⟩). Afterwards the Maruts, the givers of rain, go along with water that moves everywhere; they pervade everywhere.
notes: ವೃಷ್ಟಿ ಸೃಷ್ಟಿಷು and ಉಸಿ printed in the bhāṣya; sense uncertain
ದಾತ್ಥನ್ printed in the bhāṣya; read as ದಾತೄನ್ "givers"?

en: - यं कोशं (*yaṃ kośaṃ*)—the cloud that preserves the water like a store
- ददाशुषे (*dadāśuṣe*)—for the sacrificer who offers oblations
- आ अचुच्यवुः (*ā acucyavuḥ*)—they make it come down
- रोदसी अनु (*rodasī anu*)—so as to pervade heaven and earth wholly
- वि सृजंति (*vi sṛjaṃti*)—they loosen and let go
- धन्वना (*dhanvanā*)—with the waters that spread everywhere

The Maruts, leaders of the rains and excellent givers, make the cloud, which preserves the water like a store, come down from the atmosphere for the sacrificer who offers oblations. They loosen and let go the cloud so that it pervades heaven and earth wholly. The same Maruts, givers of rain, travel with the waters that spread everywhere.

Leaders (of the rain', munificent givers, they cause that which is the treasury (of water) to fall from the sky for (the benefit of) the donor (of the offering): they let loose the rain cloud, and the shedders of rain spread (everywhere) with (abundant) water.

In the iṣṭi called Kārīrī three balls are to be offered in the fire. It is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana-śrauta-sūtra, आ यं नरः सुदानवो ददाशुषे विद्युन्महसो नरो अश्वदिद्यवः (*ā yaṃ naraḥ sudānavo dadāśuṣe vidyunmahaso naro aśvadidyavaḥ*) (Ā. 2.13), that in the second offering this Ṛk आ यं नरः (*ā yaṃ naraḥ*) is to be recited as the anuvākyā mantra.
दिवः कोशं (*divaḥ kośaṃ*): the word कोश (*kośa*) is included among the thirty names of the cloud (Ni. 2-21). Yāska, giving the explanation of this word, has quoted the Ṛk

प्रीणीताश्वान् हितं जयाथ स्वस्तिवाहं रथमित्कृणुद्ध्वं । द्रोणाहावमवतमश्मचक्रमंसत्रकोशं सिंचता नृपाणं ॥ (*prīṇītāśvān hitaṃ jayātha svastivāhaṃ rathamitkṛṇuddhvaṃ | droṇāhāvamavatamaśmacakramaṃsatrakośaṃ siṃcatā nṛpāṇaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10.101-7)
and for the word अंगत्रकोशं (*aṃgatrakośaṃ*)⟨NOTE:448⟩ that stands there he has said:

अंसत्राणि वः कोशस्थानीयानि संतु कोशः कुष्णातेर्विकुषितो भवति । आयमपीतरः कोश एतस्मादेव संचय अचितमात्रो महान्भवति ॥ (*aṃsatrāṇi vaḥ kośasthānīyāni saṃtu kośaḥ kuṣṇātervikuṣito bhavati | āyamapītaraḥ kośa etasmādeva saṃcaya acitamātro mahānbhavati ‖*) (Ni. 5-26)

The word कोश (*kośa*) is formed from the root meaning "to draw". The meaning may be a leather bag containing many things, which are drawn out, as water is drawn or bailed out of a well. Just as water is stored in a well, so many things are stored in the bag called कोश (*kośa*) (a leather bag), as arrows are in a quiver. Just as arrows are drawn out of the quiver one by one, so by taking out the things that are in the कोश (*kośa*) (bag), the place where things are collected has received the name कोश (*kośa*). Therefore it is the custom to call a cloud in which water is collected, and any other place where other things are collected (Collected) (Store-house), a कोश (*kośa*). Here दिवः कोशं (*divaḥ kośaṃ*) means the mass of clouds gathered together in the atmosphere. The idea is that the Marut deities scatter them and make the waters that are in them fall down.
notes: ಹೃದಯ printed; the Pada text has ಹ್ವಯೆ

en: The flowing waters (सिंधवः (*siṃdhavaḥ*)), splitting the clouds (ततृदानाः (*tatṛdānāḥ*)), the Maruts, spread (प्रसरंति (*prasaraṃti*)) with the water (क्षोदसा (*kṣodasā*)) through the atmosphere (रजः (*rajaḥ*)), like cows that have newly calved and pour out milk. And there is another illustration: as swift-moving horses on the road, at the release (विमोचने (*vimocane*)), run about for the release of men from the journey, so it is: this is the meaning. When the rivers (एन्यः (*enyaḥ*), a name of rivers) move variously, or turn back and flow on, that is, swell, then they do this: so the connection with the earlier part.
- धेनवो यथा (*dhenavo yathā*)—as cows pour out and spread milk
- ततृदानाः (*tatṛdānāḥ*)—the Maruts who split the cloud
- प्र सस्रुः (*pra sasruḥ*)—they caused to spread everywhere
- वि वर्तंते (*vi vartaṃte*)—flow freely in all places

As cows pour out and spread milk, the Maruts who split the cloud caused the streams filled with water to spread everywhere. And like swift-going horses let loose freely on the road, the rivers also, at the same time, flow freely everywhere.

The gliding (torrents), issuing (from the clouds), overspread the firmament with water, as milch-cows (yield milk), and like rapid horses let loose upon the road, the rivers rush in various directions.

The Marut deities split the clouds and make their water fall upon the earth; it is described in this Ṛk that those waters become river streams and flow swiftly. As to what the swift streams are like, the seer has given two illustrations. धेनवो यथा । नवप्रसूता गाव इव । (*dhenavo yathā | navaprasūtā gāva iva |*). As cows that have newly calved pour out (give) milk to their heart's content, so the river streams flow full of abundant water: this is one illustration. अध्वनः विमोचने स्यन्ना अश्वाइव (*adhvanaḥ vimocane syannā aśvāiva*). आशुगतय अश्वाः मनुष्याणामध्वनिमोकाय यथा संचरंति तथेत्यर्थः । (*āśugataya aśvāḥ manuṣyāṇāmadhvanimokāya yathā saṃcaraṃti tathetyarthaḥ |*). When men urge swift-running horses to run quickly on the road, those horses, which by nature are swift in going, run at very great speed on the road at the urging of men; as they do, so the river streams flow with very great speed: this is the other illustration. Of these two

illustrations, by the illustration of the cows it is described here that the waters in the streams of the rivers are abundant, and by the second illustration, of the horses, that those river streams move (flow) with very great speed.

O Maruts, come from heaven, from the world of heaven, from a very distant region (परावतः (*parāvataḥ*)). In the same way come from the atmosphere. And come also from this world here (अमात् (*amāt*)). The word परावतः (*parāvataḥ*) is to be construed here also⟨NOTE:449⟩. In the distant region, there and there, in the world of heaven and so on, do not stay (माव स्थात (*māva sthāta*)): do not make a stay there.
notes: ಪೃಷ್ಟಯಜ್ವನೇ, ನೃಮ್ಮಂ, ಅರ್ಚಿತ and ಅನಜ in the Pada text differ from the Saṃhitā; printed so

en: - अमात् (*amāt*)—even though you are on this earth (come)
- परावतः (*parāvataḥ*)—remaining only in very distant regions
- मा अव स्थात (*mā ava sthāta*)—do not remain standing
O Maruts, come to us from the very distant world of heaven, or from the atmosphere, or from the earth. Do not remain standing in heaven and the other regions that are far away from us.
Come, Maruts, from heaven, from the firmaments, or from this (earth); tarry not far off.
In this Ṛk it is described that the Marut deities pervade all three places, the earth, the atmosphere and heaven. That is, the idea is that the Marut deities travel in all three worlds.

O Maruts, as to रसा (*rasā*): this is a name of rivers; the Nirukta says रसा नदी भवति (*rasā nadī bhavati*) (Ni. 11.25): the sounding river, the river with a noise. अनितभा (*anitabhā*): that of which the light has been attained is सेतभा (*setabhā*); one not of that kind is अनितभा (*anitabhā*). And कुभा (*kubhā*) is one of bad light. Let them not hinder (मा नि रीरमत् (*mā ni rīramat*); the sense is "let it not rest lowly"). क्रुमुः (*krumuḥ*) the all-moving, and सिंधुः (*siṃdhuḥ*) the ocean: let them not hinder. So also पुरीषिणी (*purīṣiṇī*): पुरीषमुदकं (*purīṣamudakaṃ*); the Sarayu too, possessing it, let it not stand around (मा परि ष्ठात् (*mā pari ṣṭhāt*)); let it not obstruct⟨NOTE:450⟩. To us alone may there be the happiness (सुम्मं (*summaṃ*)) born of your coming, belonging to you, existing in you.
notes: ಅಸ್ಮಿನ್ಪಕ್ಷೇ ಸಂಘವಾದೋಽಯಃ ; sense of the last word uncertain

en: - मा नि रीरमत् (*mā ni rīramat*)—let it not hinder
- मा परि स्थात् (*mā pari sthāt*)—let it not hinder

O Maruts, let none of the rivers Rasā, Anitabhā and Kubhā hinder you. Let the ocean, and the Sarayu, a river full of water, also not hinder you. May the happiness that is born of your coming be reserved for us.
Let not the Rasa, the Anitabha, the Kubha, or the wide-roving ocean delay you : let not the watery Sarayu oppose you : may the happiness of your (approach) be ours.

In this Ṛk the names of the rivers Rasā, Anitabhā, Kubhā and Sarayu are recited. Of these rivers, the names Anitabhā and Kubhā are recited in the Ṛgveda in this Ṛk only, and since there is no mention of them anywhere else, nothing more can be said about them. Perhaps these two rivers may have been tributaries of some large river (the Yamunā?). Therefore they are not so famous.

Sarayu: the river called Sarayū is famous in the Purāṇas. In the Rāmāyaṇa there is a description that the city of Ayodhyā stood on the bank of the Sarayū. In the Ṛgveda also the name of this river occurs in the present Ṛk, and in the Ṛk
उत त्या सद्य आर्या सरयोरिंद्र पारतः । अर्णाचित्ररथावधीः ॥ (*uta tyā sadya āryā sarayoriṃdra pārataḥ | arṇācitrarathāvadhīḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-30-18)
it is stated that Indra killed the king called Citraratha on the bank of the river called Sarayu. In the Ṛk
सरस्वती सरयुः सिंधुरूर्मिभिर्महो महीरवसा यंतु वक्षणीः । (*sarasvatī sarayuḥ siṃdhurūrmibhirmaho mahīravasā yaṃtu vakṣaṇīḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-64-9)
there is a prayer that the rivers Sarasvatī, Sarayu and Sindhu may come with their protections. The river Sarayu is mentioned in the Ṛgveda in these three Ṛks only; nowhere else.

Rasā: there must have been a well-known river called Rasā, or there is reason also to conjecture that the Sindhu, the river famous now, had this name. It was famous as a divine river, and once, when the water of this river dried up for some reason, the Aśvin deities by their power
filled it with water, this story is told in the Ṛk Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-112-12, where the qualities of the Aśvin deities are described.

अत्रेतिहासमाचक्षते । पणिभिरसुरैरपह्रियमाणा गा अनुगच्छंतः देवगोपाला रसां नामांतरिक्षनदीमगाधोदकां नोत्तरितुं शेकुः । तद्ज्ञात्वा देवाः संक्रुद्धाः रसां शेपुः निरुदका भवेति । सा प्रत्यनीतासु गोषु अश्विनौ परिचचार । तामश्विन् गत्वा पुनरगाधोदकां चक्रतुरिति ॥ (*atretihāsamācakṣate | paṇibhirasurairapahriyamāṇā gā anugacchaṃtaḥ devagopālā rasāṃ nāmāṃtarikṣanadīmagādhodakāṃ nottarituṃ śekuḥ | tadjñātvā devāḥ saṃkruddhāḥ rasāṃ śepuḥ nirudakā bhaveti | sā pratyanītāsu goṣu aśvinau paricacāra | tāmaśvin gatvā punaragādhodakāṃ cakraturiti ‖*)

When the asuras called Paṇis carried off the cows of the gods, the divine cowherds followed that track and pursued the asuras; on the way a river called Rasā, belonging to the atmosphere and filled with an unfathomable flood of water, lay across their path, and they were not able to cross it. When the gods learned of this, they were angry and cursed the river to become dry. At once all the water of that river dried up. After the cows had been driven back, the river Rasā prayed to the Aśvin deities, and they came and filled that river with abundant water. This story Skandasvāmin has explained in his commentary. Sāyaṇa's explanation is slightly different. His explanation is:

रसा नदी भवति रसतेः शब्दकर्मण इति यास्कः । नि. ११-२५ । हे अश्विनौ याभिरूतिभिर्हेतुभूताभी रसां नदीमनावृष्ट्या जलरहितां क्षोदसा कूलानि संपिंषतोद्न उदकेन पिपिन्वथुः युवां पूरितवंतौ ॥ (*rasā nadī bhavati rasateḥ śabdakarmaṇa iti yāskaḥ | Ni. 11-25 | he aśvinau yābhirūtibhirhetubhūtābhī rasāṃ nadīmanāvṛṣṭyā jalarahitāṃ kṣodasā kūlāni saṃpiṃṣatodna udakena pipinvathuḥ yuvāṃ pūritavaṃtau ‖*) (Sā. Bhā.)

Accepting the derivation of the Nirukta-writers that the word Rasā is formed from the root ras, which gives the sense "make a sound",⟨NOTE:451⟩ he says that the water of a river flows swiftly and therefore makes a noise, and for that reason this river is named Rasā. But he has said that the cause of the drying up of the water of this river was the failure of rain. In some places it is said that the water of this river was of unfathomable flood and impossible to cross.
कास्मेहितिः का परितक्त्वासीत्कथं रसाया आतरः पयांसि । (*kāsmehitiḥ kā paritaktvāsītkathaṃ rasāyā ātaraḥ payāṃsi |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-108-1)
In the past the Paṇis carried off the cows of the gods and hid them, unknown to anyone, in the cave of a mountain.

At the prayer of the gods, Indra sent Saramā, the divine bitch (the female dog of the world of the gods), to find the place where the cows were hidden. She travelled a very long way, crossed forests and wilds, passed over many rivers, and at last came to the place where the Paṇis were. Then an interesting conversation took place between the Paṇis and Saramā on the matter of giving the cows back to the gods. In it the Paṇis question Saramā: how did you cross the river Rasā, with its unfathomable flood of water, when you came here? Therefore it can be said that the river Rasā was full of an unfathomable flood of water. Besides these contexts, in the Ṛk
सिषक्तु माता मही रसा नः स्मत्सूरिभिर्ऋजुहस्त ऋजुवनिः । (*siṣaktu mātā mahī rasā naḥ smatsūribhirṛjuhasta ṛjuvaniḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-41-15)

the word Rasā is used. When he gives the meaning of this Ṛk, Sāyaṇa has said रसा सारभूता भूमिः (*rasā sārabhūtā bhūmiḥ*), "Rasā is the earth that is the essence"; but since in this Ṛk the word "let her moisten" occurs, there is room for the conjecture that the word Rasā may denote precisely the river called Rasā. And in the Ṛks Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-43-6; 10-75.6; 10-121.4; 5.53.9; 7-72.13 and others the name of the river Rasā is indicated.
notes: ಉದನ್ಯತಃ printed; Saṃhitā has ಉದನ್ಯವಃ
ಆ. ೨-೧೨ printed; the bhāṣya of the previous Ṛk cites the same sūtra as ಆ. ೨-೧೩

en: The word "that" is to be connected with "of the Maruts". "Your" means "of you": I praise the impelling strength of your new chariots, the brilliant strength, and that troop of the Maruts.⟨NOTE:453⟩ Or else: the chariots are swift-moving; of you, with these, I praise the strength that overpowers others, and the troop; this is one single sentence. Then the speech turns to the third person: the rains follow after you, they go forth vigorously. Or else: the rain-bringing Maruts go forth in accordance with their wish, favourably and excellently.
notes: ಪರ್ವತ್ಯಚ್ಯುತಃ and ಉತ್ಓಜಸಃ printed in the Pada text; ಅಶ್ವದಿದ್ಯವಃ in the Pada text and ಅಶ್ಮದಿದ್ಯವಃ in the bhāṣya differ

en: - तं मारुतं गणं (*taṃ mārutaṃ gaṇaṃ*)—that renowned troop of the Maruts (I praise)
- अनु प्र यंति (*anu pra yaṃti*)—move about according to the wish of the Maruts
O Maruts, I praise the strength of your new chariots, their brilliance, and the renowned troop of the Maruts. The rains move about according to the wish of the Maruts.
I praise that brilliant company of the Maruts, who have your strength of recent chariots, you whom the rains attend.

notes: ದುಃಽಗಾನಿ and ರಿಷ್ಯಧ printed in the Pada text; ರಿಷ್ಯತ in the Saṃhitā

en: O Maruts, of you, each strength, that is each particular strength; and each troop. A troop is a group of unspecified number; each such troop, and each company, that is each company made up of seven and seven: all these we follow, with good praises and with rites, which have the nature of offering oblations and the like.
- एषां वः (*eṣāṃ vaḥ*)—of you, the renowned (O Maruts)
- व्रातंव्रातं (*vrātaṃvrātaṃ*)—each troop defined by its strength
- गणंगणं (*gaṇaṃgaṇaṃ*)—each individual company, divided into groups of seven
- धीतिभिः (*dhītibhiḥ*)—by rites such as the offering of oblations

O Maruts, we worship your renowned individual strength, the troop defined by its strength, and the individual company divided into groups of seven, with rites such as the offering of oblations, accompanied by excellent praises.
Let us wait with sacred praises and holy rites upon your several strength, and separate troop, and individual company.
Today, on this day, to which well-born giver of oblations, one who has offered the oblation, would the Maruts go forth, that is would go vigorously, by this chariot?
- अद्य (*adya*)—on this day of the sacrifice
- एना यामेन (*enā yāmena*)—seated in this chariot
- प्र ययुः (*pra yayuḥ*)—have they set out?
On this day of the sacrifice, the Maruts, seated in this chariot, have set out to which sacrificer, of excellent birth, who has offered the oblation?
To what well-born and oblation-giving (worshipper) will the Maruts proceed to-day in this their car ?

O Maruts, with whatever compassionate mind you hold imperishable grain-seed for a son, for a grandson (or for wealth), with that mind give us that grain-seed. And the wealth that we ask of you, which is full of all food or full of a complete lifetime, and good fortune: give that also. Such is the construction.
- विश्वायु (*viśvāyu*)—lasting for the whole span of life
- धान्यं (*dhānyaṃ*)—that has the nature of grain

O Maruts, we also ask of you wealth that will last as long as the span of our life and that is auspicious. For that reason, with the same compassionate mind with which you hold imperishable seed, in the nature of grain, to distribute to a son and a grandson, share out that same grain to us also with that same compassionate mind.
With the same (goodwill) that you bestow imperishable grain-seed upon a son or grandson, bestow it upon us, for we ask of you life-sustaining and auspicious wealth.

O Maruts, we, abandoning sin through blessings of welfare, may pass beyond the revilers, the enemies who have come near; or else the word for "across" means "concealed", and the sense is that we may overcome them. By this the removal of what is unwelcome is prayed for; by what follows the attainment of what is desired is stated. When the rains impelled by you are present, may there be happiness, and the warding off of sins; and the waters, the word for waters here standing in the nominative plural by substitution. The remedy is that which is connected with cows. Although this word is a name for water, since the waters are named separately, the food produced by them is meant here. May we obtain all that together, O Maruts. Or else: may the waters impelled by you do all that has been said, and may we all be together, as your own.⟨NOTE:455⟩
notes: ಶಿಕ್ಷಸಃ printed; Saṃhitā has ಶಿಕ್ವಸಃ

en: - अति इयाम (*ati iyāma*)—may we pass beyond
- वृष्ट्वी (*vṛṣṭvī*)—by the rains impelled by you

O Maruts, by our auspicious rites may we abandon sin and pass beyond the enemies who are revilers and who lie hidden. O Maruts, through the rains impelled by you, may we obtain together happiness, freedom from sorrow, waters, and food connected with cows.
May we overcome our secret and reviling adversaries, having departed from iniquity by good deeds : may we possess, Maruts, through the rain (sent by you), unmixed happiness, water, cattle, and herbs.

O Samaha: the word is one of praise. O revered troop of the Maruts, the man becomes one who has good gods, that is, he is endowed with the gods called Maruts who bring welfare. O leaders, O Maruts, that mortal also becomes one with good heroic sons and the like, whom you protect and guard. When this is so, may we be yours.
- सुदेवः (*sudevaḥ*)—becomes one favoured by the gods
- सुवीरः (*suvīraḥ*)—is endowed with heroic sons and the like

O revered Maruts, the man whom you protect becomes one favoured by the gods. O Maruts, leaders, that same man is endowed with heroic sons and the like. May we also, like him, remain under your protection.
Renowned (host of) Maruts, leaders (of rites), that mortal is favoured by the gods, and blessed with progeny, whom you protect : may we be such as he is.

O seer, praise the Maruts, the givers, in the sacrifice of this sacrificer who offers praise. As cows going to eat grass and the like take delight, so may the Maruts also take delight. Since the Maruts are going about, call them, as one calls old friends. Praise with a hymn the Maruts who desire praise.⟨NOTE:456⟩
notes: ತೇ ಜಾಗೃಭೀತಶೋಚಿಷೋಽಗೃಹೀತತೇಜಸ್ಕಾಃ printed; ಜಾಗೃಭೀತ for ಅಗೃಭೀತ?

en: - यवसे (*yavase*)—going to eat grass and the like
- सखीन् इव (*sakhīn iva*)—as one calls friends
notes: haking printed; "shaking"?

en: O seer, in the sacrifice of this sacrificer who offers praise, praise the Maruts who are givers. May they take delight, like cows going to eat grass and the like. Call them, who are of a roving nature, as one calls friends of long-cherished friendship. Extol with praise those who desire praise.

Praise the givers of enjoyment, (the Maruts), at the sacrifice of this worshipper, (for they) delight in (pious praise), like cattle in fodder : where-fore call upon them as if upon old friends ; praise them, desirous of praise with a sacred hymn.

notes: ಕಸನಾಇವ printed; ಕಪನಾಇವ?

en: "Forth" is to be connected with "bring". Bring this praise that is being made to the strength of the Maruts: to the strength that is self-radiant, with a brilliance of its own; that makes the mountain fall (the cloud); that checks the heat; that comes from the heaven-world; that is worshipped with the six Pṛṣṭha chants, रथंतरबृहदादिभिरीजानाय (*rathaṃtarabṛhadādibhirījānāya*); and that has shining food. Offer much wealth in the form of oblation; this is the sense.
- पर्वतच्युते (*parvatacyute*)—to that which splits the cloud for the sake of rain
- शर्धाय (*śardhāya*)—to the strength in the form of a host
- दिवः आ (*divaḥ ā*)—to that which comes from the sky
- पृष्ठयज्वने (*pṛṣṭhayajvane*)—to that which is worshipped with the Pṛṣṭha praises
- द्युम्नश्रवसे (*dyumnaśravase*)—to the host of the Maruts that has shining food
- नृम्मं (*nṛmmaṃ*)—wealth in the form of oblation

Offer the praise now composed to the strength of the Maruts, in the form of a host, which is self-luminous and which splits the cloud for the sake of rain; to that which removes heat, which comes from the sky and which is worshipped with the Pṛṣṭha praises. To the host of the Maruts, which has shining food, offer wealth in the form of oblation abundantly.

Offer praise to the company of the Maruts, the self-irradiating, the precipitators of mountains : present liberal oblations to the assuagers of heat, to those who come from the sky, to whom solemn rites are familiar, to the givers of abundant food.

In the Kārīrī rite, for the first of the offerings, this Ṛk is the yājyā. It is laid down in the sūtra: प्र वो मरुतस्तविषा आ यं नरः (*pra vo marutastaviṣā ā yaṃ naraḥ*) (Ā. Sū. 2-13). O Maruts, your troops appear. Of what kind are these troops? They are shining or great; desirous of water for the protection of the world; increasers of food; yokers of horses to the chariot for going; moving all round. They join with lightning. Then Trita, the cloud or the host of the Maruts, stretched out in the three places, sounds. In this view the word for host is used in an unusual way.⟨NOTE:459⟩ Then the waters, flowing all round, fall down upon the earth.
notes: ref printed ೩ ೧-೪

en: - वयोवृधः (*vayovṛdhaḥ*)—causing increase of the wealth of food
- अश्वयुजः (*aśvayujaḥ*)—with horses yoked to the chariot
- त्रितः (*tritaḥ*)—the host of the Maruts (or the cloud), present in the three places
notes: ನ ಪ್ರೇಧತಿ printed; verse and bhāṣya have ಶ್ರೇಧತಿ / ಸ್ತ್ರೇಧತಿ

en: O Maruts, your hosts, exceedingly mighty, pouring out water for the world and causing the increase of the wealth of food, are excellent. With horses yoked to the chariot and moving everywhere, they join with lightning. Then the host of the Maruts, present in the three places, makes a noise in the form of thunder. At once the waters, spreading everywhere and flowing, fall and flow upon the earth.

Your (cohort), Maruts, is conspicuous, mighty, shedding water and augmenting food : yoking your horses (to your cars), spreading everywhere and combined with the lightning, the triple-(stationed company) roars aloud, and the circumambient waters fall upon the earth.

In the Kārīrī rite, in the offering of the first piṇḍa, this Ṛk is to be used as the yājyā mantra; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana-śrauta-sūtra प्र वो मरुतस्तविषा आ यं नरः (*pra vo marutastaviṣā ā yaṃ naraḥ*) (Ā. Sū. 2-12).⟨NOTE:461⟩
notes: ಕಾರೀರ್ಯಾಮೇವ ತೃತೀಯಸ್ಯಾಃ ಪಿಂಡ್ಯಾ: sentence begins abruptly; sense uncertain
ಮಧ್ವಃ printed; verse has ಮಧ್ಯೋ

en: This third Ṛk is the yājyā of the second piṇḍī in the same Kārīrī rite. It is laid down in the sūtra विद्युन्महसो नरोऽश्मदिद्यवः कृष्णं नियानं हरयः सुपर्णाः । (*vidyunmahaso naro 'śmadidyavaḥ kṛṣṇaṃ niyānaṃ harayaḥ suparṇāḥ |*) (Ā. Sū. 2-13). The Maruts are of shining brilliance, leaders who send the rain, with weapons far-reaching or made of the essence of stone, who have gained their splendour, who make the mountains, or the clouds, fall, and who repeatedly give waters. They set the thunderbolt in motion; they are accompanied by sound, the word meaning "together" here; that is, they are troops with noise. They strive together for the sake of rain and are of lofty strength; the sense is that the Maruts appear for the sake of rain.
- विद्युन्महसः (*vidyunmahasaḥ*)—possessed of the radiance of lightning
- अश्वदिद्यवः (*aśvadidyavaḥ*)—possessed of weapons in the form of stone
- वातत्विषः (*vātatviṣaḥ*)—possessed of a brilliance of their own
- रभसाः (*rabhasāḥ*)—who have gathered together for the sake of rain
- मरुतः (*marutaḥ*)—the Maruts (appear for the sake of rain)

The Maruts, possessed of the radiance of lightning, leaders, possessed of weapons in the form of stone and of a brilliance of their own, who split the cloud, who repeatedly give water, who wield the thunderbolt, who make noise together, who have gathered together, and who are possessed of exceeding strength, appear for the sake of rain.

The Maruts (appear) radiant with lightning, leaders (of the rain), armed with weapons of adamant, blazing with the wind, the precipitators of mountains, the repeated distributors of water, wielders of the thunder-bolt, roaring in concert, combining (to send rain), and of exceeding strength.

In the Kārīrī rite, this Ṛk is to be used as the yājyā mantra in the second piṇḍa offering; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana-śrauta-sūtra विद्युन्महसो नरोऽत्मदिद्यवः कृष्णं नियानं हरयः सुपर्णाः (*vidyunmahaso naro 'tmadidyavaḥ kṛṣṇaṃ niyānaṃ harayaḥ suparṇāḥ*) (Ā. Sū. 2-13).
चित् (*cit*): here the word has no particular meaning; the commentator says it is used to fill out the pāda. Yāska in his Nirukta gives its explanation:

चिदित्येषोऽनेककर्मा । आचार्यश्चिदिदं ब्रूयादिति पूजायां । दधिचिदित्युपमार्थे । कुल्माषांश्चिदाहरेत्यवकुत्सिते । (*cidityeṣo 'nekakarmā | ācāryaścididaṃ brūyāditi pūjāyāṃ | dadhicidityupamārthe | kulmāṣāṃścidāharetyavakutsite |*) (Ni. 1-4)

Having said that the particle चित् (*cit*) is used in many kinds of senses, he has given examples to support it. In the sentence आचार्यश्चिदिदं ब्रूयात् (*ācāryaścididaṃ brūyāt*) the word चित् (*cit*) is used in the sense of respect. In दधिचित् (*dadhicit*) it is used in the sense of comparison, and in कुल्माषांश्चित् (*kulmāṣāṃścit*) in the sense of disparagement; thus he has explained the meaning of the examples.

स्तनयदमाः (*stanayadamāḥ*): the word अमा (*amā*) is read among the names of the house (Ni. 3-13 and 11-48). Here the commentator gives the sense "together". Therefore the word means those accompanied by sound, those accompanied by lightning and thunder. The idea is that while rain is pouring, the wind blows violently and with noise, and the sound of lightning and thunder is also heard.

notes: abbreviation ತ್ರೈ. ಆ. printed; ಸಪ್ತಭಿಃ "seven" in the quotation but eight names listed and ಎಂಟು ಮಂದಿ in the Kannada

en: O Rudras, sons of Rudra, O Maruts: the word for nights is to be connected with the verb of the second half of the verse, and so everywhere; the sense of the verb is "you throw". You throw the days also. O mighty ones, able to do everything, you throw the firmament; likewise the worlds. O shakers, when you drive the clouds, as boats are driven on the sea, so you break through the strongholds, the cities of the enemy. O Maruts, you do not harm.
- धूतयः (*dhūtayaḥ*)—O Maruts, who make everything tremble
- नाव ईं यथा (*nāva īṃ yathā*)—as one drives a boat over the sea
- वि अजथ (*vi ajatha*)—you make them move (then)
- नाह रिष्यथ (*nāha riṣyatha*)—you do not harm friends
notes: ಸ್ನುಗತಯೋಽಪಿ printed after ಪಥ್ಯಾಃ; meaning unclear

en: O Maruts, sons of Rudra, you drive on the days and nights, the firmament, and likewise all the worlds. O Maruts, who are all-powerful and who make everything tremble, when you make the clouds move as a boat is driven over the sea, then you break through the cities of the enemy. O Maruts, you do not harm friends. You also are not harmed.
Powerful Rudras, you urge on the nights and days, the firmament and the worlds: agitators (of all things), you toss the clouds like ships (in
the sea), so (you throw down) the strong places (of the enemy); but, Maruts, you do no harm.

रुद्राः (*rudrāḥ*): the Maruts, sons of Rudra. Here the word Rudra itself is used to denote the sons of Rudra. The use of the father's name to indicate the sons is a special custom in the Ṛgveda. For example:
देवेभिर्विप्रा ऋषयो नृचक्षसो वि पिबध्वं कुशिकाः सोम्यं मधु । (*devebhirviprā ṛṣayo nṛcakṣaso vi pibadhvaṃ kuśikāḥ somyaṃ madhu |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-53-10)
सुदानुं देवं रथिरं वसूयवो गीर्भी रण्वं कुशिकासो हवामहे । (*sudānuṃ devaṃ rathiraṃ vasūyavo gīrbhī raṇvaṃ kuśikāso havāmahe |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-36-1)
In these and other Ṛks the sons of Kuśika are denoted by the words कुशिकाः (*kuśikāḥ*) and कुशिकासः (*kuśikāsaḥ*).
विद्याम वस्तोरवसा गृणंतो भरद्वाजा उत त इंद्र नूनं । (*vidyāma vastoravasā gṛṇaṃto bharadvājā uta ta iṃdra nūnaṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6.25-9)
एवा नपातो मम तस्य धीभिर्भरदाजा अभ्यर्चंत्यर्कॆः । (*evā napāto mama tasya dhībhirbharadājā abhyarcaṃtyarkèḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-50-15)
In these and other Ṛks the sons or descendants of Bharadvāja are addressed by the word भरद्वाजाः (*bharadvājāḥ*).
नू त्वामग्न ईमहे वसिष्ठा ईशानं सूनो सहसो वसूनां । (*nū tvāmagna īmahe vasiṣṭhā īśānaṃ sūno sahaso vasūnāṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-7-7)
वसिष्ठासः पितृवद्वाचमक्रत देवा ईळाना ऋषिवत् स्वस्तये । (*vasiṣṭhāsaḥ pitṛvadvācamakrata devā īḷānā ṛṣivat svastaye |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-66-15)
In these and other Ṛks the sons of Vasiṣṭha are called by the words वसिष्ठाः (*vasiṣṭhāḥ*) and वसिष्ठासः (*vasiṣṭhāsaḥ*).

रजांसि (*rajāṃsi*): रजो रज्यतेर्ज्योती रज उच्यते उदकं रज उच्यते । लोका रजांस्युच्यंते । (*rajo rajyaterjyotī raja ucyate udakaṃ raja ucyate | lokā rajāṃsyucyaṃte |*) (Ni. 4-19). Derived from the root रंज् (*raṃj*), which gives the sense "shine", the word रजस् (*rajas*) comes to mean light, water, and the worlds.
रजांसि चित्रा वि चरंति तन्यवो दिनः सम्राजा पयसा न उक्षतं । (*rajāṃsi citrā vi caraṃti tanyavo dinaḥ samrājā payasā na ukṣataṃ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-63-5)
Citing this Ṛk, the Niruktakāras have said that the word रजांसि (*rajāṃsi*) means the worlds. In the 44th section of the 10th chapter of the Nirukta, in explaining the Ṛk
अब्बामुक्थैरहिं गृणीषे बुद्धे नदीनां रजस्सु षीदन् (*abbāmukthairahiṃ gṛṇīṣe buddhe nadīnāṃ rajassu ṣīdan*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-34-16)
they say that the word रजस्सु (*rajassu*) means उदकेषु (*udakeṣu*), in waters; and in the 7th section of the 12th chapter, in explaining the Ṛk
एता उ त्या उषसः केतुमक्रत पूर्वे अर्धे रजसो भानुमंजते । (*etā u tyā uṣasaḥ ketumakrata pūrve ardhe rajaso bhānumaṃjate |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-92-1)
they have interpreted रजसः (*rajasaḥ*) as the firmament.
त्रीणि भांति रजांस्यस्य यत्सदानि तु तेजसा । (*trīṇi bhāṃti rajāṃsyasya yatsadāni tu tejasā |*)

The author of the Bṛhaddevatā, describing Viṣṇu's striding over the three worlds, has used the word रजांसि (*rajāṃsi*) as a synonym of the three worlds. The words रजः (*rajaḥ*) and रजांसि (*rajāṃsi*) in general are synonyms of the word for world. But in the Ṛks
यन्मा सोमासो ममदन्यदुक्कोभे भयेते रजनी अपारे (*yanmā somāso mamadanyadukkobhe bhayete rajanī apāre*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-42-6)
and others, the word is in the dual, and the technical sense of Heaven and Earth is what is stated.

O Maruts, that well-known prowess of yours has spread your greatness far and wide. As in the world the sun spreads his radiance, so do you; and there is a second comparison: as the dappled horses of the gods, in their going, stretch their course a long way, so is your greatness extended. Your lustre is not seized, that is, not held in check; or else this is simply an epithet of the Maruts. O Maruts, being of unseized lustre, you struck down the cloud that holds back the water: the word अनश्वदां (*anaśvadāṃ*) is explained as one who holds the all-pervading water, or else as one who does not give the horses carried off by the Paṇis; the mountain, the cloud, is what you struck down. ⟨NOTE:465⟩
notes: ಸೂರ್ಯ ಉದಿತ ಉದ್ದತೇ ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನೇ: ಉದ್ದತೇ unclear

en: - योजनं न (*yojanaṃ na*)—as he spreads his radiance throughout the universe
- एताः यामे न (*etāḥ yāme na*)—as the horses of the gods pervade everywhere
- अगृभीतशोचिषः (*agṛbhītaśociṣaḥ*)—you who are of unrestrained radiance
- अनश्वदां (*anaśvadāṃ*)—that does not pour out water
- न्ययातन (*nyayātana*)—you have cleft (and poured down rain)

O Maruts, as the sun spreads all his radiance throughout the universe, and as the horses of the gods pervade everywhere in their course, so your well-known prowess has extended and made famous your glory exceedingly wide. You, of unrestrained radiance, by that same greatness have cleft the cloud that does not pour out water, and have poured down rain

Your prowess, Maruts, has spread wide your glory as the sun (sends afar his) radiance, or the white (horses of the gods travel far) in their course : of unbounded lustre, you clove the cloud withholding the waters

मरुतः महित्वनं सूर्यो न योजनं दीर्घं ततान (*marutaḥ mahitvanaṃ sūryo na yojanaṃ dīrghaṃ tatāna*)—As the sun spreads his splendour or light everywhere, so the Marut deities spread their exceedingly great strength and power and their glory most widely, that is, everywhere; thus the seer has compared the sun's splendour, as an illustration, with the range of the strength and power of the Marut deities.

अनश्वदां (*anaśvadāṃ*)—व्यापकोदकादातारं (*vyāpakodakādātāraṃ*). The word aśva, formed from the root अशू व्याप्तौ (*aśū vyāptau*), is used here in the sense of water. आश्वद (*āśvada*) means the cloud that gives water; अनश्वद (*anaśvada*), on the contrary, means the cloud that holds back the water and does not pour it down as rain: this is the meaning specified here.

O Vedhasaḥ, makers of rain, O Maruts, your host shines forth, because you strike the water-laden tree. The tree is the cloud, so called because it is torn open, split. To strike it means to beat it. The word for "like" is without meaning here, so: shaking it. Or else, as worms such as wood-borers gnaw a tree, so you do. The particle स्मेति (*smeti*) is a mere filler; "us" means "me". O you of one accord, of equal affection among yourselves, lead us in due order, as we go toward wealth and the like, along an easy road. The illustration is the eye: as the eye becomes a guide by showing the way, so you do.
- सजोषसः (*sajoṣasaḥ*)—you who rejoice among yourselves with equal affection
- चक्षुरिव (*cakṣuriva*)—as the eye carries its master to the desired place

O Maruts, makers of rain, when you strike the water-laden cloud as if shaking it, then the strength of your host shines forth, manifest. You who rejoice among yourselves with equal affection, lead us on the excellent road that goes to the place of wealth, as the eye (the organ of sight) carries its master to the desired place.

Maruts, dispensers of rain, your strength is manifested when, haking the water-laden cloud, you let loose the shower: conjointly propitiated, conduct us by an easy path leading to prosperity, as the eye (shows the way). ⟨NOTE:466⟩
notes: ಮಧರಾಪುಷಾ ಆಪಃ garbled in the print

en: वृक्षं (*vṛkṣaṃ*)—Here the word vṛkṣa is given the meaning of cloud: वृश्चते विदार्यत इति वृक्षो मेघः (*vṛścate vidāryata iti vṛkṣo meghaḥ*). For the sake of rain, that is, to pour down rain, Indra splits the clouds with his thunderbolt; and the Marut deities (the violently blowing winds) split, that is, scatter, the clouds gathered together in the atmosphere and make the rain fall. Therefore, because they are split for the sake of rain, the clouds are called trees, and the etymological sense of the word vṛkṣa is thus explained with reference to the cloud.
इव (*iva*)—(कसनाइव (*kasanāiva*), चक्षुःइव (*cakṣuḥiva*)) ⟨NOTE:467⟩ The word has two or three meanings:

अथ निपाताः । उच्चावचेष्वर्थेषु निपतंति । अप्युपमार्थेऽपि कर्मोपसंग्रहार्थेऽपि पदपूरणाः । तेषामेते चत्वार उपमार्थे भवंति । इवेति भाषायां च । अन्वध्यायञ्चाग्निरिवेंद्र इवेति ॥ (*atha nipātāḥ | uccāvaceṣvartheṣu nipataṃti | apyupamārthe 'pi karmopasaṃgrahārthe 'pi padapūraṇāḥ | teṣāmete catvāra upamārthe bhavaṃti | iveti bhāṣāyāṃ ca | anvadhyāyañcāgniriveṃdra iveti ‖*) (3 1-4) ⟨NOTE:468⟩

Thus Yāska has given the explanation. Beginning with "now we shall explain the nature of the words called nipāta", and answering the question what nipātas are: certain words or letters, upasargas or indeclinables, that join with nouns and verbs, that is, with the subanta and tiṅanta words denoting agent and action, and produce many meanings, are called nipātas. Because they are used in many kinds of meanings (अनेकप्रकारेष्टर्थेषु निपतंतीति निपाताः (*anekaprakāreṣṭartheṣu nipataṃtīti nipātāḥ*)), they are called nipātas.

Of these nipātas, their use in meanings such as "and" and "comparison" is the more frequent. The four given below have the sense of comparison. Among them the word इव (*iva*) is used in the language, that is, in prose sentences not bound by metre or in modern Sanskrit, and also in chandas (the Ṛks). Thus, in अग्निरिव (*agniriva*) and इंद्र इव (*iṃdra iva*) the word is used in the sense of comparison. And it is also seen (इवोऽपि दृश्यते (*ivo 'pi dṛśyate*); sometimes it is without meaning, is the remainder of the sentence), as in सुविदुरिव (*suviduriva*), सुविज्ञायेतॆ इव (*suvijñāyetè iva*). In some contexts the word is used merely to fill out the sentence, without any specific meaning. In such contexts it has no meaning of any kind. In सुविदुरिव (*suviduriva*) the sense is only "is well known"; the word इव (*iva*) has no meaning.
notes: ಅಂಗೇಷು printed; verse has ಅಂಸೇಷು
ಭಾಷ್ಯ has ನಾಕಂ ಆದಿತ್ಯಂ; Kannada gloss ಅಂತರಿಕ್ಷ

en: O Maruts, whatever seer, a Brāhmaṇa who sees the mantra, or whatever king you rouse and impel to good works, that seer or king is not overcome, not defeated by others; जि जये ज्या वयोहानावित्यस्य (*ji jaye jyā vayohānāvityasya*): he refers to the root for conquering, or this is a form of the root for decay of life. O Maruts, he is not slain, not harmed; he is not violently separated from his life-breaths. He does not decay, does not waste away. He is not pained, not afflicted. He is not injured; here injury means mere hindrance. His riches do not fall away, and likewise his protections do not fall away.
- न जीयते (*na jīyate*)—is not overcome by anyone
- न प्रेधति (*na predhati*)—does not suffer decay ⟨NOTE:469⟩
- न उप दस्यंति (*na upa dasyaṃti*)—do not decay
notes: ಅತಿ ತ್ವಿಷ್ಟಂತ printed; verse has ಅತಿತ್ವಿಷಂತ; "(ಹುತ್ತು)" printed

en: O Maruts, whatever seer or king you impel to good works, he is not overcome by anyone. He is not slain. He does not suffer decay. He is not afflicted. He is not injured. His riches do not decay. His protections also do not fail.
The sage, or the sovereign, whom you, Maruts, direct, is never overcome nor slain: he perishes not, nor suffers pain, nor undergoes injury, nor are his riches or his safety imperilled.

In the Kārīrī alone, the verse नियुत्वंत इत्येषा (*niyutvaṃta ityeṣā*) is the yājyā of the third piṇḍī. ⟨NOTE:470⟩ It is also stated in the sūtra: नियुत्वंतो ग्रामजितो यथा नरोऽर्यमणो न मरुतः कवंधिनः । पिन्वंत्युत्सं यदिनासो अस्वरन्‌व्यंदंति पृथिवीं मध्यो अंधसा ॥ ८ ॥ नियुत्वंतः । ग्रामजितः । यथा । नरः । अर्यमणः । न । मरुतः । कवंधिनः । पिन्वंति । उत्सं । यत् । इनासः । अस्वरन् । वि । उंदंति । पृथिवीं । मध्यः । अंधसा ॥ ८ ॥ कारीर्यामेव तृतीयस्याः पिंड्या याज्या नियुत्वंत इत्येषा । सूत्रितं च । नियुत्वंतो ग्रामजितो यथा नरोऽग्ने बाधस्व वि मृधो वि दुर्गहा । (*niyutvaṃto grāmajito yathā naro 'ryamaṇo na marutaḥ kavaṃdhinaḥ | pinvaṃtyutsaṃ yadināso asvaranvyaṃdaṃti pṛthivīṃ madhyo aṃdhasā ‖ 8 ‖ niyutvaṃtaḥ | grāmajitaḥ | yathā | naraḥ | aryamaṇaḥ | na | marutaḥ | kavaṃdhinaḥ | pinvaṃti | utsaṃ | yat | ināsaḥ | asvaran | vi | uṃdaṃti | pṛthivīṃ | madhyaḥ | aṃdhasā ‖ 8 ‖ kārīryāmeva tṛtīyasyāḥ piṃḍyā yājyā niyutvaṃta ityeṣā | sūtritaṃ ca | niyutvaṃto grāmajito yathā naro 'gne bādhasva vi mṛdho vi durgahā |*) (Ā. 2-13). The Maruts are possessed of the horses called Niyut, and this word here refers to horses in general; they are those who are strongly yoked, owners of horses. They are conquerors of a multitude, that is, dissolvers of a thing that is a compound whole; they are men in form, leaders, like men who conquer a village. They are like the Ādityas beginning with Aryaman, shining. Such Maruts are water-bearing. When, as lords, they fill the well or any low place, or the cloud, with water, when they sound, and when they moisten the earth with the essence of the sweet water, then they are so. Or else: when they sound, then the lords fill the spring, and then they moisten the earth with the sustenance.
notes: radiancc printed; "radiance"?

en: - नियुत्वंतः (*niyutvaṃtaḥ*)—possessors of the horses called Niyut
- ग्रामजितः (*grāmajitaḥ*)—dissolvers of what is in compound form
- आर्यमणो न (*āryamaṇo na*)—radiant like the Ādityas beginning with Aryaman
notes: abbreviation ಕಾರಕ. ಸಂ. printed

en: The Maruts, who are possessed of the horses called Niyut, dissolvers of what is in compound form, leaders, radiant like the Ādityas beginning with Aryaman, are water-bearing. Those same Maruts, lords of all water, fill places such as wells with water. Sounding, they make the earth drenched with the essence of the water.

Lords of the Niyut steeds, overcomers of multitudes, leaders (of rites), radiant as the Adityas, are the dispensers of water : when sovereign lords, they fill the clouds, and, loud sounding, moisten the earth with sweet (watery) sustenance.

In the third piṇḍa offering of the Kārīrī sacrifice this Ṛk beginning नियुत्वंत (*niyutvaṃta*) is to be recited as the yājyā mantra; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana-śrauta-sūtra नियुत्वंतो ग्रामजितो यथा नरोऽग्ने बाधस्व वि मृधो वि दुर्गहा (*niyutvaṃto grāmajito yathā naro 'gne bādhasva vi mṛdho vi durgahā*) (Ā. 2-13).

नियुत्वंतः (*niyutvaṃtaḥ*)—The word नियुत् (*niyut*) denotes the horse that is the vehicle of the deity Vāyu; in the Nirukta (Ni. 2-28) it is read नियुतो वायोः (*niyuto vāyoḥ*). But in the present Ṛk, since it is an epithet of the word नरः (*naraḥ*), which means a man, the bhāṣyakāra has said अयं शब्दोऽत्राश्वसामान्ये वर्तते । नितरां यवनवंतोऽश्ववंतो जेतारो नर इव मनुष्या इव । (*ayaṃ śabdo 'trāśvasāmānye vartate | nitarāṃ yavanavaṃto 'śvavaṃto jetāro nara iva manuṣyā iva |*). Here this word नियुत् (*niyut*) has the general meaning of horse. नितरां यवनवंतः नियुतः (*nitarāṃ yavanavaṃtaḥ niyutaḥ*): because they have especially, that is swiftly, the nature of going (the nature of running), नियुतः (*niyutaḥ*) means horses; this is the etymological sense of the word. The meaning stated here is: like men who are provided with such horses and are victorious.

आर्यमणः (*āryamaṇaḥ*)—The deity Aryamā is one of the deities called Ādityas, the sons of Aditi. To indicate these Ādityas, or the other deities who are sons of Aditi, the plural of the word अर्यमन् (*aryaman*) is used here.

आदित्यान् विष्णुं सूर्यं ब्रह्माणं च बृहस्पतिं । इंद्रवायू बृहस्पतिं सुहवेह हवामहे । अर्यमणं बृहस्पतमिंद्रं दानाय जोदय । वातं विष्णुं सरस्वतीं सवितारं च वाजिनं ॥ (*ādityān viṣṇuṃ sūryaṃ brahmāṇaṃ ca bṛhaspatiṃ | iṃdravāyū bṛhaspatiṃ suhaveha havāmahe | aryamaṇaṃ bṛhaspatamiṃdraṃ dānāya jodaya | vātaṃ viṣṇuṃ sarasvatīṃ savitāraṃ ca vājinaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-141-3, 4, 5)

In these Ṛks the deities called Ādityas are indicated as the deities Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Brahmā, Bṛhaspati, Indra, Vāyu, Aryamā, Sarasvatī and so on. And on the question who the deities that are sons of Aditi are:

सप्तभिः पुत्रैरदितिः । उपप्रैत्पूर्व्यं युगं । प्रजायै मृत्यवे तत् । परामार्तांडमाभरदिति । ताननुक्रमिष्यामः । मित्रश्च वरुणश्च । धाता चार्यमा च । अगंशश्च भगश्च । इंद्रश्च विवस्वाग्श्चेत्येते । (*saptabhiḥ putrairaditiḥ | upapraitpūrvyaṃ yugaṃ | prajāyai mṛtyave tat | parāmārtāṃḍamābharaditi | tānanukramiṣyāmaḥ | mitraśca varuṇaśca | dhātā cāryamā ca | agaṃśaśca bhagaśca | iṃdraśca vivasvāgścetyete |*) (Tai. Ā. 1-13-2) ⟨NOTE:472⟩

In this sentence of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka it is said that Aditi has eight sons: Mitra, Varuṇa, Dhātā, Aryamā, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Indra and Vivasvān. Either these eight deities or other deities are indicated in the present Ṛk by the word आर्यमणः (*āryamaṇaḥ*).
notes: ಸ್ವಾಮಿನಃ ಕೇ! printed; garbled

en: This earth is for the Maruts, for the sake of the Maruts, prakṛṣṭa, full of wide expanses: the places in it are extensive and wide-spreading. That is, the whole earth is devoted to the Maruts; the meaning is that they pervade all of it. So too heaven becomes full of wide expanses for them as they go forth; it too is for the Maruts' movement. Likewise the paths that belong to the atmosphere, ⟨NOTE:473⟩ are also wide-spreading for the Maruts. The mountains, whether rocks or clouds, are wide-spreading, and the जीरदानवः (*jīradānavaḥ*) are those that give quickly to the Maruts.
notes: ಶಜೋಷಾಃ printed in the verse; ಸಜೋಷಾಃ in the line above

en: - प्रयद्भ्यः (*prayadbhyaḥ*)—for the Maruts, who have excellent movement
- प्रवत्वतीः (*pravatvatīḥ*)—are spread out (for their very movement)

For the easy movement of the Maruts, this earth, the atmosphere, the heavenly world, the mountains, and all the places where the Maruts move, are greatly extending their regions and helping the Maruts.

This wide-extended earth is for the Maruts: the spacious heaven is for the spreading winds; the paths of the firmament are provided (for their course); for them the expanding clouds quickly bestow (their gifts).

O Maruts, of equal strength, leaders of all, when the sun has risen, at midday, you rejoice with Soma, O leaders of the heavenly world; that is, when you wish to drink Soma, then your horses, running, do not slacken at all. ⟨NOTE:474⟩ Immediately then you reach the far end of this road, the path to the place of the gods' sacrifice; you pervade it. Or else: when you rejoice with Soma, then your horses are not slack, and you reach the end of the whole path of the three worlds.
notes: reference printed ೩ ೩೧--೧೯

en: - सूर्य्य उदिते (*sūryya udite*)—when the sun has risen
- मदथ (*madatha*)—when you rejoice with the drinking of Soma, then
- न अह श्रथयंत (*na aha śrathayaṃta*)—do not take rest at all
- अस्य अध्वनः (*asya adhvanaḥ*)—of the road that comes to this sacrificial ground

O Maruts, of combined strength, leaders of the whole universe, as soon as the sun has risen you rejoice with the drinking of Soma. At that time your swift-going horses have no rest whatever. Immediately you traverse fully the road that leads to the sacrificial ground and come here.

Maruts of combined strength, leaders of the universe, guides of heaven, when the sun has risen you rejoice (in the Soma beverage), then your rapid steeds know no relaxation, but quickly you reach the limits of this road (to the sacrifice).

O Maruts, on your shoulders the ऋष्टयः (*ṛṣṭayaḥ*), the weapons, shine (this is to be supplied). On your feet are the खादयः (*khādayaḥ*), anklets. On your breasts are the रुक्मा (*rukmā*), necklaces. In the chariot are the शुभः (*śubhaḥ*), the waters ⟨NOTE:475⟩. The lightnings, blazing with fire, shine in your arms, that is, in your hands. On the heads the हिरण्ययीः (*hiraṇyayīḥ*), golden, शिप्राः (*śiprāḥ*), turbans, are spread out. The word वितता (*vitatā*) is not to be connected with each sentence.
notes: ಶ್ರುಷ್ಟಿಮಂತಂ ॥ ೮೪ ॥ printed; Ṛk number expected ೧೪
ಸಾಮ್ಮಾಂ printed in the bhāṣya; read as ಸಾಮ್ನಾಂ "of the Sāmans"

en: O Maruts, on your arms weapons, on your feet anklets, on your breasts necklaces, in your chariot sweet waters, in your hands lightnings with the radiance of fire, and on your heads tiaras made of gold shine, widely spread.

Lances (gleam), Maruts, upon your shoulders, anklets on your feet, golden cuirasses on your breasts, and pure (waters shine) in your chariots: lightnings blazing with fire glow in your hands, and golden tiaras are towering on your heads

In this Ṛk it is explained in detail on which limbs the Marut deities wear which ornaments. Thus: on the arms they wear weapons called ऋष्टि (*ṛṣṭi*) (spears); on the legs they wear anklets or foot-rings; on the chest they wear necklaces; in the hands they wear lightning (the flash) that shines like fire, or special weapons that gleam like lightning; on the head they wear शिप्राः (*śiprāḥ*), that is, a golden head-covering or the ornament called a tiara; thus the adornments and so on of the Marut deities are described very well.

O Maruts, goers, you set in motion that well-known नाकं (*nākaṃ*), the sun: it is so called because there is no pain in it. Its lustre is not seized, that is, not carried off by the Asuras; it is bright-coloured, white, and you shake the water, the pippala, variously; the verb takes two objects. When the strengths are united, that is, when you become strong, through the oblations given by us, and afterwards become radiant, the person of the verb is changed in both cases. Or else: when the Asuras, with their strengths united, blaze, then you, desiring water, make a far-spread, fear-causing sound, घोषं (*ghoṣaṃ*). Or else the second half is to be explained as about the priest and the sacrificer: when those desiring sacrifice, the sacrificers and the rest, are gathered, their strengths blaze and they sound the stotra spread far, then the connection is that you shake the water.
- अगृभीतशोचिषं (*agṛbhītaśociṣaṃ*)—having a lustre not carried off by enemies
- वि धूनुथ (*vi dhūnutha*)—you set in motion
- ऋतायवः (*ṛtāyavaḥ*)—you who wish to pour water in the form of rain
notes: ಮೇ ಮನು ಸ್ವಭೂತಮಿದ ಮಿದಾನೀಂ: words garbled in the bhāṣya
ಋಷ್ಟರ್ಯ printed; ಋಷ್ಟಯಃ intended?

en: O Maruts, you who move about, set in motion the well-known atmosphere and the water, whose lustre is not carried off by enemies and which is bright and shining. You who wish to pour down water in the form of rain, when you gather your powers together, then, shining exceedingly, you make a far-spread sound.

Maruts, when moving, you agitate the heaven of unchecked radiancc, and (stir) the bright water : when you combine your energies and are shining brilliantly, and when purposing to send down rain, you utter a loud shout. ⟨NOTE:479⟩
notes: Ṛk number not printed after the Saṃhitā block ಅವೃತ್ಸತ॥; sequence gives 2

en: The Nirukta-writers include the word नाक (*nāka*) among six common names and explain their meaning as common: साधारणान्युत्तराणि षट् दिवश्चादित्यस्य च (*sādhāraṇānyuttarāṇi ṣaṭ divaścādityasya ca*), that is, they declare them to be synonyms common to the heavenly world and to the sun (Ni. 2-13). Afterwards, showing the explanation of this word: नाक आदित्यो भवति—नेता रसानां। नेता भासां ज्योतिषां प्रणयः । (*nāka ādityo bhavati—netā rasānāṃ| netā bhāsāṃ jyotiṣāṃ praṇayaḥ |*) (Ni. 2-14): having shown that the name नाक (*nāka*) belongs to the sun, who is the carrier of the sap and the carrier of splendour, as a synonym of the sun, they go on: अथ द्यौः। कमिति सुखनाम तत्पतिषिद्धं प्रतिषिध्येत । (*atha dyauḥ| kamiti sukhanāma tatpatiṣiddhaṃ pratiṣidhyeta |*). The word कं (*kaṃ*) is a synonym for happiness; the absence of happiness is अकं (*akaṃ*), and the absence of that, that is, the absence of the lack of happiness, means that which is free from sorrow. Explaining thus, they cite the sentence न ना अमुं लोकं जग्मु षे किं च नाकं (*na nā amuṃ lokaṃ jagmu ṣe kiṃ ca nākaṃ*) (Kāraka. Saṃ. 21.-2) ⟨NOTE:480⟩ and then न ना अमुं लोकं गतवते किंच नासुखं ; पुण्यकृतो ह्येव तत्र गच्छंति । (*na nā amuṃ lokaṃ gatavate kiṃca nāsukhaṃ ; puṇyakṛto hyeva tatra gacchaṃti |*). Those who have gone to this world (heaven) have no sorrow at all; only the virtuous have entry into this world: thus they have given the meaning of the word नाक (*nāka*). In the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā this word is used in some places as a synonym of the sun and in some places as a synonym of heaven.

त्रिरश्विना सिंधुभिः सप्तमातृभिस्त्रिय आहानास्त्रेधा हविष्कृतं । तिस्रः पृथिवीरुपरि प्रवा दिवो नाकं रक्षेथे द्युभिरक्तुभिर्हितं ॥ (*triraśvinā siṃdhubhiḥ saptamātṛbhistriya āhānāstredhā haviṣkṛtaṃ | tisraḥ pṛthivīrupari pravā divo nākaṃ rakṣethe dyubhiraktubhirhitaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-34-8)
ये नाकस्याधि रोचने दिवि देवास आसते । मरुद्भिरग्न आ गहि ॥ (*ye nākasyādhi rocane divi devāsa āsate | marudbhiragna ā gahi ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-19-6)
In these and other Ṛks the word is a synonym of the sun; and in

तेवर्धंत स्वतवसो महित्वना नाकं तस्थुरुरु चक्रिरे सदः । विष्णुरद्धावद्वृषणं मदच्युतं वयो न सीदन्नधि बर्हिषि प्रिये ॥ ( (*tevardhaṃta svatavaso mahitvanā nākaṃ tasthururu cakrire sadaḥ | viṣṇuraddhāvadvṛṣaṇaṃ madacyutaṃ vayo na sīdannadhi barhiṣi priye ‖ (*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1.85.7)

यज्ञेन यज्ञमयजंत देवास्तानि धर्माणि प्रथमान्यासन् । ते ह नाकं महिमानः सचंत यत्र पूर्वे साध्याः संति देवाः ॥ (*yajñena yajñamayajaṃta devāstāni dharmāṇi prathamānyāsan | te ha nākaṃ mahimānaḥ sacaṃta yatra pūrve sādhyāḥ saṃti devāḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-50)
and other Ṛks it is also a synonym of heaven.
व्यस्यॆव कपिलो भूत्वा यन्नाकमधिरोहति (*vyasyèva kapilo bhūtvā yannākamadhirohati*) (Bṛ. De. 2-66)
In this sentence of the Bṛhaddevatā it is clear that the atmosphere is meant.
इतोऽसावादित्यो द्वाविंशेन परमादित्याज्जयति तन्नाकं तद्विशोकं (*ito 'sāvādityo dvāviṃśena paramādityājjayati tannākaṃ tadviśokaṃ*)
इतोऽसावादित्यो द्वाविंशेन परमादित्याज्जयति तन्नाकं तद्विशोकं (*ito 'sāvādityo dvāviṃśena paramādityājjayati tannākaṃ tadviśokaṃ*) (Chā. U. 2-10-5)
In this sentence of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad it is said that the sorrowless heavenly world is better than the world of the sun.
[In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad the name नाक (*nāka*) is well known for the son of Mudgala, who knew Brahman; there it means one free from sorrow.]

In the present Ṛk, न विद्यते अकं दुःखं तत्साधनं पापं वेति नाको द्युलोकः । (*na vidyate akaṃ duḥkhaṃ tatsādhanaṃ pāpaṃ veti nāko dyulokaḥ |*): the commentator has explained it as the atmosphere, in which there is neither sorrow nor the sin that is its cause.
अच्यंत (*acyaṃta*), अतित्विषंत (*atitviṣaṃta*)—in these two verbs there is a change of person; that is, instead of the plural of the middle person, the plural of the first person is used.

यत् वृजना समच्यंत अतित्विषंत—यदा अस्मद्दत्तैर्हनिर्भिः बलिनो भवथ तदा दीप्ता भवथ । (*yat vṛjanā samacyaṃta atitviṣaṃta—yadā asmaddattairhanirbhiḥ balino bhavatha tadā dīptā bhavatha |*). O Marut deities, when you accept (eat) the oblations and the like that we offer, then, grown strong by accepting the oblations, that is, by their power, shine well: this is one kind of meaning that the commentator has stated, and he has shown that another kind of meaning is possible. यदासुरा वृजना अतित्विषंत तदा घोषं विततु स्वरंति (*yadāsurā vṛjanā atitviṣaṃta tadā ghoṣaṃ vitatu svaraṃti*): when the Asuras, grown strong with the pride of their strength, swagger about, then you (the Marut deities), to subdue them, make a terrible sound: this is another kind of meaning.

Or else, for the second half of this Ṛk, besides these two meanings, another meaning with reference to the priests and sacrificers is possible, and he has explained it also: यत् ऋतायवः समच्यंत वृजन अति त्वषंत च स्वरंति घोषं पिप्पलं विधूनुथ (*yat ṛtāyavaḥ samacyaṃta vṛjana ati tvaṣaṃta ca svaraṃti ghoṣaṃ pippalaṃ vidhūnutha*) and यदा यज्ञकामा यजमानादयो संगताः बलान्यतित्वषंत स्तोत्रं विततं स्वरंति च तदानीं पिप्पलं विधूनुथ । (*yadā yajñakāmā yajamānādayo saṃgatāḥ balānyatitvaṣaṃta stotraṃ vitataṃ svaraṃti ca tadānīṃ pippalaṃ vidhūnutha |*). When people such as the priests and sacrificers, with the wish to perform a sacrifice addressed to you, all assemble together in one place and, reciting stotras and mantras in a loud voice, extend, that is, carry forward, the sacrificial rite, then you, Marut deities, make the excellent water pour down for the satisfaction of the sacrificers: this is the chief intention.
notes: ಉರ್ವಿಯೋರವಃ ಸಂತೋ: words unclear in the bhāṣya

en: O Maruts of manifold wisdom, may we become lords of the wealth given by you, wealth that gives food, we who are owners of chariots. ⟨NOTE:481⟩ The wealth given by you does not fail, does not decay: as the sun, Tiṣya, does not fail from the sky, so grant us among us this wealth, a thousandfold, without measure. Make us delight, O Maruts.
notes: ಸಮುದ್ರವಣಸಾಧನಾತ್: words damaged in the bhāṣya

en: - तिष्यः (*tiṣyaḥ*)—the sun is imperishable, in the same way

O Maruts of manifold wisdom, may we, who are lords of chariots, become lords of the wealth given by you and endowed with food. As the sun in the atmosphere is imperishable, in the same way that wealth given by you does not perish. O Maruts, give us immeasurable wealth and make us rejoice.

May we, who are possessed of chariots, intelligent Maruts, become (proprietors) of wealth, comprising food bestowed by you : of wealth that vanishes not, as Tishya (declines not) from the sky: therefore, Maruts, gratify us with infinite (riches).

अस्मे (*asme*)—The Nirukta-writers explain that the word अस्मे (*asme*), although it has one and the same form in all the case-endings, conveys the sense of each case-ending according to the context, and show the difference in the respective examples:
(1) अस्मे ते बंधुः । वयमित्यर्थः (*asme te baṃdhuḥ | vayamityarthaḥ*)

अस्मे इत्येतत्पदं सर्वविभक्त्यंतं । तस्मादनेकार्थं । एकमेव ह्येतच्छब्दरूपं सप्तस्वपि विभक्त्यर्थेषु वर्तते । प्रकरणादिवशात् तस्य नियमो भवति । (*asme ityetatpadaṃ sarvavibhaktyaṃtaṃ | tasmādanekārthaṃ | ekameva hyetacchabdarūpaṃ saptasvapi vibhaktyartheṣu vartate | prakaraṇādivaśāt tasya niyamo bhavati |*). Thus, for the first case-ending: अस्मे ते बंधुः । वयमित्यर्थः (*asme te baṃdhuḥ | vayamityarthaḥ*). That is, the word अस्मे (*asme*) is used in the sense of all seven case-endings according to the context; that is, according to the context, this word can be said to have the meaning of any one of the seven case-endings. Thus, in the sentence अस्मे ते बंधुः (*asme te baṃdhuḥ*) the word अस्मे (*asme*) has the meaning वयं (*vayaṃ*), "we". This is an example of the sense of the first case-ending.
(2) अस्मे यातं नासत्या सजोषाः । अस्मानित्यर्थः (*asme yātaṃ nāsatyā sajoṣāḥ | asmānityarthaḥ*)
Thus, for the second case-ending: the word अस्मे (*asme*) has the meaning of the second case-ending, अस्मान् (*asmān*), "us". As an example of this meaning they have given the Ṛk

आ श्येनस्य जवसा नूतनेनास्मे यातं नासत्या शजोषाः । हवे हि वामश्विना रातहव्यः शश्वत्तमाया उषसो व्युष्टौ ॥ (*ā śyenasya javasā nūtanenāsme yātaṃ nāsatyā śajoṣāḥ | have hi vāmaśvinā rātahavyaḥ śaśvattamāyā uṣaso vyuṣṭau ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-118-11) ⟨NOTE:482⟩
In this Ṛk the word अस्मे (*asme*) means अस्मान् (*asmān*), "us".
(3) अस्मे समानेभिर्वृषभ पौंस्येभिः । अस्माभिरित्यर्थः (*asme samānebhirvṛṣabha pauṃsyebhiḥ | asmābhirityarthaḥ*)
Thus, for the third case-ending: here अस्मे (*asme*) means अस्माभिः (*asmābhiḥ*), "by us", the sense of the third case-ending. On this point

भूरि चकर्थ युज्येभिरस्मे समानेभिर्वृषभ पौंस्येभिः । भूरीणि हि कृणवामा शविष्ठेंद्र क्रत्वा मरुतो यद्वशाम ॥ (*bhūri cakartha yujyebhirasme samānebhirvṛṣabha pauṃsyebhiḥ | bhūrīṇi hi kṛṇavāmā śaviṣṭheṃdra kratvā maruto yadvaśāma ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-165-7)
this Ṛk has been given as the example. Here अस्मे (*asme*) means अस्माभिः (*asmābhiḥ*), "by us".
(4) अस्मे प्रयंधि मघवन्नृजीषिन् । अस्मभ्यमित्यर्थः (*asme prayaṃdhi maghavannṛjīṣin | asmabhyamityarthaḥ*)
Thus, for the fourth case-ending: here अस्मे (*asme*) means अस्मभ्यं (*asmabhyaṃ*), "for us", the sense of the fourth case-ending, is the example.

अस्मे प्र यंधि मघवन्नृजीषिन्निंद्र रायो विश्ववारस्य भूरेः । अस्मे शतं शरदो जीवसे धा अस्मे वीराञ्श्वत इंद्र शिप्रिन् ॥ (*asme pra yaṃdhi maghavannṛjīṣinniṃdra rāyo viśvavārasya bhūreḥ | asme śataṃ śarado jīvase dhā asme vīrāñśvata iṃdra śiprin ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-36-10)
In the words अस्मे (*asme*) of this Ṛk the sense is अस्मभ्यं (*asmabhyaṃ*), "for us", the fourth case-ending.
(5) अस्मे आराच्चिद्देषः सनुतर्युयोतु । अस्मदित्यर्थः (*asme ārācciddeṣaḥ sanutaryuyotu | asmadityarthaḥ*)
Thus, for the fifth case-ending: here अस्मे (*asme*) means अस्मत् (*asmat*), "from our side". The example:

तस्य वयं सुमता यज्ञियस्यापि भद्रे सौमनसे स्याम । स सुत्रामा स्वना इंद्रो अस्मे आराच्चिद्द्वेषः सनुतर्युयोतु ॥ (*tasya vayaṃ sumatā yajñiyasyāpi bhadre saumanase syāma | sa sutrāmā svanā iṃdro asme ārācciddveṣaḥ sanutaryuyotu ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-47-13)
In this Ṛk the word अस्मे (*asme*) has the sense of the fifth case-ending, अस्मत् (*asmat*), "from our side".
(6) ऊर्व इव पप्रथे कामो अस्मे ! अस्माकमित्यर्थः (*ūrva iva paprathe kāmo asme ! asmākamityarthaḥ*)
Thus, for the sixth case-ending: here अस्मे (*asme*) means अस्माकं (*asmākaṃ*), "to us". To explain this meaning:

आ नो भर भगमिंद्र द्युमंतं नि ते देष्णस्य धीमहि प्ररेके । ऊर्व इव पप्रथे कामो अस्मे तमा पृण वसुपते वसूनां ॥ (*ā no bhara bhagamiṃdra dyumaṃtaṃ ni te deṣṇasya dhīmahi prareke | ūrva iva paprathe kāmo asme tamā pṛṇa vasupate vasūnāṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3 31--19) ⟨NOTE:483⟩
In this Ṛk the word अस्मे (*asme*) has the sense of the sixth case-ending, अस्माकं (*asmākaṃ*), "our, to us".
(7) अस्मे धत्त वसवो वसूनि । अस्मास्वित्यर्थः (*asme dhatta vasavo vasūni | asmāsvityarthaḥ*)
Thus, for the seventh case-ending: here अस्मे (*asme*) means "in us". The example:
अग्ने वाजस्य गोमत ईशानः सहसो यहो ! अस्मे धेहि जातवेदो महि श्रवः ॥ (*agne vājasya gomata īśānaḥ sahaso yaho ! asme dhehi jātavedo mahi śravaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-69-4) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-79-4)
In this Ṛk the word अस्मे (*asme*) has the sense of the seventh case-ending, अस्मासु (*asmāsu*), "in us".
notes: ಭರಹೂತ್ printed; machine-read misprint?
ರಯಾಣಾಂ printed; Saṃhitā has ರಯೀಣಾಂ
ಹೇ ಅಗ್ನೇ ... ನಾ ಗಣಂ: ನಾ unclear; the Agni address and the verb ಆ ಹ್ವಯೇ supplied as read

en: O Maruts, you bestow wealth, that is, wealth accompanied by enviable heroes, namely sons, servants and the like; the verb धत्थ (*dhattha*) here means "you give". O Maruts, you protect the sage who is a सामविप्रं (*sāmavipraṃ*): either one who variously impels the Sāman, or one whose learned men (vipras) are accompanied by the Sāman. ⟨NOTE:485⟩ You give a horse and food to Bharata, that is, to Śyāvāśva, who bears the gods. O Maruts, you also grant a king, that is, a resplendent one or a master, who is endowed with happiness (श्रुष्टिमंतं (*śruṣṭimaṃtaṃ*)); the meaning is a son.
notes: ಚಿತ್ತೂರಣಃ ಅವಾವಸ್ತಾತ್ damaged; the sense of ಚಿತ್ ಅವ left unsettled

en: - स्पार्हवीरं (*spārhavīraṃ*)—enviable heroic sons and the like
- सामविप्रं (*sāmavipraṃ*)—who praises, knowing the nature of the Sāma mantras
- भरताय (*bharatāya*)—to me, who bear the gods
- श्रुष्टिमंतं (*śruṣṭimaṃtaṃ*)—you make him endowed with prosperity and happiness

O Maruts, you give wealth and enviable heroic sons and the like. You protect the sage who praises, knowing the nature of the Sāma mantras. To me, who bear the gods, you give a horse and food. You make the king endowed with prosperity and happiness.
You bestow, Maruts, wealth and enviable posterity: you protect the sage learned in the Sama: you grant horses and food to (me) the ministrant priest; you render a prince prosperous.

In this Ṛk, which is the conclusion of the sūkta, and in the next Ṛk, the seer Śyāvāśva prays to the Marut deities to grant wealth, horses, food and other nourishment, sons, grandsons and the like, and long life, so that he may live up to a hundred years.

O you who are सद्यऊतयः (*sadyaūtayaḥ*), that is, whose protection comes at that very moment, or whose coming is immediate: from you we ask that wealth, by which we may extend our sons, servants and the rest, as the sun extends his rays. O Maruts, desire well this praise now being made by me ⟨NOTE:486⟩; by the strength of this praise we may pass a hundred winters, that is, live a hundred years.
notes: ಪಿಷಮ್ printed; Saṃhitā has ಪಿಷ್ಟಂ

en: - सद्यऊतयः (*sadyaūtayaḥ*)—O Maruts, who give protection at once
- स्वर्ण (*svarṇa*)—as the sun spreads out his rays
- नृन् (*nṛn*)—our sons and the rest of our progeny
- अभि (*abhi*) ततनाम (*tatanāma*)—we may extend and increase

O Maruts, who give protection as soon as you are prayed to, I ask of you that wealth by whose help we may extend and increase our sons and the rest of our progeny, as the sun spreads out his rays. O Maruts, desire exceedingly this praise made by me, by the strength of which we may live a hundred years.

Therefore do I solicit wealth of you, who are prompt to grant protection, whereby we may multiply our descendants, as the sun (spreads wide his rays): be propitiated, Maruts, by this my praise, by the efficacy whereof may we pass over a hundred winters.

तदानीमेव रक्षा येषां ते तादृशाः । सद्योगमना ना (*tadānīmeva rakṣā yeṣāṃ te tādṛśāḥ | sadyogamanā nā*) (on सद्यऊतयः (*sadyaūtayaḥ*)). The word सद्यऊतयः (*sadyaūtayaḥ*) suggests two meanings: that you should give us your protection at once, immediately; or that you should come to this place of sacrifice at once.

येन धनेन अस्मत्पुत्रभृत्यादीन् आदित्यरशीनिव ततनाम (*yena dhanena asmatputrabhṛtyādīn ādityaraśīniva tatanāma*). What is expressed here is the hope: just as the sun spreads his rays widely, so by the wealth and other gifts that the Marut deities give us, may we increase and extend our line of sons, grandsons and so on.

स्तोत्रवचसः बलेन वयं शतसंख्याकान् हेमंतान् शतसंवत्सरं जीवेमेत्यर्थः । (*stotravacasaḥ balena vayaṃ śatasaṃkhyākān hemaṃtān śatasaṃvatsaraṃ jīvemetyarthaḥ |*). The seer prays that, by the power of the hymns we recite addressed to the Marut deities, we may live up to a hundred years. The word हिमाः (*himāḥ*) means Hemanta, the Hemanta seasons. The Hemanta season comes only once in a

year, and therefore शतं हिमाः (*śataṃ himāḥ*) means a hundred years. In the same way the use of the words शरदः शतं (*śaradaḥ śataṃ*) also indicates the sense of a hundred years. Such usages are especially frequent in the Ṛgveda.

The Maruts are प्रयज्यवः (*prayajyavaḥ*), eminent sacrificers, and भ्राजदृष्टयः (*bhrājadṛṣṭayaḥ*), having shining weapons. They bear abundant वयः (*vayaḥ*), which is either the youthful age that is their mark or abundant food. They are रुक्ष्मवक्षसः (*rukṣmavakṣasaḥ*), having necklaces spread over their chests. Those Maruts are brought by swift horses that can be easily controlled, and they come splendidly. Or else: aiming at the water, the chariots of the Maruts as they go also follow them.
- सुयमेभिः (*suyamebhiḥ*)—capable of bearing them with ease

The Maruts, eminent sacrificers, having shining weapons and necklaces on their chests, possess abundant food. They are brought by swift-moving horses that are capable of bearing them with ease. As bringers of well-being, they go, and their chariots also follow them.
The adorable Maruts, armed with bright lances and cuirassed with golden breast-plates, enjoy vigorous existence: may the cars of the quick-moving (Maruts) arrive for our good.

भ्राजदृष्टयः (*bhrājadṛṣṭayaḥ*)—भ्राजत् ऋष्टर्य (*bhrājat ṛṣṭarya*) ⟨NOTE:487⟩. ऋष्टि (*ṛṣṭi*) is a particular weapon of the Marut deities. It is said to be sharp, shining and spear-shaped. The meaning of the word भ्राजदृष्टयः (*bhrājadṛṣṭayaḥ*) is those who bear such shining weapons. The use of this word in describing the qualities of the Marut deities is special to them, and it indicates their distinction. This word is not much used of the other deities.

बृहत् (*bṛhat*) वयः (*vayaḥ*)—The commentator gives two kinds of meaning for these words. बृहत् (*bṛhat*) means large, much, abundant. If वयः (*vayaḥ*) is taken to mean food (Ni. 3-9), the sense is that they have abundant wealth of food, or that they give abundant food and other sustenance to the sacrificers who praise them. If वयः (*vayaḥ*) is taken to mean age, then बृहत् (*bṛhat*) means greater, and वयः (*vayaḥ*) means having age; that is, not young children but those who are like young men, endowed with the marks of youth; this is the intended sense.

रुक्मवक्षसः (*rukmavakṣasaḥ*)—Like the word भ्राजदृष्टयः (*bhrājadṛṣṭayaḥ*), the word रुक्मवक्षसः (*rukmavakṣasaḥ*) also is used only of the Marut deities. It too describes their distinction. The meaning is those who wear golden necklaces and other ornaments on their chests.

सुयमेभिः आशुभिः अश्वैः ईयंते (*suyamebhiḥ āśubhiḥ aśvaiḥ īyaṃte*)—The word सुयमेभिः (*suyamebhiḥ*) means horses that have the strength to carry the Marut deities easily, that is, without difficulty or effort. Or the meaning may be given as having easy control, that is, "Well-Controlled", subject to the charioteer's hold. The word आशुभिः (*āśubhiḥ*) means able to run swiftly. Therefore the chief meaning of this sentence is that these Marut deities are carried by their chariot horses, which bear the load easily and go quickly.

शुभं यातां रथाः अनु आवृत्सत (*śubhaṃ yātāṃ rathāḥ anu āvṛtsata*)—The chariots of the Marut deities, which travel happily, follow them. That is, the chariots carry them, according to their wish, to wherever the Marut deities desire to go. Or for the word शुभं (*śubhaṃ*) the sense water

is taken (Ni. 2.24), then the sense can also be given that the chariots of the Maruts, going toward the clouds for the sake of water, carry them there. It is well known that the chariot of the Maruts is made of water. The last pāda of this Ṛk, शुभं यातामनु रथा अवृत्सत (*śubhaṃ yātāmanu rathā avṛtsata*), is repeated again and again, like a refrain, as the last pāda in all the Ṛks of this sūkta.
notes: reference (೨. ೧-೯) printed; abbreviation ೨. not in list, Nirukta?
