en: O Maruts, on your shoulders special weapons, the spears, are placed, that is, rest; the word "placed", which is to be mentioned later, must be changed in form to fit, and the word "upon" only repeats the sense of the locative. Likewise in your arms there is a force that overpowers enemies; the word for vigour is the name of the eighth bodily element, and strength in that form is placed there. On your heads golden things, turbans of silk and the like, are placed. In your chariots weapons, instruments of battle, are placed. Your splendour, your lustre, is spread over your bodies, that is, rests upon them.
- नृम्मा (*nṛmmā*)—attractive turbans and the like shine
- तनूषु अधि (*tanūṣu adhi*)—also on the limbs of the body

O Maruts, spears shine upon your shoulders. In your arms the vigour and strength that can face the enemy are placed. Attractive turbans and the like shine on your heads. In your chariots there are weapons, and on all your limbs splendour pervades and shines.

Lances rest, Maruts, upon your shoulders; strength (of) foe-destroy ing powor is seated in your arms; golden (tiaras) are on your heads weapons are placed in your chariots, all glory is assembled in your limbs.⟨NOTE:528⟩
notes: printed English "eonferred" for conferred; no closing full stop

en: In this Ṛk the ornaments worn by the Maruts and their special weapons are described. Likewise, in the Ṛk

अंसेषु व ऋष्टयः पत्सु खादयो वक्षःसु रुक्मा मरुतो रथे शुभः । अग्निभ्राजसो विद्युतो गभस्योः शिप्राः शीर्षसु वितता हिरण्ययाः ॥ (*aṃseṣu va ṛṣṭayaḥ patsu khādayo vakṣaḥsu rukmā maruto rathe śubhaḥ | agnibhrājaso vidyuto gabhasyoḥ śiprāḥ śīrṣasu vitatā hiraṇyayāḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-24-11)⟨NOTE:529⟩
the description is, with a little more or less, the same as that of the present Ṛk.
notes: ಮರುತೋ ನಾ—ನೇತೃಗಳಾದ: the last Sanskrit word ನಾ is glued to the Kannada and not quoted

en: O Maruts, give us wealth, food, accompanied by cattle, that is, furnished with many cows, with horses, that is, furnished with many horses, with chariots, with good sons, that is, furnished with excellent sons, and with gold. The verb is given in the singular by a change of number; or else it is the perfect in the sense of the imperative, second person plural. O sons of Rudra, Maruts, make for us praise, that is, prosperity. May I partake of your own protection, which is divine, that is, fit for gods.
- सुवीरं (*suvīraṃ*)—filled with excellent sons and the like
notes: ಉಲ್ಲೇಖ ೨ ೧೨-೧೩ printed without the name of the work

en: O Maruts, give us wealth that is accompanied by cows, distinguished by horses, furnished with chariots, filled with excellent sons and the like, and rich in gold. O Maruts, sons of Rudra, create for us prosperity of a special kind. Grant that we may always enjoy your worshipful protection.
Maruts, bestow upon us affluence, comprehending cattle,horses, cars, treasure, and male descendants ; sons of Rudra, grant us distinction : may I ever enjoy your divine protection.
In this Ṛk, which is the conclusion of the sūkta, and in the next Ṛk also, the seer Śyāvāśva has prayed to the Maruts to give wealth in the form of cows and the like.

गोमत् अश्वावत्, रथवत्, सुवीरं चंद्रवत् राधः (*gomat aśvāvat, rathavat, suvīraṃ caṃdravat rādhaḥ*)—When the seer Śyāvāśva prays to the Maruts to give him the things he needs, he has prayed that they give राधः (*rādhaḥ*), wealth or riches. In what form that wealth should be, he has explained in the same place. He has asked that they give cows, horses, chariots, good sons and wealth in the form of gold, all of these. Wealth does not mean only property. That animal wealth such as cows and horses has been counted as wealth from ancient times is the established custom. The custom of calling wealth any thing that people need most urgently has come down from earlier times. In the Ṛgveda also it is just so.

O leaders, Maruts, make us happy; or else be happy for our good. O you of abundant wealth, immortal, that is, of a nature not subject to death, knowers of water or of sacrifice, that is, doers of it.⟨NOTE:531⟩ Renowned for truth, that is, famed for the truth of the fruit of what you do; wise; ever young; of abundant praises; and, being served with oblations in great measure, or sprinkling water: such as you are, be gracious to us.
notes: ಋ. ಸಂ. ೫-೮,೨ reference does not fit the verse

en: - उक्षमाणाः (*ukṣamāṇāḥ*)—those to whom oblations are offered

O Maruts, who possess abundant wealth, who are free from death, who know the truth, who have true fame, who are wise, ever young, worthy of abundant praises, to whom oblations are offered in great measure, and who are leaders: make us happy.

Ho, Maruts, leaders (of rites), be propitious to us, you who are infinitely opulent, immortal, shedders of rain, renowned for truth, wise, young, greatly glorified and worshipped with copious oblations.

हये (*haye*)—The word हये (*haye*) is used in the vocative sense like the word हे (*he*). Therefore here हये मरुतः (*haye marutaḥ*) means हे मरुतः (*he marutaḥ*), that is, O Maruts. The word हये (*haye*) occurs in
हये देवा यूयमिदापयः स्थ ते मृळत नाधमानाय मह्यं । (*haye devā yūyamidāpayaḥ stha te mṛḷata nādhamānāya mahyaṃ |*) (Mṛ. Saṃ. 2-29-4)⟨NOTE:532⟩
हये नरो मरुतो मृळता नस्तु वीमघासो अमृता ऋतज्ञाः । (*haye naro maruto mṛḷatā nastu vīmaghāso amṛtā ṛtajñāḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5 57-8)⟨NOTE:533⟩
हये जाये मनसा तिष्ठ घोरे वचांसि मिश्रा कृणवावहै नु । (*haye jāye manasā tiṣṭha ghore vacāṃsi miśrā kṛṇavāvahai nu |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-95-1)
and in these three Ṛks only. This word is not used anywhere else in the Ṛgveda. In all three places it is used in the vocative sense of हे (*he*).

en: "Him": that very Mārut host which was praised before, belonging to the Maruts, radiant, I praise today. Of what Maruts? Of the more praiseworthy ones; he notes a change of gender, and says the word means newer or worthy of praise. Of these Maruts, the host: the Maruts are the members that make up the host. What kind are they? Those Maruts who, furnished with swift horses, move along in such a way that they are strong. And they are also lords of the immortal, that is, of water, self-radiant, shining of themselves. I praise the host of those.

Those Maruts who move about with swift horses and with exceeding strength, and who, self-dependent and radiant, are lords of water: of such worshipful Maruts I now praise the luminous and well-known host.
I praise to-day that brilliant company of the adorable Maruts, lords of swift horses, who pass along in strength, who, self-radiant, preside over the ambrosial rain.
उ (*u*)—Concerning the particle उ (*u*) Yāska has spoken thus:

अथाप्युकार एतस्मिन्नेवार्थ उत्तरेण मृषेमे वदंति सत्यमु ते (मे) वदंतीति । अथापि पदपूरण इदमु तदु ॥ (*athāpyukāra etasminnevārtha uttareṇa mṛṣeme vadaṃti satyamu te (me) vadaṃtīti | athāpi padapūraṇa idamu tadu ‖*) (Ni. 1-5)

The particle उ (*u*) is used in the sense of restraint, that is, in a context that indicates mutual opposition. For example, in the sentence मृषेमे वदंति सत्यमु ते (*mṛṣeme vadaṃti satyamu te*), "These speak falsehood; those speak only truth", there are two matters indicating mutual opposition, speaking falsehood and speaking truth. The use of the word उ (*u*) is in a context in which these two are said in comparison with each other. Besides this, the word उ (*u*) is used also for completing a sentence, or a foot of a metre, by adding a syllable that is lacking. In such a context this word has only the sense of "this" or "that", and no other definite meaning. In the sentence तदु प्रयक्षतममस्य कर्म (*tadu prayakṣatamamasya karma*), "that very act of Indra, worthy of worship or praise", when the words that are joined indicate "that very act" or "that itself", the word उ (*u*) merges into the sense of the word for "that"; it has no separate meaning. Therefore the chief intention of the Nirukta statement is that in such a context the word is used for filling out the word. On the use of the word उ (*u*) for filling out the word, the author of the Nirukta has stated another Nirukta passage:

ये प्रवृत्तेऽर्थेऽमिताक्षरेषु ग्रंथेषु वाक्यपूरणा आगच्छंति पदपूरणास्ते मिताक्षरेष्वनर्थकाः कमीमिद्विति । (*ye pravṛtte 'rthe 'mitākṣareṣu graṃtheṣu vākyapūraṇā āgacchaṃti padapūraṇāste mitākṣareṣvanarthakāḥ kamīmidviti |*) (Ni. 1-9)⟨NOTE:535⟩

That is, the particles कं (*kaṃ*), ईं (*īṃ*), इत् (*it*) and उ (*u*) are used in prose works not bound by metre for completing a sentence, and in metres of a fixed number of syllables for completing a foot. It is explained that these need not have a separate definite meaning; thus the use of these words is described.
विचिकित्सार्थीयो भाषायामुभयमन्वध्यायं विचिकित्सार्थीयश्च पदपूरणश्च । (*vicikitsārthīyo bhāṣāyāmubhayamanvadhyāyaṃ vicikitsārthīyaśca padapūraṇaśca |*) (Ni. 1-5)⟨NOTE:536⟩

The word नूनं (*nūnaṃ*) is used in the sense of deliberation in places other than the Vedic verses also. In the Vedic metre he has described it as used both in the sense of deliberation and in the sense of filling out the word.

Durgācārya has explained: विवेकपूर्वको अवधारणाभिप्रायः (*vivekapūrvako avadhāraṇābhiprāyaḥ*). The determining of a matter by discernment, in situations where doubt has arisen, is called deliberation. Sāyaṇa has supported that in the Ṛk न नूनमस्ति (*na nūnamasti*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-170-1), which is given as an example for this word, it is used in the sense of deliberation and also in the sense of determination.

en: The radiant host of the Maruts, the strong one, that has bracelets on its hands, whose work is shaking, that is intelligent, whose given wealth is bestowed: O wise priest, the hotṛ, praise it; this is the connection. O Maruts, causers of happiness, unbounded, that is, unlimited, in greatness: praise them, the leaders of abundant wealth.
- धुनिव्रतं (*dhunivrataṃ*)—whose chief activity is making trees and the like tremble
- दातिवारं (*dātivāraṃ*)—of a nature to give wealth in gift
- तुविराधसः (*tuvirādhasaḥ*)—possessing abundant wealth: praise the host of such Maruts

O wise hotṛ, praise the host of the Maruts, which is radiant, powerful, has hands adorned with bracelets, has as its chief activity the making of trees and the like tremble, is endowed with wisdom, and is of a nature to give wealth in gift. Praise that host of the Maruts, who are makers of happiness and of unmeasured nature by their greatness, who are leaders and possess abundant wealth.

Adore, priest, the resplendent and powerful company, whose arms (are decorated) with bracelets, whose function is the agitation (of the trees), who are wise and by whom wealth is eonferred: they who are bestowers of felicity, whose greatness is unbounded: glorify the opulent leaders (of rites)⟨NOTE:537⟩
notes: ಚಿಕ್ರಿರೇ printed; the Saṃhitā block has ಚಕ್ರಿರೇ

en: गणं (*gaṇaṃ*)—मारुतं गणं (*mārutaṃ gaṇaṃ*). In contexts in which the Maruts are indicated, it is the custom to denote the Maruts, who are accompanied by seven groups, by मारुतं गणं (*mārutaṃ gaṇaṃ*) and मारुतं शर्धः (*mārutaṃ śardhaḥ*). सप्तगणा वै मरुतः (*saptagaṇā vai marutaḥ*): the groups of the Maruts are seven. In each group there are seven Maruts. In all there are forty-nine deities in the seven groups. All of them together are called by the words मारुतं गणं (*mārutaṃ gaṇaṃ*), मारुतं शर्धः (*mārutaṃ śardhaḥ*) or मरुतः (*marutaḥ*). Although in the present Ṛk there is only the word गणं (*gaṇaṃ*), yet because in the previous Ṛk it is मारुतं गणं (*mārutaṃ gaṇaṃ*), it should be understood that here too it is indicated as मारुतं गणं (*mārutaṃ gaṇaṃ*). In the first half of this Ṛk the Maruts are praised collectively by the word गणं (*gaṇaṃ*). In the second half they are praised, as मरुतः (*marutaḥ*), by words ending in the accusative plural, such as नैन् (*nain*). Although there is a change of number, both sentences have the same meaning.

अमिताः (*amitāḥ*)—अपरिच्छिन्नाः । (*aparicchinnāḥ |*) Those who are free from limitation. The intention is that these Maruts never leave one another but always remain together; or, when the words महित्वा अमिताः (*mahitvā amitāḥ*) are construed together, those who excel in greatness, that is, without the difference that one is greater and another smaller in greatness, all are of one and the same, equal kind of greatness.

विप्र (*vipra*)—होतः । (*hotaḥ |*) Here the word विप्र (*vipra*) denotes the hotṛ in the sense of wise. The sacrificer who performs the yajña addresses the hotṛ, who is the chief among the priests, by the word विप्र (*vipra*) and directs him to praise the Maruts, who are endowed with glory.

मायिनं (*māyinaṃ*)—Although the word from which this is formed has several meanings, such as wisdom and stratagem, here it is used in the sense of wisdom. It means possessing wisdom, of much intellect.

धुनिव्रतं (*dhunivrataṃ*)—कंपयितृकर्माणं । (*kaṃpayitṛkarmāṇaṃ |*) The second member of the compound is read among the names of action. From the root धूज् कंपने (*dhūj kaṃpane*) the first member is formed, meaning to shake, to cause to tremble. Because the Maruts, blowing with very great violence as storms, are of a nature to make trees and the like tremble (sway), they are described by this word.

For the word नैन् (*nain*) Sāyaṇa has given two kinds of meaning, नेत्यन् मनुष्यान्यस्मान् मरुतो (*netyan manuṣyānyasmān maruto*)⟨NOTE:538⟩: us, who are leaders, or the Maruts. The qualification मयोभुवः (*mayobhuvaḥ*), "causers of happiness", fits both meanings. If the seer has said it with reference to himself and his family, the meaning is that by the grace of the Maruts powerful happiness was obtained by them. Or, if it is a qualification of मरुतः (*marutaḥ*), it amounts to a description of the natural power of the Maruts. The natural and collective power of the Maruts, and the heroic deeds accomplished by that power, are indicated by the many qualifications such as अमिता महित्वा (*amitā mahitvā*).
सप्त सप्त हि मरुतो गणस्तस्मान्मारुतः सप्तकपालः। (*sapta sapta hi maruto gaṇastasmānmārutaḥ saptakapālaḥ|*) (Śa. Brā. 2-5-1-13)
सप्त सप्त हि मारुतो गणः सर्वमेवैतेन रथं प्रीणाति । (*sapta sapta hi māruto gaṇaḥ sarvamevaitena rathaṃ prīṇāti |*) (Śa. Brā. 5-4-3-17) (Śa. Brā. 5-4-3-17)

From such sentences it is understood that the Maruts always remain in groups, and that in such a group a kind of vitality and strength is natural to them. Therefore the qualification अमिता (*amitā*) is appropriate in the present Ṛk.
नैन् (*nain*) has been explained also as the Maruts, who are leaders and of the nature of subjects. The Maruts are well known as the subjects of the gods.

स एतामैंद्रीं मरुत्वतीमज्ञ पत् । क्षत्रं ना इंद्रो विशो मरुतः क्षत्रं वै विशो निषेद्धा ॥ (*sa etāmaiṃdrīṃ marutvatīmajña pat | kṣatraṃ nā iṃdro viśo marutaḥ kṣatraṃ vai viśo niṣeddhā ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 2-5-2-27)

This meaning is stated in such sentences. Therefore there is propriety in giving to the word नृन् (*nṛn*) also the other meaning, मरुतः (*marutaḥ*). It can be noticed that the word नरः (*naraḥ*) is used as a qualification of the Maruts in many places in the Ṛksaṃhitā itself. For example,

चित्रैरंजिभिर्वपुषे व्यंजते वक्षःसु रुक्मा अधि येतिरे शुभे । अंसेष्वेषां नि मिमृक्षुर्ऋष्टयः साकं जज्जिरे स्वधया दिवो नरः । (*citrairaṃjibhirvapuṣe vyaṃjate vakṣaḥsu rukmā adhi yetire śubhe | aṃseṣveṣāṃ ni mimṛkṣurṛṣṭayaḥ sākaṃ jajjire svadhayā divo naraḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-64-4)

विश्ववेदसो रयिभिः समोकसः संमिश्ला सस्तविषीभिर्विरप्यनः । आस्तार इषुं दधिरे गभस्त्योरनंतशुष्मा वृषखादयो नरः ॥ (*viśvavedaso rayibhiḥ samokasaḥ saṃmiślā sastaviṣībhirvirapyanaḥ | āstāra iṣuṃ dadhire gabhastyoranaṃtaśuṣmā vṛṣakhādayo naraḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-64-10)
In many such Ṛks the word नरः (*naraḥ*) shows the nature of the Maruts; in the same way in the present Ṛk also the word नन् (*nan*) may have the meaning "the Maruts".

en: Those all-pervading Maruts who impel rain, who are the carriers of water, may they come to you today, O priests and sacrificers. Now he turns to direct address: O Maruts, this well-known Agni is kindled, that is, well lit; enjoy this Agni, serve it, O wise ones, O ever-young ones, who are pervading everywhere.
- जुनंति (*junaṃti*)—who urge on and pour down (the rain), such
- आ यंतु (*ā yaṃtu*)—may they graciously come

O priests and sacrificers, may those Maruts who, being all-pervading, urge on and pour down the rain, come to your sacrifice now, bearing waters. O Maruts, wise and ever young, enjoy this Agni which is blazing here.
May the universal Maruts, who urge on the rain, come to you to-day laden with water: Maruts who are wise and young, be pleased by this fire which is kindled for you.

अद्य—इदानीं । अस्मिन् यज्ञे । (*adya—idānīṃ | asmin yajñe |*) "Now", or at the time of this sacrifice that we are performing: that is, an invitation is stated here, "come to this sacrifice that we are performing and enjoy Agni." In this sacrifice of ours Agni is kindled and shining. A prayer is stated that you, the Marut deities, should come through such an Agni to the sacrificial ground to receive the oblations and the rest.

In the first half of this Ṛk the Marut deities are praised with a sentence of the indirect kind, and in the second half with a sentence of the direct kind. Yāska has explained what परोक्षकृत, प्रत्यक्षकृत (*parokṣakṛta, pratyakṣakṛta*) mean, in the following way. Yāska, the great sage and author of the Nirukta, has spoken thus on the interpretation of the Vedic mantras.

तद्यानि नामानि प्राधान्यस्तु तीनां देवतानां तद्दैवतमित्याचक्षते ॥ यत्काम ऋषियस्क्यां देवतायावार्थपत्यमिच्छन्सुतिं प्रयुं (*tadyāni nāmāni prādhānyastu tīnāṃ devatānāṃ taddaivatamityācakṣate ‖ yatkāma ṛṣiyaskyāṃ devatāyāvārthapatyamicchansutiṃ prayuṃ*)

क्ते तद्दैवतः स मंत्रो भवति ॥ (*kte taddaivataḥ sa maṃtro bhavati ‖*) तास्त्रिविधा ऋचः परोक्षकृताः प्रत्यक्षकृता आध्यात्मिकाश्च । तत्र परोक्षकृताः सर्वाभिर्नामविभक्तिभिर्युज्यंतॆ, प्रथमपुरुषैश्चाख्यातस्य ॥ अथ प्रत्यक्षकृता मध्यमपुरुषोपयोगास्त्वमिति चैतेन सर्वनाम्ना ॥ अथाध्यात्मिक्य उत्त मपुरुषयोगा अहमिति चैतेन सर्वनाम्ना॥ परोक्षकृताः प्रत्यक्षकृताश्च मंत्रा भूयिष्ठा अल्पश आध्यात्मिकाः ॥ (*tāstrividhā ṛcaḥ parokṣakṛtāḥ pratyakṣakṛtā ādhyātmikāśca | tatra parokṣakṛtāḥ sarvābhirnāmavibhaktibhiryujyaṃtè, prathamapuruṣaiścākhyātasya ‖ atha pratyakṣakṛtā madhyamapuruṣopayogāstvamiti caitena sarvanāmnā ‖ athādhyātmikya utta mapuruṣayogā ahamiti caitena sarvanāmnā‖ parokṣakṛtāḥ pratyakṣakṛtāśca maṃtrā bhūyiṣṭhā alpaśa ādhyātmikāḥ ‖*) (Nirukta, the section on deities, chapter 7, sections 1-3)

That is, among mantras there are many kinds: the mantra of a deity, the mantra of praise, the mantra of blessing, oath, curse, exposition of some matter, lament, censure, eulogy, दानस्तुति (*dānastuti*) and so on. A deity-mantra is one that describes the greatness of the deities; praise means a hymn, a mantra containing prayers; blessing is a mantra that wishes good; an oath is a vow; a curse is an evil wish; the exposition of some matter is the explanation of a subject or principle; lament is grief; censure is blame; eulogy is praise.

Among the many kinds mentioned above, the Ṛks that are deity-mantras are of three kinds: indirect, direct and personal. The indirect kind: since the deity who is praised is not present before the speaker, the mantras that in praising that deity use third-person nouns and verbs (Third person both in subject and predicate). The direct kind: mantras in which the deity who is praised is imagined as actually present in front, and is addressed and praised with second-person words (Second person) such as "thou" and "thy". The personal kind: mantras that praise by using the first person (First person). Of these three kinds, the two kinds, indirect and direct, are the more numerous, and the personal mantras are only few.

कवयः:—क्रांतदर्शिनः मेधाविनो ना (*kavayaḥ:—krāṃtadarśinaḥ medhāvino nā*) Thus Sāyaṇa has given the meaning of this word. In some other places Sāyaṇa has explained the meaning of this word in two ways: first, following the Veda sentence ये वा अनूचानास्ते कवयः (*ye vā anūcānāste kavayaḥ*), as scholars who have studied the Veda together with its limbs; second, following the Nirukta sentence कविः, मनीषी (*kaviḥ, manīṣī*) (Ni. 3-15), as a wise man. The author of the Nirukta says:
मेधावी कविः क्रांतदर्शनो भवति कवतेर्ना (*medhāvī kaviḥ krāṃtadarśano bhavati kavaternā*) (2 12-13)⟨NOTE:539⟩

Thus the author of the Nirukta has stated the derivation of the word kavi. Derived from the root क्रम् (*kram*) it can mean one possessed of far-reaching vision; or derived from the root कम् (*kam*) it can mean the praiser who is to praise: so the derivation of the Nirukta author explains. What is the nature of a kavi? What is his power? In what nature and power is the word kavi used in the Ṛk-saṃhitā? It is necessary to understand this.

It may be said that the word kavi is useful for conveying the same distinctive nature that the words ऋषि, सुमेध, धीर, रेभ (*ṛṣi, sumedha, dhīra, rebha*) show. One who has the extraordinary and supernatural power of knowing all the doings of past, future and present times is the wise one; he is the seer, and he is the kavi. One who has this power is also fit for the creation of poetry in the form of hymns. Therefore the praiser also has names such as kavi and रेभ (*rebha*). In worldly literature and in treatises on poetics the words kavi and poem likewise stand for a name indicating an extraordinary power of this kind, but it is to be understood, according to the context, that the explanation there differs somewhat from this one. To make known the true nature of the kavi, the author of the Nirukta quotes the Ṛk

विश्वा रूपाणि प्रति मुंचते कविः प्रासावीद्भद्रं द्विपदे चतुष्पदे । नि नाकमख्यत्सविता वरेण्योऽनु प्रयाणमुषसो वि राजति ॥ (*viśvā rūpāṇi prati muṃcate kaviḥ prāsāvīdbhadraṃ dvipade catuṣpade | ni nākamakhyatsavitā vareṇyo 'nu prayāṇamuṣaso vi rājati ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-8,2)⟨NOTE:540⟩

and explains what nature of Savitṛ the word kavi, which is here an epithet of Savitṛ, shows. It is understood that this epithet belongs to Savitṛ because he brings to light all the forms of the world; that is, he has the power by his own might to light up those aspects that lie hidden and are not visible to the eye of the world, and to make them fall within the sight of the world. In this same sense the name kavi is well known also for the praiser, the one who praises. This idea is indicated in the Ṛk of the Ṛk-saṃhitā,

ब्रह्मा कृणोति वरुणो गातुविदं तमीमहे । व्यूर्णोति हृदा मतिं नव्यो जायतामृतं वित्तं मे अस्य रोदसी ॥ (*brahmā kṛṇoti varuṇo gātuvidaṃ tamīmahe | vyūrṇoti hṛdā matiṃ navyo jāyatāmṛtaṃ vittaṃ me asya rodasī ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-105-15)

and likewise in other Ṛks. In this quoted Ṛk Sāyaṇa has explained the word व्यूर्णोति (*vyūrṇoti*) as उच्चारयति, प्रकाशयति (*uccārayati, prakāśayati*). The root ऊर्णु (*ūrṇu*), meaning to cover or to veil, becomes ऊर्णोति (*ūrṇoti*). Here, joined with the prefix vi, it gives the meaning of removal of covering, that is, of taking away the veil,

and the purport is: to make manifest. It is understood from this that the power to create, in the form of making manifest a thought hidden in the mind, and the power to reveal what is hidden by bringing it to light, are the special quality of the kavi or praiser. Therefore the word kavi is an epithet that conveys to both Savitṛ and the praiser the quality they have in common. Explaining this same characteristic and the work of a kavi, the Ṛk-saṃhitā says:

समानं नीळं वृषणो वसानाः सं जग्मिरे महिषा अर्वतीभिः । ऋतस्य पदं कवयो नि पांति गुहा नामानि दधिरे पराणि । (*samānaṃ nīḷaṃ vṛṣaṇo vasānāḥ saṃ jagmire mahiṣā arvatībhiḥ | ṛtasya padaṃ kavayo ni pāṃti guhā nāmāni dadhire parāṇi |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-5-2)

बृहस्पते प्रथमं वाचो अग्रं यत्प्रैरत नामधेयं दधानाः । यदेषां श्रेष्ठं यदरिप्रमासीत्प्रेणा तदेषां निहितं गुहाविः ॥ (*bṛhaspate prathamaṃ vāco agraṃ yatprairata nāmadheyaṃ dadhānāḥ | yadeṣāṃ śreṣṭhaṃ yadaripramāsītpreṇā tadeṣāṃ nihitaṃ guhāviḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-71-1)

This idea is expressed in all such Ṛks. It is described that the kavis, entering the path of the cosmic order, have borne in the most hidden heart the most excellent secret names, and make them manifest so that the world may know. The vision of this kavi too is possible only through the means that has the form of making manifest.

यज्ञेन वाचः पदवीयमायन् तामन्वनिंदन्नृषिसु प्रविष्टां । तामाभृत्या व्यदधुः पुरुत्रा तां सप्त रेभा अभि सं नवंते ॥ (*yajñena vācaḥ padavīyamāyan tāmanvaniṃdannṛṣisu praviṣṭāṃ | tāmābhṛtyā vyadadhuḥ purutrā tāṃ sapta rebhā abhi saṃ navaṃte ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-71-3)

The kavis obtained, by the means that has the form of sacrifice, speech that lay dormant in the seers who see beyond the senses. Afterwards, for the benefit of the people of the world, they taught it to them also. The metres such as the Gāyatrī serve this speech, which is of the nature of the principle of the universe. Thus, in some places the identity, and in others the relation of cause and effect, is shown between creation, which has the form of the manifestation of speech, and the rite, which has the form of sacrifice. The same idea is stated in this way in the Brāhmaṇas, the Śatapatha and others:
आयुरेतज्योतिः प्रविशति य एतमनु ना ब्रूते भक्षयति वा तस्य व्रतचर्या या सृष्टौ ॥ (*āyuretajyotiḥ praviśati ya etamanu nā brūte bhakṣayati vā tasya vratacaryā yā sṛṣṭau ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 14-1-2-26)

Here the identity of the rite accompanied by the utterance of mantras with new creation is stated. In the present Ṛk the word is an epithet that shows the extraordinary quality of the Marut deities, who are endowed with knowledge of matters beyond the senses and are all-knowing. Since this epithet is used in many places, it should be interpreted according to each context.

en: O Maruts, you beget for the sacrificer a son who is a ruler, that is, a lord, shining; an urger of enemies, one who makes them fall away; and विभ्वतष्टं (*vibhvataṣṭaṃ*). Vibhvan is the middle one of the Ṛbhus; he is skilled, and the son made by him is exceedingly handsome. O worshipful ones, you bring forth, that is, produce, such a son. O Maruts, from you there comes a son. What kind of son? मुष्टिहा (*muṣṭihā*): the word "fist" stands for the arm; he is the slayer of enemies by the strength of his own arms. The same is said again: बाहुजूतः (*bāhujūtaḥ*), one whose arm is the impeller of enemies; such a son comes. Likewise, from you comes a son who has good horses, that is, an existing horse or many horses, and who is of excellent valour. That is, such a son is born.
- विभ्वतष्टं (*vibhvataṣṭaṃ*)—made by Vibhvan, such a son
- मुष्टिहा (*muṣṭihā*)—one who destroys enemies with blows of the fist
- बाहुजूतः (*bāhujūtaḥ*)—one who conquers enemies with the strength of his arms, such a son
- सदश्वः (*sadaśvaḥ*)—one who has an excellent horse
- सुवीरः (*suvīraḥ*)—one who has excellent valour, such a son is born

O worshipful Maruts, you cause to be born to the sacrificer a son who is shining, a destroyer of enemies, and made by Vibhvan. O Maruts, by your favour a son is born who destroys enemies by the strength of his fist, wins victory by the strength of his arms, and has an excellent horse and excellent valour.

Adorable Maruts, you cause (a son) to be born to the man (who worships you), a ruler, an over-comer of foes, and modelled by Vibhwan: from you, Maruts comes a valiant descendant, strong-fisted, mighty-armed; from you (he acquires) an excellent steed.

विभ्वतष्टं—विश्वानाम ऋभूणां मध्यमः । स कुशली । तेन निर्मितं । अत्यंतरूपवंतमित्यर्थः। (*vibhvataṣṭaṃ—viśvānāma ṛbhūṇāṃ madhyamaḥ | sa kuśalī | tena nirmitaṃ | atyaṃtarūpavaṃtamityarthaḥ|*) In former times the sage Aṅgiras had a son named Nītimañjarī. In his line the sage Sudhanvan had three sons, Ṛbhu, Vibhu and Vāja. By good works such as the performance of righteous rites and the helping of the gods, they obtained the birth of gods, or became gods, so it is traditionally held. It is the custom to call all three sons of Sudhanvan, Ṛbhu and the others, together by the name of the eldest son, the Ṛbhus. The Vibhu named in the present Ṛk is neither the eldest nor the youngest of these Ṛbhus, but the middle one. Since he is very skilled in the making of things, the son made, or given, by him is renowned as exceedingly handsome. By the use of the word विभ्वतष्टं (*vibhvataṣṭaṃ*) here, the Maruts are prayed to bring forth such a son.

मुष्टिहा, बाहुजूतः—मुष्टिशब्दो बाहूपलक्षकः ॥ स्वभुजबलेनैव हंता शत्रूणां । तदेवोच्यते । बाहुजूतः बाहुः प्रेरकः शत्रूणां यस्य तादृशः पुत्र इति । (*muṣṭihā, bāhujūtaḥ—muṣṭiśabdo bāhūpalakṣakaḥ ‖ svabhujabalenaiva haṃtā śatrūṇāṃ | tadevocyate | bāhujūtaḥ bāhuḥ prerakaḥ śatrūṇāṃ yasya tādṛśaḥ putra iti |*) The word "fist" also means the arm; or else, "fist" is the name for folding the five fingers of the hand inwards and using that hand itself as a weapon. The meaning is a son who has the power to slay enemies by using the fist itself as a weapon, by the strength of his arm alone, without using any kind of weapon. To fight a wrestling bout by blows of the fist alone, without the help of weapons, much sturdiness and strength are needed in the body. In order to pray to the Marut deities to grant such an exceedingly strong and firm-limbed son, the words मुष्टिहा, बाहुजूतः (*muṣṭihā, bāhujūtaḥ*) are used in the present Ṛk.

At the Varuṇa-praghāsa rite, for the Marut offering of curds (āmikṣā), अरा इव (*arā iva*) is the yājyā verse; and the sūtra says: अरा इवेदचरमा अहेवेमं मे वरुण श्रुधि (*arā ivedacaramā ahevemaṃ me varuṇa śrudhi*) (Ā. 2-17). It is also the yājyā verse of the animal-cake offering in the Marut animal sacrifice of the eleven-stake kind⟨NOTE:541⟩; and the sūtra says: अरा इवेदचरमा अहेव या व शर्म शशमानाय संति । (*arā ivedacaramā aheva yā va śarma śaśamānāya saṃti |*) (Ā. 3-7).

अरा इवेत् (*arā ivet*): like the spokes of a chariot wheel; अचरमाः (*acaramāḥ*): not inferior, that is, all alike, born together. अहेवाहानीव (*ahevāhānīva*): like the days; as all days consist of sixty ghaṭikās, so they are equal in the form of seven groups of seven each. By these two examples the absence of any dissimilarity is shown. Being of this nature, they are born forth with their splendours (mahas), that is, they appear in glory. The prefix is repeated to fill out the foot of the verse, and the repeated prefix is a filler. They are अकवा (*akavā*), not small. Or else it is an epithet of महोभिः (*mahobhiḥ*). Pṛśni is the middle speech in the form of a cow, that is, the atmosphere; those who stand as her sons are उपमासः (*upamāsaḥ*), each one like the other, and रभिष्ठाः (*rabhiṣṭhāḥ*), of surpassing speed. Such mighty Maruts, by their own mind, that is, by their own intention of showing favour, संमिमिक्षुः (*saṃmimikṣuḥ*): they pour down rain well.
notes: ಇವತ್ತೊಂಭತ್ತನೆಯ printed for ಐವತ್ತೊಂಭತ್ತನೆಯ

en: - अरा इवेत् (*arā ivet*)—like the spokes of a chariot wheel
- अहेव (*aheva*)—the Maruts, all equal like the days
- प्रप्र जायंते (*prapra jāyaṃte*)—appear together in the same manner
- स्वया मत्या (*svayā matyā*)—by their own self-prompted intention of favour

The Maruts, who like the spokes of a chariot wheel are none inferior to another, and who like the days are all equal, being great appear together in the same manner with their great splendours. The Maruts, who resemble one another, are of excellent speed and are the sons of Pṛśni, pour down rain by their own self-prompted intention of favour.

Like the spokes of a wheel, none (of you) are inferior (to the rest), but equal as days (of like duration): the sons of Prishni are born all alike, none inferior in splendour: rapid in speed, the Maruts, of their own free favour, send down (the rains).

In the rite called वरुणप्रघास (*varuṇapraghāsa*), in the offering made to the deities Āmikṣā and the Maruts, this Ṛk अरा इवेदचरमा (*arā ivedacaramā*) is to be used as the yājyā mantra, as is set out by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, अरा इवेदचरमा अहेवेनुं मे वरुण श्रुधि (*arā ivedacaramā ahevenuṃ me varuṇa śrudhi*) (Ā. 2-17). In the animal sacrifice connected with the eleven-stake Marut rite also, this very Ṛk is to be used as the yājyā mantra in the offering of the animal-cake, as is set out by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra, अरा इवेदचरमा अहेव या वः शर्म शशमानाय संति (*arā ivedacaramā aheva yā vaḥ śarma śaśamānāya saṃti*) (Ā. 3-7).

In this Ṛk two comparisons are given for the point that all the Marut deities are alike. अराइवेत् अचरमाः (*arāivet acaramāḥ*): as the spokes (spokes) of a chariot wheel are all equal, neither more nor less, and all of one kind, so each one of the Marut deities is of one kind. There is no difference whatever among them in form, in quality, in shape, in greatness or in origin. It is fitting that this has been explained by the example of the spokes of a chariot wheel. In the same way the other example, अहेव (*aheva*), is also most fitting. The days are all of one kind. As yesterday, so today; as today, so tomorrow; as tomorrow, so the day after, and so on: every day is of one kind without any difference, whether in brightness,
or in measure. Therefore these two kinds of example suit the Marut deities very well.

स्वया मत्या मरुतः सं मिमिक्षुः—स्वकीयैवानुग्रहबुद्ध्या वृष्टा सम्यक् सिंचंति । (*svayā matyā marutaḥ saṃ mimikṣuḥ—svakīyaivānugrahabuddhyā vṛṣṭā samyak siṃcaṃti |*) These Marut deities pour down rain by their own mind, that is, without the compulsion or prompting of others, by the good intention that they should show favour to the people: this is the meaning.

O Maruts, when you set out with spotted horses, horses called pṛṣat, which are the means of conveyance (the word horse here is a general word for a conveyance, hence the masculine form). So elsewhere also: यदश्वान्सूष्टु पृषतीरयुग्ध्वं (*yadaśvānsūṣṭu pṛṣatīrayugdhvaṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-55-6)⟨NOTE:542⟩; रोहिदश्वोऽजाश्व (*rohidaśvo 'jāśva*) are similar usages in the same case. You set out with chariots yoked with such horses and having firm wheel-rims. Or else: when the Maruts set out together with horses and chariots, then the waters flow forth, the clusters of trees are damaged, that is, broken by the speed. उस्रियः (*usriyaḥ*) are the rays of the sun; Parjanya connected with them, the showerer of the waters, the shining heaven, let him roar downward, let him sound with his face turned down, for the sake of rain.
notes: ಶ್ಯಾವಾತ್ವಸ್ಯಾರ್ಷಂ printed; ಶ್ಯಾವಾಶ್ವ in the Anuvāda

en: - उस्रियः (*usriyaḥ*)—one impelled by the sun's rays
- अवक्रंदतु (*avakraṃdatu*)—let him sound with his face turned down
notes: ನಿಪಾತಭಾಜೌ — sense of the phrase doubtful

en: O Maruts, when you set out with chariots yoked with the horses called pṛṣat and having firm wheel-rims, then the waters flow forth and run, the clusters of trees are damaged. Let Parjanya, impelled by the sun's rays and the maker of rain, shining, make a sound with his face turned down, for the sake of rain.

When, Maruts, you come with stout-axled cars drawn by spotted steeds, then the waters descend, the forests are damaged, and the bright showerer (of the rain), influenced by the solar rays, may emit a downward sound.

In this Ṛk the pouring down of rain is described. When the Marut deities set out seated in their chariots, that is, when the atmosphere is covered with black clouds and the storm wind is blowing with the utmost force, the rain falls from the atmosphere upon the earth and runs in the form of floods. As the wind blows with the utmost speed, the trees shake, and sometimes are overthrown with their roots, and so suffer damage. In such a situation Parjanya, the maker of creation, produces fearful sounds such as thunder and lightning as signs of rain: this description of rain is stated here.

पृषतीभिः अश्वैः— पृषत्संज्ञकैरश्वैर्वाहनसाधनैरश्वैः। अश्वशब्दोऽत्र वाहनसामान्यवचनः । (*pṛṣatībhiḥ aśvaiḥ— pṛṣatsaṃjñakairaśvairvāhanasādhanairaśvaiḥ| aśvaśabdo 'tra vāhanasāmānyavacanaḥ |*) In describing the various vehicles of the deities, Yāska has said पृषत्यो (*pṛṣatyo*): the deer with white spots are themselves the vehicles of the Marut deities (Ni. 2.28).
यदश्यान्नूर्षु पृषतीरयुग्ध्वं हिरण्ययान्यत्या अमुग्धं (*yadaśyānnūrṣu pṛṣatīrayugdhvaṃ hiraṇyayānyatyā amugdhaṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-55-6)

In this Ṛk it is said, "yoke to the chariot your horses called पृषतीः (*pṛṣatīḥ*)." In the present Ṛk there are the two words पृषतीभिः (*pṛṣatībhiḥ*) and अश्वैः (*aśvaiḥ*). If पृषतीभिः (*pṛṣatībhiḥ*) means the vehicles of the Marut deities,

is not the use of the word अश्वैः (*aśvaiḥ*) useless? To this: the commentator has explained the word horse here as a general word for a vehicle. That is, the meaning of these two words is to be understood as the horses (deer) called pṛṣatī that carry the Marut deities.

In the going of these Maruts, the earth became renowned, that is, became fit for conception; चित् (*cit*) is a filler. And those Maruts, as a worldly husband places an embryo in his wife, so placed in the earth their own embryo-like water (शव (*śava*) means water). Because they have yoked to the yoke of the chariot horses swift as the wind⟨NOTE:544⟩, therefore they make rain, which stands in the place of sweat⟨NOTE:545⟩. रुद्रियासो (*rudriyāso*) means the sons of Rudra.
notes: abbreviation ಖ. ಸಂ printed
ಈ ಮಕ್ಕಳಲ್ಲಿ printed; read as ಈ ಋಕ್ಕಿನಲ್ಲಿ

en: - गर्भं इव (*garbhaṃ iva*)—as he places the embryo in his wife (so the Maruts also)
- स्वमित् (*svamit*)—their own, in the form of an embryo
- धुरि (*dhuri*)—to the yoke of the chariot
- आ युयुज्रे (*ā yuyujre*)—have joined and tied
- स्वेदं (*svedaṃ*)—their own, in the form of sweat
notes: ಯೂಯುಂ printed for ಯೂಯಂ

en: At the time of the going of these Maruts the earth becomes fertile. As a worldly husband places an embryo in his wife, the Maruts also have placed in the earth their own water, which is like an embryo. Therefore they have joined and tied their horses, swift as the wind, to the yoke of the chariot. The Maruts, sons of Rudra, pour down their rain, which is like sweat.

On their approach the earth becomes capable of fertility, and they deposit in her water as their germ, as the husband generates the embryo of the child : they have harnessed their horses fleet as the wind: the sons of Rudra have emitted their perspiration, (the rain).

एषां यामन् पृथिवी प्रथिष्टा चित्—मरुतां गमने भूमिः प्रख्याताभवत् । (*eṣāṃ yāman pṛthivī prathiṣṭā cit—marutāṃ gamane bhūmiḥ prakhyātābhavat |*) It is said here that by the coming of the Marut deities the earth became fertile. With the coming of the Marut deities the rain pours down abundantly, the earth becomes wet, and this helps plants and the like to sprout. Therefore the assertion that the coming of the Marut deities is the cause of the earth's fertility is only natural. In this matter the Ṛṣi has here given an example:

भर्तेव गर्भं स्वमिच्छवो धुः—ते च मरुतो लौकिकः पतिः गर्भमिव भार्यायास्तथा भूम्याः स्वमित् स्वभूतं गर्भं गर्भस्थानीयं शव उदकं धुः स्थापितवंतः । (*bharteva garbhaṃ svamicchavo dhuḥ—te ca maruto laukikaḥ patiḥ garbhamiva bhāryāyāstathā bhūmyāḥ svamit svabhūtaṃ garbhaṃ garbhasthānīyaṃ śava udakaṃ dhuḥ sthāpitavaṃtaḥ |*)

The idea stated here is that, as in the ways of the world a husband places an embryo in his wife and from it a son is born, so the Marut deities, by pouring water (rain) on the earth, which stands in the place of the wife, are the cause of the birth of plants and the like.
स्वेदं वर्षं-स्वेदस्थानीयं वृष्टिसंत्यायं (*svedaṃ varṣaṃ-svedasthānīyaṃ vṛṣṭisaṃtyāyaṃ*)⟨NOTE:547⟩ Here the water in the form of rain

is compared to the sweat of the Marut deities. As sweat comes out of a man's body and oozes when he moves about in the sun, so, the Ṛṣi describes, when the Marut deities come, the water in the form of rain pours down upon the earth.
notes: reference printed as సి. ೧-೪ in Telugu script, apparently for ನಿ.; kept as printed

en: O leaders, O Maruts, make us happy; become happy for our good. O you of abundant wealth (तुवीमघासः (*tuvīmaghāsaḥ*)), you immortal ones, of deathless nature, you who know the water or the sacrifice, that is, who accomplish them; renowned for truth, that is, famed for the truth of the fruit you give; wise; ever young; of abundant praises; and, in great measure, served with oblations or sprinkling water: such as you are, make us happy.
- उक्षमाणाः (*ukṣamāṇāḥ*)—those to whom oblations are offered
notes: ಪ್ರಾಯುಧಃ printed for ಪ್ರಯುಧಃ

en: O Maruts, you of abundant wealth, deathless, knowers of the truth, of true fame, wise, ever young, worthy of abundant praises, to whom oblations are offered in great measure, and leaders: make us happy.

Ho, Maruts, leaders (of rites), be propitious to us, you who are infinitely opulent, immortal, shedders of rain, renowned for truth, wise, young, greatly glorified, and worshipped with copious oblations.
हये (*haye*): the word is used in the vocative sense, like the word हे (*he*). Therefore हये मरुतः (*haye marutaḥ*) here means O Maruts, O Marut deities. This word is found only in these three Ṛks:
हये देवा यूयमिदापयः स्थ ते मृळत नाधमानाय मह्यं (*haye devā yūyamidāpayaḥ stha te mṛḷata nādhamānāya mahyaṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-29-4)
हये नरो मरुतो मृळता नस्तुवीमघासो अमृता ऋतज्ञाः (*haye naro maruto mṛḷatā nastuvīmaghāso amṛtā ṛtajñāḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 557-8)⟨NOTE:549⟩
हये जाये मनसा शिष्ठ घोरे वचांसि मिश्रा कृणवावहै नु (*haye jāye manasā śiṣṭha ghore vacāṃsi miśrā kṛṇavāvahai nu*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-95-1)
This word is not used anywhere else in the Ṛgveda. In all three places it is used in the vocative sense of हे (*he*).
notes: Sāyaṇa's words ಆ ಜಿಗಾತನ। ಸರ್ವತಃ ಪ್ರಶಂಸತ ಸಾಧ್ವನುಷ್ಠಿತಮಿತಿ । ಉತ್ತರಾರ್ಧಃ ಪ್ರತ್ಯಕ್ಷಕೃತಃ read as: praise on all sides, saying "well performed"; the latter half is in direct address; construction not certain
ದಕ್ಷಿಣ printed in the bhāṣya for the word glossed by the Kannada as "birds", probably ಪಕ್ಷಿಣ

en: O Maruts, for you, for the giver of oblations, who is well reached, the clear-voiced Hotṛ priest cries out aloud, that is, praises you; or he cries out for the well-reached gift to you. O Hotṛ, to the shining heaven, the deity of heaven, offer praise aloud, O my self. And to the earth I bring the hymn of praise, that is, I accomplish it; since heaven and earth are the support of the Maruts, they too come in as sharers here⟨NOTE:552⟩. Moreover those Maruts sprinkle the pervading hosts of water; they cross the atmosphere on all sides, that is, they roam; they cause their own light to cling together with the clouds, that is, they bring it favourably.
notes: abbreviation ಅ. printed; the bhāṣya has ಆ.

en: - उक्षंते (*ukṣaṃte*)—(the Maruts) cause to pour down
- आ तरुषंते (*ā taruṣaṃte*)—go round and roam

O Maruts, the Hotṛ priest praises you exceedingly for the sake of a gift that he may happily obtain. O Hotṛ, offer exceeding praise to the shining atmosphere. I offer praise addressed to the earth. The Maruts cause the all-pervading waters to pour down. And they go round and roam through the whole atmosphere, uniting their own radiance with the clouds.

The priest glorfies you, Maruts, for the good of the donor of the oblation : offer worsip to the shining (heaven): I bring offerings to the earth : they, the Maruts, scatter the rapid (rain); they traverse the firmment ; they combine their own radiance with (that of) the clouds.
स्पट्—स्पष्ट होता । (*spaṭ—spaṣṭa hotā |*) Since he touches the oblations and the like at the time of the homa, the priest called Hotṛ is here called स्पट् (*spaṭ*).

अश्वान् (*aśvān*): the word aśva, formed from the root अशू व्याप्तौ (*aśū vyāptau*), is explained here as the all-pervading waters. Since when rain falls water spreads everywhere, the all-pervading water is indicated by the word अश्वान् (*aśvān*).
रजः (*rajaḥ*): it is explained here as the atmosphere. The word has many meanings. Yāska, on this word, says:
रजो रज्यतेर्ज्योती रज उच्यते उदकं रज उच्यते । लोका रजांस्युच्यंते । (*rajo rajyaterjyotī raja ucyate udakaṃ raja ucyate | lokā rajāṃsyucyaṃte |*) (Ni. 4-19)
The word रजस् (*rajas*), formed from the root रंज् (*raṃj*) which gives the sense of shining, means light, and water, and also the worlds.
रजांसि चित्रा वि चरंति तन्यवो दिवः सम्राजा पयसा न उक्षतं । (*rajāṃsi citrā vi caraṃti tanyavo divaḥ samrājā payasā na ukṣataṃ |*) (Kha. Saṃ. 5-63-5)⟨NOTE:553⟩
Quoting this Ṛk, the author of the Nirukta has said that रजांसि (*rajāṃsi*) means the worlds; in the 44th section of the 10th chapter of the Nirukta,
अज्जामुक्थैरहिं गृणीषे बुद्धे नदीनां रजस्सु षीदन् (*ajjāmukthairahiṃ gṛṇīṣe buddhe nadīnāṃ rajassu ṣīdan*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-34-16)
in explaining this Ṛk, he says that रजस्सु (*rajassu*) means उदकेषु (*udakeṣu*), that is, in the waters; and in the 7th section of the 12th chapter,
एता उ त्या उषसः केतुमक्रत पूर्वे अर्धे रजसो भानुमंजते । (*etā u tyā uṣasaḥ ketumakrata pūrve ardhe rajaso bhānumaṃjate |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-92-1)
in explaining this Ṛk, he explains रजसः (*rajasaḥ*) as the atmosphere.

श्रीणि भांति रजांस्यस्य यत्पदानि तु तेजसा (*śrīṇi bhāṃti rajāṃsyasya yatpadāni tu tejasā*) so the author of the Bṛhaddevatā, describing Viṣṇu's striding over the three worlds, used the word रजांसि (*rajāṃsi*) as a synonym for the three worlds.
Generally रजः, रजांसि (*rajaḥ, rajāṃsi*) is a word that is a synonym of the worlds. But in Ṛks such as
यन्ना सोमासो ममदन्यदुक्कोभे भयेते रजसी अपारे (*yannā somāso mamadanyadukkobhe bhayete rajasī apāre*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-42-6)
this word is in the dual and only the technical meaning, heaven and earth, is stated. Only in some places, that is, in a couple of Ṛks such as
अहश्च कृष्णमहरर्जुनं च वि वर्तेते रजसी वेद्याभिः (*ahaśca kṛṣṇamahararjunaṃ ca vi vartete rajasī vedyābhiḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-9-1)
the original meaning of the root is primary, as in रजसी जगद्रंजयंतौ (*rajasī jagadraṃjayaṃtau*). In the present Ṛk it means the shining atmosphere.

भानुं (*bhānuṃ*): the word भानु (*bhānu*) is read among the names of the day (2-20). भानु (*bhānu*) has several meanings: the sun, a ray of the sun, light, the day. Here the word is used in the sense of light.
notes: ಶ್ಯಾನಾಶ್ವಃ printed in the bhāṣya

en: Of these Maruts, through fear, the earth trembles, like a boat full of living beings, which, going through the midst of the water, sways and moves, being shaken; both these are epithets of the boat. Those Maruts who, though seen far away, are known by their goings: those great Maruts strive between heaven and earth in the sacrifice, for the great oblation, to eat the oblation. They are leaders: the Maruts.
- दूरेदृशाः (*dūredṛśāḥ*)—even though seen very far away
- अंतः (*aṃtaḥ*)—in the midst of heaven and earth

As a boat full of people trembles and, as it moves forward, is alarmed, so the earth trembles through the fear of these Maruts. The Maruts who, though seen very far away, are exactly known by their individual goings, those Maruts, the leaders, go about and come between heaven and earth to eat the great oblation in the sacrifice.

From their approach the earth trembles with fear, as a crowded boat goes quivering (through the water) : visible from afar, they are recog- nized by their movements : the Maruts, leaders (of rites), pass between (heaven and earth) to the solemn sacrifice.
When the storm wind blows with force, not only do trees and the like tremble and fall uprooted, but rain also falls in torrents, with thunder, lightning, flashes of

lightning, and the like, it appears terrifying. This terrifying sight, the shaking of the earth, the seer describes by the illustration of a boat. If a boat carries more people than it should ordinarily carry, it is struck by the beating of the waves, rocks to and fro, and becomes an occasion of fear as to where it may sink. The people seated in it feel great alarm and fear. When the wind blows violently and pours down rain, such events as rain, wind, thunderbolt, lightning and trees falling uprooted are truly terrifying. It is most fitting that the seer has described this state by the illustration of a boat full of people. In both there is occasion for fear, for alarm and for agitation. Besides, it is also said here that the forewarning of the coming of the Marut deities is known from afar. It is described here that, by the gathering of clouds in the atmosphere, by the swift blowing of the wind and by the lightning flashing from time to time, the sign of the coming of the Marut deities is known from afar, that is, beforehand.

Sāyaṇa addresses the Maruts. You bear, for splendour, an excellent head-ornament such as a turban-band, like the horn of cattle. Like the sun: as the sun, at the dispersal of light, bears the orb that is the means of sight, so you, at the release of rain, bear the light that illuminates everything. Like horses, being swift and everywhere present, you are graceful, pleasing to behold. Like mortals, that is, sacrificers: as they know the sacrifice and the like for their prosperity, so you, O leaders, the Maruts, know it for glory.
- गवां शृंगं इव (*gavāṃ śṛṃgaṃ iva*)—like the horn of cattle
- श्रियसे (*śriyase*)—for the increase of your beauty (you wear them)
- सूरो न (*sūro na*)—as the sun spreads and diffuses the light of his orb (so you also)
- चक्षुः (*cakṣuḥ*)—the light visible to all (you have put on)
- श्रियसे (*śriyase*)—(knowing) that sacrifices and the like bring welfare

O Maruts, you wear excellent turbans and the like, like the horn of cattle, for the increase of your beauty. As the sun spreads and diffuses the light of his orb, so you also have put on, for the release of water, a light visible to all. Swift like horses, you are charming. O Maruts, leaders, like human sacrificers you also have known that sacrifices and the like bring welfare.

You bear for your decoration, an excellent (diadem) like the horn of cattle : as the sun, the eye (of day, dispenses light), so (are you diligent) in the distribution of the rains : graceful are you, and rapid as horses, and, like (pious) mortals, you, leaders (of rites), consider (holy ceremo- nies) for their glory.
In this Ṛk ⟨NOTE:554⟩ four illustrations are stated.

(1) गवामिव शृंगं श्रियसे—हे मरुतः गवां शृंगमिन उत्कृष्टमुष्टीषपटादिकं श्रिये धारयथ । (*gavāmiva śṛṃgaṃ śriyase—he marutaḥ gavāṃ śṛṃgamina utkṛṣṭamuṣṭīṣapaṭādikaṃ śriye dhārayatha |*) As the horns shine on the head of cattle, so you, O Marut deities, shine wearing a head-ornament on your heads. The horn of cattle is given as the illustration in order to describe things worn on the head for adornment.

In the Ṛk अग्निभ्राजसो विद्युतो गभस्तोः शिप्राः शीर्षसु वितता हिरण्ययीः । (*agnibhrājaso vidyuto gabhastoḥ śiprāḥ śīrṣasu vitatā hiraṇyayīḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-54-11) the head-ornaments of the Marut deities are described by the words शिप्राः शीर्षसु (*śiprāḥ śīrṣasu*).

(2) सूर्यो न रजसः विसर्जने चक्षुः—सूर्यो यथा तेजसो विसर्जने चक्षुर्दर्शनसाधनं मंडलं धत्ते तथा मरुतः वृष्टेविसर्जने सर्वस्य प्रकाशकं तेजो धारयथ । (*sūryo na rajasaḥ visarjane cakṣuḥ—sūryo yathā tejaso visarjane cakṣurdarśanasādhanaṃ maṃḍalaṃ dhatte tathā marutaḥ vṛṣṭevisarjane sarvasya prakāśakaṃ tejo dhārayatha |*) As the sun spreads and diffuses the light (radiance) of his orb so that it is visible to all, so you also, Marut deities, spread your radiance everywhere for the pouring of rain. That the sun's radiance spreads and diffuses everywhere is within the experience of all. In the same way, the radiance of the Marut deities, that is, their lightning, spreads everywhere at the time of rain and is seen by all: this is the main purport of this illustration.

(3) अत्याइव सुभ्वः चारवः— अश्वा इव सुष्टु सर्वत्र भवंतो वेगवंतश्चारवो दर्शनीयाः भवथ । (*atyāiva subhvaḥ cāravaḥ— aśvā iva suṣṭu sarvatra bhavaṃto vegavaṃtaścāravo darśanīyāḥ bhavatha |*) As horses that move swiftly are attractive by their gait, so the Marut deities are attractive to all by their swift movement and their nature of pervading everywhere: this is the main purport. It is the very nature of a horse to move swiftly; the going of the Marut deities is likewise swift. Since swift movement is a common property of horses and Maruts, the Marut deities are here described by comparison with horses.

(4) मर्या इव श्रियसे चेतथ—मर्त्या यजमाना यज्ञादिकं यथा श्रियसे जानंति तद्वच्छ्रिये नेतारो मरुतः चेतथ । (*maryā iva śriyase cetatha—martyā yajamānā yajñādikaṃ yathā śriyase jānaṃti tadvacchriye netāro marutaḥ cetatha |*) As human sacrificers know that sacrifices and other rites are conducive to welfare, so the Marut deities also have obtained this kind of knowledge: this is the meaning stated here.
notes: ಸ್ವಾಯುತ್ತರಕ್ಷಣಂ printed; sense of the gloss doubtful

en: O Maruts, which sacrificer among you, the great and adorable, would attain great and excellent blessings? And who, to that end, would offer your poetic praises, those of the seers? And who your manly deeds? The repetition of the question is for respect. You indeed make the earth tremble like a ray: as a ray is made to move for the sake of rain, so you make the earth tremble. Since you bring forth rain abundantly for the giving of wealth that is well to be obtained, or of water, therefore the meaning is: who else does thus?
- उदश्ववत् (*udaśvavat*)—can make it still more glorious
- काव्या (*kāvyā*)—can offer praise in poetic form
- पौंस्या (*pauṃsyā*)—can know and praise your valour
- किरणं न (*kiraṇaṃ na*)—as a ray trembles
notes: ಪೂರ್ವಾರ್ಧೇ ಯ ಏವಮಕುರ್ವನ ತೇಷಾಂ ಸ್ತೋಮಮೃಧ್ಯಾಮಿತಿ ಪೂರ್ವತ್ರಾನ್ವಯಃ printed; the clause is damaged; it links the first half with the preceding Ṛk: "may I exalt the praise of those who act thus"

en: O Maruts, which sacrificer can praise well your greatness, you who are adorable? Who can offer poetic praise befitting it? Who indeed can know your valour and extol it? Because, by that greatness of yours, you pour rain to make the earth fruitful and to produce abundance in it, therefore you make the earth tremble as a ray trembles.

Who may exalt the great excellencies of you who are adorable ? who may (offer you fitting) praises ? who (glorify your) manly (deeds) ? for you make the earth tremble like a ray (of light) when you confer the gift (of rain) for (the diffusion of) fertility.

यूयं ह भूमिं किरणं न (*yūyaṃ ha bhūmiṃ kiraṇaṃ na*) Here it is described that you, O Marut deities, make the earth shake as a ray of the sun trembles. Although the ray of the sun appears to tremble, in reality it does not tremble. As that ray passes through the atmosphere it appears to tremble. Therefore the seer here describes the trembling of the earth by the illustration of the trembling of a ray.

In the first half of this Ṛk the power, ability and greatness of the Marut deities are described by way of a question. को महतां वः महांति उत् (*ko mahatāṃ vaḥ mahāṃti ut*) O Marut deities, who can describe the greatness of you who are endowed with great glory? In saying this the seer asks the question in this manner, expecting the answer that no person can describe it; that your greatness is so excessive that it cannot be reached by the power and ability of any person. The questions that follow should be understood to be of the same kind.
Concerning the meaning and use of the word न (*na*) Yāska has spoken thus:

नेति प्रतिषेधार्थीयो भाषायां । उभयमन्वध्यायं । नेंद्रं देवममंसत इति प्रतिषेधार्थीयः पुरस्तादुपचारस्तस्य यत्प्रतिषेधति । दुर्मदासो न सुरायां इत्युपमार्थीयः । उपरिष्टादुपचारस्तस्य येनोपमिमीते ॥ (*neti pratiṣedhārthīyo bhāṣāyāṃ | ubhayamanvadhyāyaṃ | neṃdraṃ devamamaṃsata iti pratiṣedhārthīyaḥ purastādupacārastasya yatpratiṣedhati | durmadāso na surāyāṃ ityupamārthīyaḥ | upariṣṭādupacārastasya yenopamimīte ‖*) (Ni. 1-4)⟨NOTE:556⟩

This he has said. The particle न (*na*) has two kinds of meaning and use. In the language of ordinary usage the word is used only in the sense of prohibition or negation, that is, "not". But in the Chandas, that is, in Vedic sentences, the word न (*na*) is used both in the sense of negation and in the sense of comparison. How? In the sentence नेंद्रं देवममंसत (*neṃdraṃ devamamaṃsata*) "they did not regard Indra as a god", the word न (*na*) is used in the sense of negation (in the sense of "not"). In such a context the word न (*na*) is used before the word that is to be negated. In the example above, since it is Indra that is negated, the word न (*na*) is used before the word Indra, as नेंद्रं (*neṃdraṃ*). Next, in the sentence दुर्मदासो न सुरायां (*durmadāso na surāyāṃ*) "like those who, having drunk liquor in excess, are intoxicated", the word न (*na*) has the meaning "like" and is used in the sense of comparison. In this context the word न (*na*) is placed after the word that denotes the standard of comparison, as in दुर्मदासो न (*durmadāso na*).
notes: ವಿ printed; the Pada has ನಿ

en: These Maruts are swift in going like horses, and shining. They are सबंधवः (*sabaṃdhavaḥ*): the one common kinsman, the binder, of whom Rudra is, is theirs; or they are kinsmen to one another, full of affection. Like warriors, brave fighters, they fight strenuously with their enemies. As mortals grow, so these leaders, who are good promoters of growth or are themselves growing, grow. So, being great, they with their showers vanquish, that is, cover, the eye of the sun, meaning the mass of his light or his orb.
- अरुषासः (*aruṣāsaḥ*)—those of attractive colour and gait
- सबंधवः (*sabaṃdhavaḥ*)—those who have equal affection for one another
- शूरा इव (*śūrā iva*)—like excellent heroic warriors
- प्र युयुधुः (*pra yuyudhuḥ*)—fight exceedingly with enemies
- प्र मिनंति (*pra minaṃti*)—cause to be covered
notes: ಸುದುಘ್ನಾಸುಷ್ಟು in the bhāṣya is a machine-read joining; read as ಸುದುಘಾ ಸುಷ್ಠು; the Pada has ವವೃಧುಃ while the Saṃhitā has ವಾವೃಧುಃ

en: The Maruts, who like excellent horses are of attractive colour and gait, who have equal affection for one another, and who like excellent heroic warriors are skilled in battle, fight exceedingly with their enemies. Like human beings they have attained fullness, and as leaders they increase. They cause the sun's orb of splendour to be hidden by showers.

Resplendent as steeds, of one kindred, they engage in combat like valiant heroes : like (prosperous) men, they, the leaders (of rites), have increased (in power), and cover the eye of the sun with showers.

अश्वा इव-शीघ्रगंतारः (*aśvā iva-śīghragaṃtāraḥ*) Since the speed of the Marut deities is exceedingly great, they are compared to horses of swift gait. शूरा इव प्रायुधः (*śūrā iva prāyudhaḥ*) Like warriors skilled in battle, the Marut deities, skilled in the work of war, fight exceedingly with their enemies. Here "enemies" means

the clouds. Scattering the clouds by their impetuous motion, they make them rain. At the time of rain there are lightning, thunderbolt and thunder. These are the roars that warriors make in battle. This is described here as the war that the Marut deities wage with their enemies.

सबंधवः—समान एक एव बंधुर्बंधको रुद्रो येषां ते तादृशाः । परस्परं बंधवः स्नेहयुक्ता वा । (*sabaṃdhavaḥ—samāna eka eva baṃdhurbaṃdhako rudro yeṣāṃ te tādṛśāḥ | parasparaṃ baṃdhavaḥ snehayuktā vā |*) Since Rudra is the father of every one of these Maruts, they are bound to one another by the tie of brotherhood: this is the meaning. In this kind of relationship there is equality; that is, there is not, as in the relation of father and son, the difference that the father is superior and the son inferior. The meaning is that among the Marut deities there are no distinctions of high and low, one greater and another lesser, but all stand in one and the same relationship. Or it may be said that they are friendly to one another, free from hatred and envy: thus two explanations of the meaning have been given.

सूरस्य चक्षुः वृष्टिभिः प्र मिनंति—सूरस्य तेजस्समूहं मंडलं वा प्रकर्षण हिंसंति आवृण्वंतीत्यर्थः । (*sūrasya cakṣuḥ vṛṣṭibhiḥ pra minaṃti—sūrasya tejassamūhaṃ maṃḍalaṃ vā prakarṣaṇa hiṃsaṃti āvṛṇvaṃtītyarthaḥ |*) By their acts in the form of rain these Marut deities injure the light of the sun or the orb of the sun, that is, they cover it so that the sun is not seen. The meaning is that, since at the time of rain the atmosphere is covered with clouds, the orb of the sun is seen by no one.

Those Maruts are not eldest, not youngest, breakers-forth against their enemies, not middle ones: in every way equal, they grow by their splendour. They are well born by birth, sons of Pṛśni, beneficial to mortals; you come to us from heaven, turned towards us. ⟨NOTE:558⟩ Or else: those who are well born by birth and sons of Pṛśni, those who have come from heaven, O priests, you mortals, come to them; that is, come towards us.
notes: ಪೃತ್ನಿಯೂ printed in the gloss for ಪೃಶ್ನಿಃ

en: - अज्येष्णाः (*ajyeṣṇāḥ*)—though none is older than another
- अकनिष्ठासः (*akaniṣṭhāsaḥ*)—though none is younger than another
- उद्भिदः (*udbhidaḥ*)—(all, with equal strength) destroyers of enemies
- पृश्निमातरः (*pṛśnimātaraḥ*)—those who have Pṛśni for their mother
- मर्याः (*maryāḥ*)—O Maruts, beneficial to human beings

Among the Maruts none is greater than another, none is smaller than another, and none of them has taken a middle position. All are destroyers of enemies by equal strength, and have grown by their own individual splendour. O Maruts, of excellent birth by nature, having Pṛśni for mother, beneficial to human beings, come to us from the atmosphere.

None of them are older, none younger (than the others) : the destroyers of (foes), none hold a middle (rank), but all excel in glory : honourable by birth, having Prisni for your mother, you, Maruts, favourable to man, come from heaven to our presence.

In ordinary usage, when speaking of brothers, it is the custom to call the one born first the eldest, the one born after him the middle one, and the one born after him the youngest. Thus many differences in age, in qualities and in strength and capacity are commonly seen in the world among those who are brothers. But with the Marut deities it is not so. Since Rudra is father and Pṛśni is mother of them all, they are all related as brothers. Even so, since they were all born at the same time, there is among them no distinction that one is eldest, another middle and another youngest. All are of the same age, of the same qualities, of the same form and appearance. All grow in one and the same manner: this is the common nature of the Marut deities, and it is clearly set forth in this Ṛk. The seer prays that such Marut deities may come towards us.

The Maruts who, in rows like birds ⟨NOTE:559⟩, fly with their strength all round the ends of heaven, that is, of the atmosphere or of the sun, and of the great, swelling circle of the sky. Their horses make the नभनून् (*nabhanūn*) of the cloud fall: this word is derived from the root meaning "to sound", as in नभ्राडितिवत् (*nabhrāḍitivat*), and means waters. As both gods and men know it: men's knowledge is well known, and the gods know of the rain from the offering of oblations at the Āgrayaṇa and similar rites. The gods' knowledge of the completion of the rain is stated by Āśvalāyana (Ā. 2. 9): beginning with "when one is satisfied with the rain, then one should sacrifice with the Āgrayaṇa", he continues that the gods too say, "surely he is satisfied with the rain, for he sacrifices with the Āgrayaṇa".
notes: ಉತ್ಕಮೇ in the Pada against ಉತ್ತಮೇ in the Saṃhitā

en: - सानुनः (*sānunaḥ*)—of the summit of the sky

Those same Maruts, forming rows like birds, move by their strength through all the border regions of the atmosphere lying round the great circle of the sky. The horses of these Maruts pour down the waters of the cloud, as both gods and men know.

Like birds (that fly) in rows they pass along in their strength above the vast summit (of the sky) to the ends of the firmament : their horses have caused the waters of the cloud to descend, as both (gods and mortals) know.

वयो न (*vayo na*) Concerning the movement of the Marut deities in the atmosphere the seer gives the illustration of birds. As birds of one kind fly in the atmosphere gathered together in row after row,
so the Maruts, who have the same nature, also move in the highest regions of the atmosphere gathered together in rows: thus it is described.

उभये यथा (*ubhaye yathā*) It is said here that both gods and men know that these Marut deities pour down rain. That men who are on the earth know the pouring of rain is natural. But as to how this becomes known to the gods, who dwell in heaven, it is said that they know it from the oblation that sacrificing sacrificers offer to the gods in the Āgrayaṇa and other Iṣṭis. On this subject the great sage Āśvalāyana has spoken thus:

देवानां वृष्टिसंपूर्तिपरिज्ञानमाश्वलायनेनोक्तं—यदा वर्षस्य तृप्तः स्यादथाग्रयणेन यजेतेत्युपक्रम्यापि हि देवा आहुस्तृप्तो नूनं वर्षस्याग्रयणेन यजते । (*devānāṃ vṛṣṭisaṃpūrtiparijñānamāśvalāyanenoktaṃ—yadā varṣasya tṛptaḥ syādathāgrayaṇena yajetetyupakramyāpi hi devā āhustṛpto nūnaṃ varṣasyāgrayaṇena yajate |*) (A. 2.9)⟨NOTE:560⟩

How the gods come to know of the rain is this: after the rain has fallen abundantly, it is the custom for the sacrificer who performs a sacrifice to perform the Iṣṭi called Āgrayaṇa and to offer in it oblations and the like for the gratification of the gods. By this the gods are gratified. Therefore it is explained here that the gods come to know of the pouring of rain that has taken place on the earth through the offering of oblations in the Āgrayaṇa Iṣṭi that the sacrificers perform.
notes: ಉತ್ತಮೇ ಚರಮೇ ನಾ ದಿವಿ and ಮಧ್ಯಮೇ ನಾ ದಿವಿ: ನಾ where ವಾ is expected

en: May heaven, that is, the atmosphere, send down rain for us; that is, may it make the rain favourable. Of what kind is it? Aditi, the undiminished. Or else: may heaven and Aditi, the earth, bring well-being. For what purpose? For origination, or for procreation. May the dawns, of wonderful light and generous gifts, strive together. O seer, the Maruts, praised by you, the sons of Rudra, make the heavenly store, the water of the cloud, to pour down.
- वीतये (*vītaye*)—for our welfare and course of life
- दानुचित्राः (*dānucitrāḥ*)—those who spread lights in many ways
- सं यतंतां (*saṃ yataṃtāṃ*)—let them strive (for our good)
- कोशं (*kośaṃ*)—the water that lies in the cloud
- आ अचुच्यवु: (*ā acucyavu:*)—let them pour down

For our welfare and course of life, may the earth and the atmosphere pour down rain. May the dawns also, which spread lights in many ways and give to the world, strive for our good. O seer, may these Maruts, praised by you and sons of Rudra, pour down the water that is born of the heavenly world and lies in the cloud.

May the heaven and the earth yield (rain) for our sustenance : may the wonderfully bounteous dawns exert themselves (for our good) : may these sons of Rudra, lauded, Rishi, (by you), send down the celestial rain.

In this last Ṛk, which is the conclusion of the hymn, the seer prays to the Marut deities and expresses the wish that the earth, the atmosphere, the goddess Dawn and the Maruts, all of them, may pour down rain upon the earth.

I, Śyāvāśva⟨NOTE:562⟩, praise Agni, the good protector ⟨NOTE:563⟩, with hymns of praise. This hymn is now made; may he, pleased and having come to the sacrifice, take notice of it for us. As by chariots people reach what they desire, so by hymns of praise, which are the means of speed and are sought by those who desire food, I accomplish my desire exceedingly. Going round the fire from left to right, may I promote the praise of the Maruts.
notes: ಉದಾಹರಿಸಿ printed as ದಹರಿಸಿ; the quoted text has ನಾ for ವಾ and ends ಪೃಥಿವೀ without ಃ
ಯುಕ್ವಭಿಃ in the sūtra as quoted, ಋಕ್ವಭಿಃ in the bhāṣya; ಯುಕ್ಕಿನಲ್ಲಿಯೂ for ಋಕ್ಕಿನಲ್ಲಿಯೂ

en: - स्ववसं (*svavasaṃ*)—who gives his protection to all
- प्रसत्तः (*prasattaḥ*)—Agni, who is gracious in mind
- वि चयत् (*vi cayat*)—may he know fully
- रथैः इव (*rathaiḥ iva*)—like chariots that easily carry one to the desired place
- ऋध्यां (*ṛdhyāṃ*)—I make it increase (I compose it in abundance)

I praise with hymns Agni, who gives his protection to all. May Agni, gracious in mind, know fully the rites performed by us at this time of sacrifice. With praises that are like chariots that easily carry one to the desired place, and that seek food, I offer worship. Saluting Agni with circumambulation, I compose praises addressed to the Maruts and extol them exceedingly.

I adore the protecting Agni with hymns: may he, propitiated on this occasion, approve of our acts: I offer (worship with praises), inten- ded to obtain food, as if (proceeding) with cars (to the goal), circumam- bulating (the fire): may I exalt the praise of the Maruts.

रथैरिव प्र भरे वाजयद्भिः- अन्न मिच्छद्भिः स्तोत्रै रथैर्यथाभिमतं प्राप्पुवंति तद्वद्रंहणसाधनैः प्रकर्षेण संपादयाम्यभिमतं । (*rathairiva pra bhare vājayadbhiḥ- anna micchadbhiḥ stotrai rathairyathābhimataṃ prāppuvaṃti tadvadraṃhaṇasādhanaiḥ prakarṣeṇa saṃpādayāmyabhimataṃ |*) As by chariots, which have the nature of gladdening or delighting the mind, we reach what we desire or the places we desire, so, says the seer, by hymns that contain a prayer for food and the like, I praise Agni and the Marut deities and obtain the fruit I desire. That is, travelling in chariots and the like not only brings delight to the mind but we also reach quickly the place to which we must go. In the same way, may Agni and the Marut deities, gratified by the hymns that we make desiring food, grant us food and the like and the accomplishment of what we desire: this prayer is stated here.

The Maruts, sons of Rudra, mount their mares, the vehicles of the Maruts, which are renowned, or tired, in the chariots whose axle-holes are good: the word for sky is the empty space, a hole; they mount the chariots with well-formed axle-holes. O fierce Maruts of impetuous strength, when you ride your chariot, then even the forests bow down in fear of you; the earth too trembles, and the mountain also trembles. The latter half is addressed directly. ⟨NOTE:564⟩
notes: garbled letters in the verses, e.g. ಸುನರ್ಗೃಹಂ, ತದ್ಭಾರ್ರ್ಯಾ, ತತ್ಕೇ ಶ್ರೇತ್ಯತ್ರ

en: - पृषतीषु (*pṛṣatīṣu*)—in those that have horses named Pṛṣat
- वना चित् (*vanā cit*)—even the masses of trees
- वि जिहते (*vi jihate*)⟨NOTE:565⟩—bend (as if indicating humility)
notes: ವೈಧದಶ್ವೀ, ಶ್ವಾನಾಶ್ವ, ಪಂಚಮ್ಯನುಷ್ಟುಪ್ with ಸತೋಬೃಹತೀ as printed; ಪುರುಮೀಳ್ವೋ and ಪುರುಮೀಳ್ಹಾ in the same passage

en: The Maruts, sons of Rudra, mount and sit in the renowned and comfortable chariots, which have horses named Pṛṣat. O Maruts of terrible speed, at that time, through fear of you, the trees bend as if indicating humility. The mountain trembles. The earth too shakes.
Fierce Maruts, sons of Rudra, who ride in easy chariots (drawn by) celebrated steeds, (at your coming) the woods bow down with fear, the earth trembles, and the mountains (shake).

At the time of the coming of the Marut deities, the sons of Rudra (that is, when the storm wind blows violently), trees and the like, struck by the force of the wind, shake and bend. This bending is as if it indicated humility through fear of the Marut deities. The mountain and the earth also seem to shake. Thus it is stated here that the coming of the Marut deities is terrible.

In the Kārīrī Iṣṭi, for the seven-potsherd cake offered to the Maruts, this Ṛk beginning with पर्वतश्चि (*parvataści*) is the yājyā. It is laid down in the sūtra पर्वतश्चिन्महि वृद्धो बिभाय सृजंति रश्मिमोजसा (*parvataścinmahi vṛddho bibhāya sṛjaṃti raśmimojasā*) (Ā. 2. 13). O Maruts, when your fearful sound is heard, even the mountain, though great and grown, is afraid; even the summit, the lofty region, of the atmosphere trembles. When you sport, O Maruts, armed with spears, then you rush together like waters, that is, you go.
- सानुः (*sānuḥ*)—also the lofty region that is like a summit
- ऋष्टिमंतः (*ṛṣṭimaṃtaḥ*)—you who are armed with weapons
- आप इव (*āpa iva*)—like streams of water

O Maruts, even the mountain, which has attained a great form, is afraid at the sound produced at the time of your sport. The very lofty region, like a summit, of the atmosphere trembles. O Maruts, armed with weapons, you go forward gathered together like streams of water.
The mountain, vast and lofty (though it be), is alarmed at your noise, and the summit of the firmament trembles when, lance-armed Maruts, you are sporting: you rush along together like waters.

In the Iṣṭi called Kārīrī, when oblations are offered to the Marut deities with the seven-potsherd cake, this Ṛk पर्वतश्चिन्महि (*parvataścinmahi*) is to be recited as the yājyā mantra; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta-sūtra, पर्वतश्चिन्महि वृद्दो बिभाय सृजंति रश्मिमोजसा (*parvataścinmahi vṛddo bibhāya sṛjaṃti raśmimojasā*) (Ā. 2-13).

In this Ṛk also there is a description of the going of the Marut deities. When the storm wind blows with great force, a certain kind of sound arises. It is the custom to describe this blowing, accompanied by sound, as the sport of the Marut deities:
क्रीळं वः शर्धो मारुतमनर्वाणं रथे शुभं । कण्वा अभि प्र गायत ॥ (*krīḷaṃ vaḥ śardho mārutamanarvāṇaṃ rathe śubhaṃ | kaṇvā abhi pra gāyata ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-37-1)
नित्यं न सूनुं मधु बिभ्रत उप क्रीळंति क्रीळा विदथेषु घृष्टयः । (*nityaṃ na sūnuṃ madhu bibhrata upa krīḷaṃti krīḷā vidatheṣu ghṛṣṭayaḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-166-2)
In Ṛks such as these there is a description that the Marut deities are sporting.

ऋष्टिमंतः मरुतः आप इव सध्रंचः (*ṛṣṭimaṃtaḥ marutaḥ āpa iva sadhraṃcaḥ*) and the verb that follows: when the Marut deities, bearing their weapons, are sporting (or moving), waters flow from various places and

come together and flow in the form of a stream without any obstruction, in the same way the Marut deities gather together and rush forward without any hindrance or obstacle. Not even mountains and the like can check their movement. Not only that, it is described that even though a mountain is very large, it trembles through fear of the Marut deities.

Sāyaṇa explains वरा इव (*varā iva*) as "like young men fit for marriage". Just as wealthy men adorn their own bodies with golden ornaments, that is, special ornaments made of gold, and with waters, so these Maruts too, being wealthy, adorn their own bodies with ornaments that stand in the place of gold, namely lightning, and with waters. "For splendour" means for beauty; the excellent and mighty Maruts, in their chariots, together (or truly), have made great things in their bodies. The meaning is that, furnished with all ornaments and with waters and mounted on their chariots, they bore splendours in their bodies.
- वराः (*varāḥ*)—young men who are ready for marriage
- रथेषु सत्रा (*ratheṣu satrā*)—stationed in their chariots

Just as wealthy young men, ready for marriage, adorn their bodies with golden ornaments and with the help of waters, so the excellent and powerful Maruts, stationed in their chariots, made, or make, many excellent preparations for their adornment.

Like wealthy bridegrooms who have decorated their persons with golden (ornaments) and purifying waters, so the noble and powerful Maruts, associated together in their chariots, have made great(preparation) in their several persons for their embellishment.

In this Ṛk it is described that the Marut deities adorn their bodies with ornaments and the like and with waters, and shine seated in their chariots. Their manner of adorning themselves is compared to that of wealthy bridegrooms. Just as rich and youthful young men, at the time of their marriage, adorn themselves in many ways with golden ornaments and shine seated on vehicles and the like, so the Marut deities too adorn their bodies with ornaments such as lightning and with waters, and shine seated in their chariots. Here the lightning is the special ornament of the Marut deities. The water itself is the means of adornment. Sitting in the chariot is swift movement. That is to say, the wind blowing with great force in the time of rain, with lightning flashing now and then, is compared to the ornaments of the Marut deities. The rain-water is said to be the thing that serves as the means of adornment. That is, the seer describes the scene in which rain pours down in torrents, the wind blows with force, and rain-water falls accompanied by lightning and thunder, by comparing it to the adornment of newly grown young men ready for marriage.

"Not elder, not younger" means that these Maruts are free of any relation of elder and younger among themselves, born together and of equal strength; being brothers to one another they grow together for good fortune. Rudra, ever young, the doer of good deeds, is the father of these Maruts; Pṛśni, the cow-deity who is their mother and yields milk well, made good days for the Maruts, that is, for the sake of the Maruts. The verb "made" is to be supplied.⟨NOTE:566⟩
notes: ಅಭೀಶವೋ ಬಂಧನರಜ್ಜವಂ with ಂ for ಃ in the bhāṣya

en: - एते भ्रातरः (*ete bhrātaraḥ*)—these brothers, who are of the form of Maruts
- सौभगाय (*saubhagāya*)—for their own welfare and growth
notes: ಸಕ್ಷ್ಯಾನ್ in the bhāṣya against ಸಕ್ತಾನಿ in the verse; ಅರಾಗ್ರಕಾಷ್ಠವಿಶೇಷೋ ನಾ ವರ್ತತೇ, ನಾ as printed

en: These brothers, of the form of Maruts, of whom none is elder to another and none younger to another, grew up together for their own welfare. May Rudra, ever young, the doer of excellent deeds, the father of the Maruts, and their mother Pṛśni, who yields excellent fruits, make good days for these Maruts.

They are brothers, of whom no one is the elder, no one the younger, but who grew up together for their mutual prosperity : may their father, Rudra, ever youthful, the doer of good deeds, and Prishni, ( their mother), easy to be milked, grant favourable days for ( the sake of ) the Maruts.

The matters described in this Ṛk are these: among the Marut deities there is no feeling of higher and lower, no difference of elder and younger; all are equal and brothers of equal origin. These points, already stated before, that is, in the Ṛk ते अजेष्ठा अकनिष्ठा (*te ajeṣṭhā akaniṣṭhā*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-59-6), the seer describes again. There is no difference in meaning or in description.

notes: Pada has ಮಾರ್ಯಾಸಃ against ಮರ್ಯಾಸೋ in the Saṃhitā and bhāṣya

en: "O Maruts, whether you are in the highest heaven, that is, the topmost, in the heavenly world, or in the middle heaven, or in the lowest heaven, O fortunate ones, you are." ⟨NOTE:569⟩ By the Vedic text which says that these three worlds are threefold, that there are three heavens and three earths, and so on, the heavenly world is of three kinds. "From this, from these three places, come to us, O Rudras" (the word "come" is to be supplied). "Or else": whatever oblation we now offer, O Agni, know that oblation, that is, accept it.
notes: ಶ್ಯಾವಾಶ್ವಸ್ತು ತಾಯ and ಯಾ- । in the Pada

en: - यदुत्तमे दिवि (*yaduttame divi*)—whether you are in the best world, the heaven-world
- मध्यमे वा (*madhyame vā*)—or in the middle world, the atmosphere
- अवमे ना (*avame nā*)—(heaven) in the worldly earth-world⟨NOTE:570⟩
- यत् यजाम (*yat yajāma*)—whatever oblation we offer
notes: ತರುತರಾಯ in the bhāṣya as printed, perhaps ತರುಣತರಾಯ

en: O Maruts, sons of Rudra, whether you are in the best world, the heaven-world, or in the middle world, the atmosphere, or in the worldly earth-world, from all those regions be gracious to us. Moreover, O Agni, know fully whatever oblation we offer at this time of sacrifice.
Auspicious Maruts, whether you abide in the upper, the middle, or the lower heaven, (come), Rudras, to us from thence ; and Agni, accept the oblation which this day we offer.

उत्तमे मध्यमे अवमे ना (*uttame madhyame avame nā*)—for these words Sāyaṇa has explained the meaning as the intermediate subdivisions of the heavenly world: the lower, the middle and the upper. In this matter, quoting the Vedic sentence त्रयो ना इमे त्रिवृतो लोकास्तिस्रो दिवः पृथिवी (*trayo nā ime trivṛto lokāstisro divaḥ pṛthivī*), he has supported the existence of three kinds of difference of position in the heavenly world.⟨NOTE:571⟩ Or else the meaning may be said to be: the highest place, the heavenly world; the middle place, the atmospheric world; the lower place, the earth-world. In whichever region among these three worlds you may now be, you are prayed to come from there toward us.
रुद्राः (*rudrāḥ*)—रुद्रपुत्रा मरुतः (*rudraputrā marutaḥ*). The Maruts, sons of Rudra, are here addressed by their father's name.
