notes: text breaks off at the end of p. 803: ತರಂತರಾಜನ; the sentence ತನಗೆ ಗೋವುಗಳನ್ನು ಕೊಟ್ಟು ಸ್ತ್ರೀಯು ಯಾರೆಂದರೆ is damaged

en: "O all-knowing ones", that is, knowers of everything, or else possessors of all wealth, O Maruts: since you and Agni are carried above the higher heaven, above the ridges, that is, in the region above the ridges, the meaning is that you dwell there. Or else, by the word for ridge, horses resembling ridges are meant, and you are carried by them. You, rejoicing in our hymns and oblations, shakers of your enemies and destroyers of those who harm us, bestow desirable wealth upon the sacrificer who presses the soma.
- मंदसानाः (*maṃdasānāḥ*)—those who are satisfied with our praise
- रिशादसः (*riśādasaḥ*)—who bring about the destruction of those who harm us
- सुन्वते (*sunvate*)—who presses the soma juice and offers the oblation

O omniscient Maruts, you and Agni who move about above the excellent summits of the heavenly world, in the loftiest region: being such, satisfied with our praise, causing enemies to tremble and destroying those who do us harm, bestow attractive wealth upon the sacrificer who presses the juice and offers the oblation.

Maruts, who are omniscient, since you and Agni abide above the summits of the upper (region) of the sky, you who cause (your enemies) to tremble, and are the consumers of (our) foes, being pleased, bestow upon the sacrificer who offers you oblations desirable wealth.

As is commonly the case in the last Ṛk of a sūkta, where a prayer for the fulfilment of wishes is stated, in this Ṛk too a prayer is stated that the sacrificer who prepares and offers soma juice to the Marut deities be favoured with the gift of wealth.

The eighth Ṛk, beginning अग्ने मरुद्भिः (*agne marudbhiḥ*), is the yājyā of the offering to Agni and the Maruts, since it is laid down in the sūtra अग्ने मरुद्भिः शुभयद्भिर्यक्वभिः (*agne marudbhiḥ śubhayadbhiryakvabhiḥ*) (Ā. 5 - 20). O Agni, drink the soma, rejoicing together with the Maruts. Of what kind are these Maruts? They are shining, or they make others shine; praiseworthy, worthy of hymns; those who take on the condition of a troop; purifiers; those who gratify the whole world with rain; and endowed with long life. O Vaiśvānara, Agni, benefactor of all men, you are accompanied by your ancient banner, the mass of flame.
- गणश्रिभिः (*gaṇaśribhiḥ*)—gathered together in the form of a troop
- विश्वमिन्वेभिः (*viśvaminvebhiḥ*)—who gratify the world with rain
- वैश्वानर (*vaiśvānara*)—O Agni, who are of the form of Vaiśvānara
- केतुना (*ketunā*)—with your banner of the form of flame (a mass of flame)

O Agni, rejoicing together with the Maruts, who are shining, praiseworthy, gathered together in troops, purifying, gratifying the world with rain, and long-lived, drink the soma. O Agni, who are of the form of Vaiśvānara, united with your ancient banner of the form of flame, drink the soma.
Agni, drink the Soma-juice, rejoicing, along with the Maruts,
resplendent, adorable, associated in troops, purifying all, animating and long-lived : drink, Vaiswanara, who are identified with the ancient emblem (of flame).

When offering oblation to the deities Agni and the Maruts, this Ṛk beginning अग्ने मरुद्भिः (*agne marudbhiḥ*) is to be recited as the yājyā mantra, as is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta-sūtra अग्ने मरुद्भिः शुभयद्भिर्युक्वभिः (*agne marudbhiḥ śubhayadbhiryukvabhiḥ*) (Ā. 5-20).⟨NOTE:572⟩ In this Ṛk too Agni is prayed to drink the soma, delighted, together with the Maruts.
notes: ಹೇಳುತ್ತಾಉತ: the Kannada word ಹೇಳುತ್ತಾ is glued to the first word ಉತ of the Ṛk, so the quotation as copied lacks its first word

en: O leaders, Maruts, most excellent, who are you? Being uncertain of their true nature, he asks in doubt: who are you? You who come one by one, each separately, from the farthest distance, from a very remote region, that is, from the atmosphere.
- के ष्ठ (*ke ṣṭha*)—where were you? from where have you come?
O Maruts, leaders, you who come individually from a very distant region, you who are most excellent, where were you? From where have you come?
Who are you, most excellent leaders (of rites), who come one by one from a region exceedingly remote?
O Maruts, although you are separate, you have all gathered together and come here. Moreover, you have come from a very distant region. Where were you until now? From where have you now come, thus

the seer asks the Marut deities, who have come toward him, at the very beginning. In the introduction it is said that when the seer Śyāvāśva was going through the forest the Marut deities came and appeared before him, and that Śyāvāśva praised them. Śyāvāśva has put questions, as stated above, to these deities who came toward him. In the ways of the world, when kinsmen, friends and other dear ones have been separated for some time for some reason and then meet again, it is the custom to welcome them with questions about their welfare, beginning: where were you? where have you come from? when did you come? In the same way it should be understood that the seer Śyāvāśva has welcomed the Marut deities with affectionate questions in this Ṛk and in the next.

O Maruts, where are your horses, of what place are they? And where are the reins, the binding cords? How are you able to go swiftly? How have you come? On the back of the horses there is seen the saddle, पर्याणं (*paryāṇaṃ*), so called because one sits there; and in the nostrils there is seen the restrainer that prevents flight, as with an animal. Therefore, by such marks as horses, you appear as if going somewhere in haste. Not ascertaining their divinity, he says: who are you?⟨NOTE:575⟩
notes: ಮರುತಾಂ ದಾನಪ್ರಶಂಸಾಯಾ ಅಪೇಕ್ಷಿತತ್ವಾನ್ನ ಪ್ರಾರ್ಥನೋಚಿತಾ: the closing sentence reads as "since praise of the Maruts' giving is what is required, a prayer is not fitting"; sense doubtful

en: - शेक (*śeka*)—you are able to move about
- कथा यय (*kathā yaya*)—where will you go
- पृष्ठे (*pṛṣṭhe*)—on the backs of the horses
- यमः (*yamaḥ*)—the bridle that holds the horses and stops them is here

O Maruts, where are your horses? Where are the bridles of your horses? In what manner are you able to move about? Where will you go? The saddle that is placed on the backs of your horses, and the bridles that hold them and stop them in their muzzles, are here.
Where are your horses? where your reins ? what is your capability ? where are you going ? the saddle is on the back (of the steeds), the bridle in their nostrils.
Just as in the previous Ṛk, in this Ṛk too the seer puts questions about the welfare of the Marut deities, concerning their coming and concerning their horses.

On the hindquarters of these horses, the place to be struck, the goad is applied, that is, the whip that urges them on, or a special piece of wood with a pointed end; the meaning is that it is applied, striking, for swift going. The leaders, the Maruts, separate and restrain their thighs; the meaning is that by running swiftly they become spread apart. The example for the spreading is given: like women who bring forth offspring, who at the time of begetting sons, at the time of union, make the thighs spread apart; so too the horses.⟨NOTE:576⟩
notes: ದಾರ್ಭ್ಯಾಯ ಶ್ಯಾವಾಶ್ವಾಯ: the two datives stand together though Dārbhya is Rathavīti and Śyāvāśva the speaker; the following words read ದಾರ್ಭ್ಯಾಭಿಮುಖೀ

en: - चोदः (*codaḥ*)—the goad, the means of urging them to go swiftly, is applied
- पुत्रकृथे (*putrakṛthe*)—at the time of begetting a son
- जनयो न (*janayo na*)—as women spread their thighs apart
- वि यमुः (*vi yamuḥ*)—cause to spread apart

The goad is applied to the flank regions of these horses, that is, to the sides of the belly. The Maruts, urging their horses to run swiftly, make the horses spread their feet apart, just as women at the time of childbirth spread their thighs apart.
The goad is (applied) to their flanks : the drivers force them to spread their thinghs apart, like women in bringing forth children.

जघने चोदः (*jaghane codaḥ*)—here the flank is the region where the feet and the belly meet. It may be called the lower belly of horses. The चोद (*coda*) is the goad or stirrup, the object like an iron ring which serves the rider to place his feet when he rides. To fit both feet of the rider, these are on both sides of the horse. They are joined to a leather strap and hung down on both sides of the horse. The rider, placing his feet in them, rides. When the rider wishes the horse to go swiftly, he presses the sides of the horse with his feet, using these rings in which he has placed his two feet. From this, urging arises and the horse runs swiftly. This is the matter that is explained here by the words जघने चोदः (*jaghane codaḥ*).

एषां सक्तानि नरः वि यमुः (*eṣāṃ saktāni naraḥ vi yamuḥ*)—these Marut deities make the thighs of their horses spread apart as they run. Whatever the animal, when it runs at full gallop its thighs or legs are seen to spread far apart as it runs. Therefore, to make the thighs of the horses spread apart means to make the horses run swiftly, spreading their legs far apart. The seer has given an example concerning the spreading of the thighs.

पुत्रकृथे न जनयः (*putrakṛthe na janayaḥ*)—पुत्रोत्पादने अपत्योत्पादयित्र्यो योषित इव (*putrotpādane apatyotpādayitryo yoṣita iva*). At the time of begetting a son, that is, when women give birth to a son, at the time of delivery, they spread their thighs so that the child may come out easily from the region of the womb. In the same way the seer has described the going of the horses by comparing it to the childbirth of women, saying that the Marut deities urge their horses so that, in order to run swiftly, they spread their thighs or legs far apart.

Taking them to wish to go, from such marks as the lashing of the whip, he says: O heroes, senders-forth of enemies, O Maruts, beneficial to mortals, O भद्रजानयः (*bhadrajānayaḥ*), those whose birth is auspicious, praiseworthy, that is, sons of Rudra: as copper and other metals heated by fire are bright, so you are blazing. Or else: as those whose bodies are burnt by fire flee, so you are.⟨NOTE:577⟩
notes: ಕಸ್ಯಾರ್ಥವಾಗಿ printed; read here as ಕನ್ಯಾರ್ಥವಾಗಿ "for the sake of the maiden"?

en: - भद्रजानयः (*bhadrajānayaḥ*)—those of auspicious origin, O Maruts
- परा इतन (*parā itana*)—set out for your work
- अग्नितपो यथा (*agnitapo yathā*)—as copper and other metals heated by fire shine
O Maruts, heroes, benefactors of men, of auspicious origin, set out for your work. As copper and other metals heated by fire shine, you too are shining.
Heroes, friendly to man, of honourable birth, you are as if blazing with fire.

अग्नितपो यथासथ-अग्निना तप्तास्ताम्रादयो यथा दीप्तास्तद्वत् प्रदीप्ता भवथ । अथवाग्नि तप्ता दग्धदेहा यथा पलायंते तथा भवथेत्यर्थः । (*agnitapo yathāsatha-agninā taptāstāmrādayo yathā dīptāstadvat pradīptā bhavatha | athavāgni taptā dagdhadehā yathā palāyaṃte tathā bhavathetyarthaḥ |*). In this Ṛk the Marut deities are described by comparison with copper and other metals heated by fire. Just as copper and other metals, heated so as to melt in the fire, shine brightly, so you, Marut deities, shine with your own light: this is the description. Or else another meaning has been given for the word अग्नितप (*agnitapa*). When a forest fire spreads in a forest, the animals there, as their bodies begin to burn in the fire, run wherever they find a way, looking neither backward nor forward; in the same way, the seer describes, you move swiftly. Although the commentator has arranged these two kinds of explanation so that sense results, it cannot be stated precisely what the intention or meaning of the seer, the seer of the mantra, is in the simile अग्नितपो यथासथ (*agnitapo yathāsatha*).

notes: ಶ್ಯಾನಾಶ್ವೋಽಥ and ಸಂಪ್ರೇಕ್ಷ್ಯಾರ್ಷಣ printed; the bhāṣya has ಶ್ಯಾವಾಶ್ವೋಽಥ and ಸಂಪ್ರೇಕ್ಷ್ಯರ್ಷೇಣ

en: That queen of Taranta gave me, सनत् (*sanat*), she bestowed. What did she give? A horse, that is, a stock of horses, a herd of them; "animal" is a singular used in the generic sense. And also cattle, a stock of cows, a herd; and a stock accompanied by a hundred sheep, many sheep. Who is she who is spoken of as "she"? He says: she who, for the hero, the younger, who was praised by me, Śyāvāśva, stretched out her own arm for the embrace; that is the "she" who gave. Since she is the abode of her husband's love, for that very reason she is able to give much wealth.⟨NOTE:579⟩
notes: ೬ ನೇ ಸೂಕ್ತದಿಂದ ೨ನೆಯ ಸೂಕ್ತದವರೆಗೆ printed; presumably 62nd to 72nd

en: - वीराय (*vīrāya*)—and is a hero, for the embrace of Taranta
- शतावयं (*śatāvayaṃ*)—that which consists of a hundred sheep
She, Śaśīyasī, who extended her arm for the embrace of Taranta, who was praised by Śyāvāśva, gave me wealth of cattle, consisting of horses, of cows, and of a hundred sheep.
(She. Sasiyasi), who has thrown her arms round the hero Taranta who was eulogized by Syavaswa, has given me cattle comprising horses, and cows, and hundreds of sheep.

In this Ṛk the great seer Śyāvāśva has described the praise of Śaśīyasī, the queen of King Taranta, for her gift, saying that she gave him cows, horses and goats. श्यावाश्वस्तुताय वीराय उपबर्बृहत् सा मह्यं (*śyāvāśvastutāya vīrāya upabarbṛhat sā mahyaṃ*) ... the queen of Taranta gave him wealth of cattle such as cows; in describing the praise of that royal wife for her gift, the seer has praised her qualities. Who is the woman who gave him cows? She is the wife of King Taranta, who was praised by him (by Śyāvāśva) and who is valiant,⟨NOTE:580⟩

that queen herself. And this woman extended her arms to the embrace of her husband, King Taranta, and so helped him; that is, when her husband embraced her with affection, she too, in return for his embrace and out of mutual affection, offered her arms, that is, embraced him in turn, and showed the love that each had for the other. From the seer's description it becomes evident that the king behaved with the greatest affection towards this wife of his, Śaśīyasī, and that the loving couple had a mutual attachment. The chief meaning is that his wife was worthy of the embraces and the like that show a husband's love. Such a queen, worthy of her husband's affection and regard, with the king's permission gave the seer many horses, cattle, cows and goats, by the hundred; thus the seer has praised the generosity of the king's wife.
notes: abbreviation ಭಾ. printed

en: उत (*uta*) means "and also": and that one Śaśīyasī. Śaśīyasī is the name of the king's chief queen; she alone is the woman. Or else उत (*uta*) is used in the sense of emphasis: among women she alone is to be praised. She is more excellent than a man. Than what kind of man? Than one by whom the gods are not protected, since he does not please them with praise and the like, and who therefore lacks राधो धनं (*rādho dhanaṃ*), that is, wealth: one without wealth fit for giving, a miser.
- अदेवत्रात् (*adevatrāt*)—from not worshipping the gods, one who is not fit for their protection
- अराधसः (*arādhasaḥ*)—one who has no wealth useful for giving
- उत त्वा शशीयसी (*uta tvā śaśīyasī*)—Śaśīyasī alone
Than a man who, by not worshipping the gods, is not fit for their protection and who has no wealth useful for giving, Śaśīyasī, though a woman, is the more excellent.
Sasiyasi, though a female, is more excellent than a man who reverences not the gods, nor bestows wealth.

It is the common notion that men are superior to women in strength, ability and the like, in valour and in qualities. But even among men, those who do not worship the gods, that is, who perform no sacrifices and the like, who practise no charity or righteous conduct, who do no kind of good to people, and who behave only with miserliness, are not excellent, though they belong to the class of men. People feel no respect or regard for them. A woman whose mind is set on charity, righteous conduct and doing good to others is better than men of such bad nature. The seer has described that Śaśīyasī, wife of King Taranta, though a woman, is endowed with such good qualities that she is far superior to many men who are men only in name and who perform neither worship of the gods nor charity and righteous conduct. Here the special statement is made plain that, contrary to the general rule that men are superior to women, Taranta's queen is superior to many men.
उत (*uta*)—"also" and "and". The word उत (*uta*) is used in the sense of conjunction (the meaning "and") and in the sense of emphasis. In the present Ṛk either meaning may be given.

The Śaśīyasī who "discerns" the afflicted, that is, the troubled man. The root जसि (*jasi*) is used in the sense of striking and casting out. She discerns that one; likewise she discerns the thirsty one, and she discerns the desirous one, that is, one who longs for wealth and the like; the meaning is that out of compassion she gives what is wished for. देवत्रा (*devatrā*): she turns her mind towards the gods, that is, she forms the intention of giving for the gods' pleasure. The woman who does this alone is excellent; the connection is with what went before.
- जसुरिं (*jasuriṃ*)—the suffering of one who is distressed; she is able to discern it
- तृष्यंतं (*tṛṣyaṃtaṃ*)—the need of a man who wants wealth
- कामिनं (*kāminaṃ*)—the condition of a man who has other wishes
- देवत्रा (*devatrā*)—in the worship of the gods

The Śaśīyasī who is able to discern the suffering of one who is distressed, who, knowing the need of a man who wants wealth, can help so that his other wishes too are fulfilled, and whose mind is devoted to the worship of the gods, she alone is excellent.
For she discerns one who suffers pain, one who is in want, or one desirous (of any thing), and directs her mind towards the gods.

In this Ṛk too there is a description of the qualities of Śaśīyasī, queen of Taranta. This king's wife is not only of a nature to give gifts with a generous mind. She understands the sorrows of others, that is, the grief of people who are in distress, shows pity towards them and is of a nature to help them: she gives wealth to those who have none and other kinds of help to those who need help, and so does good to others; knowing the condition of poor people who suffer from lack of wealth and the like, she helps them by giving wealth and so on.

Besides these qualities, her mind also turns towards worshipping the gods; that is, she is also devoted to the worship of the gods (to sacrifices and the like). Thus the seer has described the qualities of Śaśīyasī.

जसुरिं (*jasuriṃ*)—For the word जसुरि (*jasuri*) Yāska gives an explanation, citing the Ṛk स्मैनं वस्त्रमथिं न तायुमनु क्रोशंति क्षितयो भरेषु । नीचायमानं जसुरिं श्येनं श्रवश्चाच्छा पशुमच्च यूथं ॥ (*smainaṃ vastramathiṃ na tāyumanu krośaṃti kṣitayo bhareṣu | nīcāyamānaṃ jasuriṃ śyenaṃ śravaścācchā paśumacca yūthaṃ ‖*) ⟨NOTE:581⟩ (Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-38-5), and he explains the meaning of this word. There जसुरिं (*jasuriṃ*) means one oppressed by hunger, hungry. In the present Ṛk one may give that meaning, and also the general meaning "oppressed, suffering": that is, one who is in agony from the pain of hunger for want of food, or who grieves from falling into some other kind of trouble.
notes: abbreviation ಸಾ. ಭಾ printed

en: उत (*uta*) means "and also"; घा (*ghā*) is a filler. The word नेमः (*nemaḥ*) means half, as in the Nirukta (Ni. 3-20): it is explained as "half". Wife and husband, doing one work in union, are one and the same thing, according to the smṛti saying that the wife is half of the body. So Taranta, who is half of Śaśīyasī, is called "a man". The speaker says: "I, the praiser, say that he is unpraised"; though he has been praised in many ways, because of the great abundance of his qualities he is still unpraised. And that Taranta is "equal" in the giving of wealth by such givers: heroes are those who impel wealth, the generous; the wealth to be given by them is what is to be given; in that wealth he is equal, that is, a giver to all. इत् (*it*) is a filler.
- नेमः (*nemaḥ*)—the other half of Śaśīyasī (her husband)
- अस्तुत इति (*astuta iti*)—(though he is praised in many ways) as unpraised
- वैरदेये (*vairadeye*)—in the giving of abundant wealth
- समः इत् (*samaḥ it*)—is the same to all, at all times

Though I praise Śaśīyasī's husband Taranta in many ways, my feeling is that he is still unpraised. His qualities are endless; however much one praises, it remains little. When that Taranta gives wealth he shows no difference to anyone; he is the same to all, at all times.
And, eulogizing (him), I proclaim that the man, her ( other ) half is (as it were), uncommended, for he is ever the same in munificent donations.

In this Ṛk the description of Śaśīyasī's qualities is made indirectly, that is, by praising her husband. The commentator, saying अर्धं शरीरस्य भार्येत्यादि स्मृतेः (*ardhaṃ śarīrasya bhāryetyādi smṛteḥ*), points out that husband and wife share the body in equal parts, that to describe one of them is to describe only half, and that the description of the qualities of the husband, King Taranta, is therefore to be taken as a description of the qualities of the wife Śaśīyasī (the other half). So it should be understood that the praise of the qualities of King Taranta in this Ṛk applies also to Śaśīyasī.

घ (*gha*)—This word is used here as a filler, that is, to complete the number of syllables that a foot must have. It has no fixed meaning. Still, if one wishes, the sense of emphasis may be given. This word is customarily used in the Saṃhitā text with a long vowel as घा (*ghā*) and in the Pada text with a short vowel as घ (*gha*).

नेमः (*nemaḥ*)—The word नेमः (*nemaḥ*) is read among the twenty-six द्विशनामगळल्लि (*dviśanāmagaḷalli*) beginning with प्रपित्वे, अभीके (*prapitve, abhīke*) (Ni. 320) ⟨NOTE:582⟩. That is, this word is used when only an incomplete or half portion of a matter is described.

त्वो नेम इत्यर्धस्य । त्वोऽपततः । नेमोऽपनीतः । अर्धं हरतीर्वि परीताद्धारयतेर्वा स्यादुद्धृतं भवति । ऋध्नोतेर्वा स्यादृद्धमो विभागः । पीयति त्वो अनु त्वो गृणाति । नेमे देवा नेमेऽसुराः । इत्यपि निगमौ भवतः ॥ (*tvo nema ityardhasya | tvo 'patataḥ | nemo 'panītaḥ | ardhaṃ haratīrvi parītāddhārayatervā syāduddhṛtaṃ bhavati | ṛdhnotervā syādṛddhamo vibhāgaḥ | pīyati tvo anu tvo gṛṇāti | neme devā neme 'surāḥ | ityapi nigamau bhavataḥ ‖*) (Ni. 3-20). In this way Yāska has given the explanation of the word नेमः (*nemaḥ*). That is: the words त्वः (*tvaḥ*) and नेमः (*nemaḥ*) are words that indicate the meaning "half". त्वः (*tvaḥ*) means what is not wholly spread out, that is, what is half and half. नेमः (*nemaḥ*) means what is not wholly carried off, that is, what is only a half portion. The word for "half" (अर्ध (*ardha*)) may be formed (1) from the root हृ (*hṛ*) (हरति (*harati*)) meaning to carry off, take away, or (2) from the root धृ (*dhṛ*), meaning to hold, bear, or (3) from the root ऋथ् (*ṛth*), meaning to prosper, increase. If the letters of the root हरति (*harati*) or the root meaning "bears" are changed or transposed, the word for "half" is formed; or it may be formed from the root ऋध्योति (*ṛdhyoti*) as well. For example, in the sentence पीयति त्वो अनु त्वो गृणाति (*pīyati tvo anu tvo gṛṇāti*) ("one half reviles, the other half praises") the word त्व (*tva*) is used in the sense of "one half, the other half". In the same way, in the sentence नेमे देवा नेमेऽसुराः (*neme devā neme 'surāḥ*) ("half of them gods, the other half asuras") the word नेम (*nema*) is used in the sense of "half".

अस्तुतः पुमान् इति ब्रुवे पणि (*astutaḥ pumān iti bruve paṇi*)—The seer Śyāvāśva has said of himself: "I, who am praising King Taranta, say that however much I praise him he is अस्तुतः (*astutaḥ*), not fully praised." Since the generosity and other qualities of King Taranta are endless, I have described only some small part here and there; because I am not able, I could not describe his qualities in full. Therefore "not praised", not described; thus the seer has spoken of the greatness of King Taranta and of his own smallness.

वैरदेये इत् समः (*vairadeye it samaḥ*)—स च तरुंतो वैरदेये! वीरा धनानां प्रेरयितारो दानशीलाः । तैर्दातव्यं धनं देयं । तस्मिन्थनॆ: समः । सर्वेभ्यो दातेत्यर्थः । इदिति पूरणः । (*sa ca taruṃto vairadeye! vīrā dhanānāṃ prerayitāro dānaśīlāḥ | tairdātavyaṃ dhanaṃ deyaṃ | tasminthanè: samaḥ | sarvebhyo dātetyarthaḥ | iditi pūraṇaḥ |*). Describing the generosity and other qualities of that King Taranta, the seer has said वैरदेये इत् समः (*vairadeye it samaḥ*). Heroes are those who urge that gifts be given, that is, the generous. The wealth that such generous people give is called the hero-gift. Among such givers of wealth King Taranta is the foremost. He gives wealth to all alike, without partiality, that is, without saying "no" to anyone; in this way the seer praises King Taranta's generosity. The word इत् (*it*) is used here to fill the foot; it has no fixed meaning here.
notes: abbreviation ಋಗ್ವೇ printed

en: उत (*uta*) means "and also". To Śyāva, that is, to me, Śyāvāśva, she अरपत् (*arapat*), that is, अलपत् (*alapat*), declared clearly the way. What kind of woman is she? Young, one whose youth has set in, and rejoicing in return, delighting. For whom did she do this? For the one of long fame, or of abundant food, called Purumīḷha, a man of wisdom and of abundant possessions. The dative is said to be used here after a word that serves the purpose of an action, with the meaning "who has reached Purumīḷha". For that purpose the two red horses given by Śaśīyasī "held", that is, bore him; she, setting him in a chariot yoked with those two horses and going ahead of him, showing the way to Purumīḷha's house, is the one who is more excellent than a man; the connection is with what went before.
- प्रति ममंदुषी (*prati mamaṃduṣī*)—being full of kindness
The young Śaśīyasī, full of kindness, explained and told the way to me, Śyāvāśva. The horses given by her carried me to Purumīḷha, who is wise and of widespread fame.
Young and affable, she has explained to me, Syavaswa, the road and two ruddy horses have borne me to the valiant and renowned Purumilha,

Since this Ṛk speaks of a king named Purumīḷha, Purumīḷha himself is the seer of this Ṛk. The commentator says in the introduction he has written for this sūkta that this Purumīḷha was the younger brother of King Taranta. Purumīḷha is a well-known royal seer. In the Ṛgveda there are two seers of the name Purumīḷha. One Purumīḷha, born in the Aṅgirasa lineage, is a seer who saw the mantras of the seventy-first sūkta of the eighth Maṇḍala (fifteen Ṛks) together with one named Sudīti. The other seer of the name Purumīḷha was the son of a king named Vidadaśva, who was famous in the lineage of Suhotra of the Gotama line. This Purumīḷha and one named Ajamīḷha (he too a son of Suhotra) together are the seers of the forty-third and forty-fourth sūktas of the fourth Maṇḍala (fourteen Ṛks in all). Although there is room for doubt as to which of these two Purumīḷhas is the one spoken of in the present sūkta, on certain grounds it may be said that the king mentioned here is the Purumīḷha who was the son of Vidadaśva, of Suhotra's line.

As stated in the introduction to this sūkta, Śaśīyasī, the chief queen of King Taranta, not only honoured Śyāvāśva by giving him cows and other things, but, so that he might also obtain wealth and the like from Purumīḷha, King Taranta's brother, who lived close by, she herself showed Śyāvāśva the way to the town where Purumīḷha was, and gave him excellent horses to reach it. This Ṛk describes in detail that those horses carried the seer Śyāvāśva to the presence of King Purumīḷha.

This is praise of Purumīḷha. Purumīḷha, the son of Vidadaśva, who gave me a hundred cows in the way that was stated, likewise gave desirable riches as well, like Taranta. As Taranta gave a hundred cows and wealth of many kinds, so Purumīḷha, son of Vidadaśva, gave also. The words "I praise him" are to be supplied.
As soon as I reached Purumīḷha with the help of the horses given by Śaśīyasī, he too gave me a hundred cows and priceless riches, just as Taranta had given to me.
Who the sons of Vidaswa, has given me a hundred (head) of cattle, and, like Taranta, many precious gifts.

In this Ṛk too the seer Śyāvāśva praises Purumīḷha's generosity, saying that he gave him hundreds of cows. Therefore, according to the statement या तेनोक्ता सा देवता (*yā tenoktā sā devatā*), that the subject propounded in a Ṛk is the deity of that Ṛk, Purumīḷha himself should be the deity. The commentator Sāyaṇa too says plainly in the opening sentence of his commentary on this Ṛk: इयं पुरुमाळ्हस्तुतिः (*iyaṃ purumāḷhastutiḥ*), that is, this Ṛk is praise of Purumīḷha. Yet in the Anukramaṇikā it is said: यो मे धेनूनामित्यस्या वैददश्विस्तरंतो राजा देवता (*yo me dhenūnāmityasyā vaidadaśvistaraṃto rājā devatā*), and the rest.

For the tenth Ṛk of this sūkta, यो मे धेनूनां (*yo me dhenūnāṃ*), it is said that its deity is the king named Taranta, son of Vidadaśva. In the Ṛk the mention of Taranta, "as Taranta gave", is only incidental; the matter mainly propounded in the Ṛk is the praise of Purumīḷha's gift. Hence there is room for doubt whether it is right to say that Taranta is the deity instead of saying that Purumīḷha is the deity of this Ṛk.

Having now concluded that these are the Maruts themselves, he praises them with their greatnesses known among the people. The Maruts who are now borne by swift-moving horses. Doing what? Drinking the intoxicating मधु (*madhu*), the Soma juice; the meaning is the Soma held as provision for the journey. Those Maruts here, in this place, bear glories, that is, fame produced by praise.
The Maruts who are borne by swift-moving horses drink the intoxicating Soma juice in this sacrifice and are praised with hymns.
Those (Maruts) who are brought hither by swift horses, drinking the inebriating juice, receive here glorification.

Up to now the seer Śyāvāśva has praised the Maruts, Śaśīyasī the chief queen of Taranta, Taranta, and Purumīḷha; he now praises the Maruts again in this Ṛk and in the next five Ṛks. The explanation of the meaning of the Ṛk is plain.

By the splendour, the radiance, of whichever Maruts, heaven and earth stand supported; the word "stand" is to be supplied. For these Maruts shine in a special way in their chariots; the word आ (*ā*) is in the sense of "and". The illustration: like the radiant sun in heaven, in the world of the sky that is above, higher and higher. Or else the word उपरि (*upari*) is to be construed as "upon the chariot".
- रुक्ष्मः इव (*rukṣmaḥ iva*)—like the shining sun
- विभ्राजंते (*vibhrājaṃte*)—shine; those Maruts are praised here
The Maruts, by whose splendour alone heaven and earth both stand, and who shine in their chariots like the sun shining in the high region of heaven, are praised here.
They by whose glory heaven and earth are surpassed : who shine splendid in their chariots like the radiant (sun) in the heaven above.

In this Ṛk there is a description of two kinds of greatness of the Maruts. येषां श्रिया रोदसी अधि (*yeṣāṃ śriyā rodasī adhi*): by the splendour of the Maruts, that is, by their strength and power, heaven and earth stand resting on them; and उपरि दिवि रुक्ष्म इव रथेषु विभ्राजंते (*upari divi rukṣma iva ratheṣu vibhrājaṃte*): like the sun shining in the heaven above the atmosphere, the Maruts seated in their chariots blaze with splendour. Thus the qualities of the Maruts are described.

That group of Maruts is youthful: one that joins together everywhere, or ever young. Its chariot is bright, with a shining chariot. It is without reproach, not to be blamed. It goes well, one who goes auspiciously. It is "not gone against" or "not answered by a counter-sound". Thus the group, of such great power, shines.
- सः मारुतो गणः (*saḥ māruto gaṇaḥ*)—that same company of Maruts (is praised)
That same company of Maruts, which is ceaselessly and always united, has a shining chariot, is faultless and has an excellent course, is praised.
That company of Maruts, ever young, riding in bright chariots, irreproachable, ausspicious, motive unobstructed.

युवा (*yuvā*)—मिश्रायिता नित्यतरुणो वा (*miśrāyitā nityataruṇo vā*). The word युवा (*yuvā*) means that the Maruts are ever young, or that when they move about in the atmosphere they all move together, joined as one. Therefore they are described by the word युवा (*yuvā*). The word युवा (*yuvā*) is a singular form and is an adjective of the word गणः (*gaṇaḥ*). गण (*gaṇa*) means the company of Maruts, the host or group of the Marut gods. Although this word is in the singular, it indicates a multitude and so points to all the Marut gods.

अप्रतिमः (*apratimaḥ*)⟨NOTE:583⟩—For this word Yāska says: अप्रतिष्टुतोऽप्रतिष्ठुतोऽप्रतिस्खलितो वा । अस्मभ्यमप्रतिष्टुत इत्यपि निगमो भवति ॥ (*apratiṣṭuto 'pratiṣṭhuto 'pratiskhalito vā | asmabhyamapratiṣṭuta ityapi nigamo bhavati ‖*) (Ni. 6-16), and so he has given the explanation. That is, this word has the meanings "that cannot be faced", "that cannot be stopped", "having an extraordinary sound", and the like. He says that the Vedic text अस्मभ्यमम्रतिष्कुतः (*asmabhyamamratiṣkutaḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-7-6) is given as an example.
notes: ಋತು printed; read as ಋತಂ

en: Who knows the abode of these Maruts? Who knows it, now? The place where the shakers of their enemies rejoice, that is, are glad; they who are born for the sake of water, who have been manifested by the sacrifice, and who are sinless.
- धूतयः (*dhūtayaḥ*)—making their enemies tremble with fear
- को वेद (*ko veda*)—who knows? (these same Maruts)
- ऋतजाताः (*ṛtajātāḥ*)—and are born for the sake of water
Who certainly knows the abode of these Maruts, in which they are glad while making their enemies tremble with fear? These same Maruts are sinless and are born for the sake of water.
Who knows of a certainty their (abode), where the intimidators (of their foes) rejoice? born for (the distribution of) water, exempt from defects.

The greatness of the Marut gods cannot be known by ordinary people. Though they make their enemies tremble, they themselves are always glad. They are sinless. They are born for the sake of water in the form of rain; that is, it is by their grace that rain falls upon the earth and from it the plants flourish. Such Marut gods are of a nature that is always moving
about. No man knows their true place of abode; thus the seer has praised the extraordinary qualities of the Marut gods.

O Maruts, desirous of praise, you are, for the mortal, the sacrificer, the leaders who carry him forward to the wished-for heaven and the like, by this attitude of favour such as has now been shown, or by this kind of act of praise as the cause. In the sacrifices, called by that name because the going (of the gods) is the purpose for which the invocations are made in them, you are the hearers of the invocations.
- प्रणीतारः (*praṇītāraḥ*)—you are those who lead to heaven and the like
- श्रोतारः (*śrotāraḥ*)—you are those who listen to the praises

O Maruts, who desire praises, you are those who lead the sacrificer to heaven and the like by the thought of favour that is manifest in the present case. In the sacrifices and the like you are those who listen to the praises.
Desirous of praise, you are the guides (to happiness) of the man who propitiates (you) by this pious rite: you are bearers of invocations to the sacrifice.

इदानीं कृतप्रकारयानुग्रहबुद्ध्या, ईदृशेन स्तुति कर्मणा (*idānīṃ kṛtaprakārayānugrahabuddhyā, īdṛśena stuti karmaṇā*) वा (*vā*). The commentator has explained the words इत्था धिया (*itthā dhiyā*) in two ways: by the thought of favour which you are now showing towards us, or by the act in the form of praise which we are now performing.

यामहूतिषु (*yāmahūtiṣu*)—यानो गमनं। तदर्था हूतयो यस्मिन्निति यामहूतयो याज्ञाः। (*yāno gamanaṃ| tadarthā hūtayo yasminniti yāmahūtayo yājñāḥ|*) The word for going means "going"; the act for which such going is intended gets the name of the word explained. Since the going of the gods is for the sake of the sacrifice, that is, since the gods, being invoked in the sacrifices, go there, the commentator has explained the parts of this word as meaning "in the sacrifices".

श्रोतारः (*śrotāraḥ*)—श्रोतार आह्वानानां (*śrotāra āhvānānāṃ*): because they are hearers of the invocation that the sacrificers make in those sacrifices (the calling to come to the sacrificial ground), it is said here "hearers".

O devourers of the harmful enemies, O you worthy of the sacrifice, O you whose wealth is abundant and delightful, you, to us, desirable, enviable riches fit to dwell in: bring them about, that is, cause them to turn towards us. ⟨NOTE:584⟩
notes: abbreviation ತೈ. ಉ. printed

en: - पुरुश्चंद्राः (*puruścaṃdrāḥ*)—O Maruts, who have delightful wealth
- वसूनि (*vasūni*)—and fit to dwell in, the riches
O Maruts, destroyers of enemies, worthy of the sacrifice, who have delightful wealth, bring about for us the riches that we desire and that are fit to dwell in.
You, are destroyers of the malevolent, abounding in wealth and entitled to adoration, bestow upon us desirable riches.
In this Ṛk, the last of those that praise the Maruts, the seer prays that they give the wealth and the like that we desire. Since the meaning is clear, no explanation is needed.

Śaunaka told of the marriage of Śyāvāśva Arcanānas, who had attained the state of a seer, and of the daughter of Rathavīti. How? When the Maruts had departed, Śyāvāśva, very famous, the delight of the three families, knowing himself to have become manifest as a seer, in his mind approached the daughter of Rathavīti. Intending to tell Rathavīti truly that he was a seer, with the two verses beginning एतं मे स्तोमं (*etaṃ me stomaṃ*) he entrusted a message to Night as messenger. Rathavīti, knowing the seer's command and urged by the goddess Night, took his daughter and went to Arcanānas to give her; clasping his feet, standing humble with folded hands, he declared his name, saying that he was Rathavīti Dārbhya, asked forgiveness for what he had said before, when Śyāvāśva wished a union with him, bowed to him and begged him not to be angry; he said that Śyāvāśva was the seer's son and a seer himself, and his father a revered seer, and bade him accept this daughter-in-law. That king gave him a hundred horses and his well-adorned daughter as daughter-in-law; at the time of the marriage the king also gave a hundred horses and a thousand for the daughter, a thousand cows and abundant wealth; and when his austerities were completed he went to the forest.

The words are then explained. हे ऊर्मै रात्रि देवि (*he ūrmai rātri devi*): ऊर्मै (*ūrmai*) is a name of night. The meaning: this hymn of mine, made for the Maruts, the praise that I, having become a seer of the mantra, offered to the Maruts: carry it, turned away from me and turned towards Dārbhya, Śyāvāśva; that is, convey it. ⟨NOTE:585⟩ The same is said again, for respect: O goddess Night, carry the praises concerning the Maruts, like a charioteer: as a charioteer places the wealth he intends in the chariot and conveys it to the intended place, so.
notes: ವಾಂಯು ವಸೋಸ್ತನ್ಮಹಿತ್ವಂ printed; the words are damaged, read as "of you two, that greatness"

en: - रथीः इव (*rathīḥ iva*)—as the master of a chariot carries heavy things in the chariot

O goddess of night, carry this hymn composed by me, turned away from me and turned towards Dārbhya, and bring it to him. O goddess, as the master of a chariot carries heavy things in his chariot, carry my praises.
Bear to Darbhya, oh night, turning away (from me to him), this my eulogy (of the Maruts) : convey my praises, goddess, as charioteer (conveys the contents of his vehicle to their destination.

Up to now, that is, through the eleven sūktas from the fifty-second sūkta of this Maṇḍala to the sixty-second, Śyāvāśva praised the Marut gods and through the grace of those gods attained the state of a seer; and King Rathavīti too gave his daughter to this seer Śyāvāśva in marriage. The commentator says that the great seer Śaunaka has narrated this matter in the following way:
संपन्नऋषिभावस्य श्यावाश्वस्यार्चनानसः । रथवीतिसुतायाश्च विवाहं शौनकोऽब्रवीत् ॥ (*saṃpannaṛṣibhāvasya śyāvāśvasyārcanānasaḥ | rathavītisutāyāśca vivāhaṃ śaunako 'bravīt ‖*)

मरुत्सु तु प्रयातेषु श्वावाश्वः सुमहायशाः । प्रादुर्भूतार्षमात्मानं ज्ञात्वा त्रिकुलनंदनः ॥ रथवीतेर्दुहितरमगच्छन्मना तदा । स सत्यमृषिमात्मानं प्रवक्ष्यनथवीतये ॥ एतं मे स्तोममित्याभ्यां दौत्ये रात्रिं न्यवेदयत् । ऋषेर्नियोगमाज्ञाय देव्या रात्रा प्रचोदितः ॥ आदाय कन्यकां दातुमुपेयायार्चनानसं । पादौ तस्योपसंगृह्य स्थित्वा प्रह्वः कृतांजलिः ॥ रथवीतिरहं दार्भ्य इति नाम शशंस सः । मया संयोगमिच्छंतं त्वां प्रत्याचक्षि यत्पुरा ॥ तत्क्षमस्व नमस्तेऽस्तु मे मा स्म भगवन् क्रुद्धः । यषेः पुत्रः स्वयमृषिः पितासि भगवानृषेः । हंत प्रतिगृहाणेमां स्नुषामित्येनमब्रवीत् ॥ तस्मै ददावश्वशतं स राजा स्वलंकृतां चापि सुतां स्नुषार्थं । विवाहकालेऽपि ददौ नरेंद : शतं हयानां दुहितुः सहस्रं ॥ (*marutsu tu prayāteṣu śvāvāśvaḥ sumahāyaśāḥ | prādurbhūtārṣamātmānaṃ jñātvā trikulanaṃdanaḥ ‖ rathavīterduhitaramagacchanmanā tadā | sa satyamṛṣimātmānaṃ pravakṣyanathavītaye ‖ etaṃ me stomamityābhyāṃ dautye rātriṃ nyavedayat | ṛṣerniyogamājñāya devyā rātrā pracoditaḥ ‖ ādāya kanyakāṃ dātumupeyāyārcanānasaṃ | pādau tasyopasaṃgṛhya sthitvā prahvaḥ kṛtāṃjaliḥ ‖ rathavītirahaṃ dārbhya iti nāma śaśaṃsa saḥ | mayā saṃyogamicchaṃtaṃ tvāṃ pratyācakṣi yatpurā ‖ tatkṣamasva namaste 'stu me mā sma bhagavan kruddhaḥ | yaṣeḥ putraḥ svayamṛṣiḥ pitāsi bhagavānṛṣeḥ | haṃta pratigṛhāṇemāṃ snuṣāmityenamabravīt ‖ tasmai dadāvaśvaśataṃ sa rājā svalaṃkṛtāṃ cāpi sutāṃ snuṣārthaṃ | vivāhakāle 'pi dadau nareṃda : śataṃ hayānāṃ duhituḥ sahasraṃ ‖*)
गवां सहस्रं वसु च प्रभूतं तप्तुं तपोऽन्तेऽथ वनं जगाम ॥ (*gavāṃ sahasraṃ vasu ca prabhūtaṃ taptuṃ tapo 'nte 'tha vanaṃ jagāma ‖*) Thus (it is said).

Śaunaka Maharṣi has narrated in this way the account of how Śyāvāśva, son of the seer Arcanānas, who had attained the rank of a seer by praising the Marut deities, married the daughter of King Rathavīti. After Śyāvāśva had praised the Maruts with eleven sūktas, as said before, they favoured Śyāvāśva and departed to their own place. Then Śyāvāśva, knowing that he had become a seer and that three families had been sanctified through him, was delighted, and kept thinking in his mind of the daughter of King Rathavīti whom he had earlier desired. Thereupon the seer Śyāvāśva thought of sending the goddess Night as messenger to King Rathavīti, and prayed to the goddess Night that she should let that king know that he had now truly attained the rank of a seer through the grace of the Maruts. This matter is set forth in two Ṛks beginning with एतं मे स्तोमं (*etaṃ me stomaṃ*) (the 17th and 18th Ṛks of this sūkta). When the goddess Night consented to the seer Śyāvāśva's word and conveyed his errand to King Rathavīti, the king took his daughter with him and came to the presence of the seer Arcanānas, the father of Śyāvāśva. Holding his feet and bowing, with folded hands and in a humble manner, he said: "O seer Arcanānas, I am the king named Rathavīti, of the Dārbha line. Behold, I now bow to you. Formerly, that is, at the time of the sacrifice I performed, when you wished to build a bond with my house and asked that my daughter be given to your son, I refused your word, saying that it was not possible. Forgive that now; do not be angry with me. Behold, I bow to you again. You are a seer's son born in a line of seers, that is, your father too is a seer and you too are a seer, and you are the father of the (newly made) seer Śyāvāśva, that is, your son too is a seer. Therefore forgive the fault I committed formerly, and accept this my daughter as your daughter-in-law." Having prayed thus, he gave that seer a hundred horses and appeased him, and gave his daughter, adorned with divine ornaments, to that seer to be accepted as a daughter-in-law; that is, he gave his daughter in marriage to Śyāvāśva, the son of the seer Arcanānas. At the time of the wedding too, the king gave his daughter, as a gift, horses and cows by the hundred; along with these he gave much wealth and the like. Thereafter that king, having fulfilled his purpose, went to the forest to practise austerity. Śaunaka Maharṣi's description of this account is mentioned here.

ऊर्मॆ मे एतं स्तोमं परा दार्भ्याय वह-हे रात्रि देवि मरुद्भः कृतं स्तोत्रमहं मंत्रदृत् भूत्वा मरुतः स्तुतवानित्येवं दार्भ्यायाभिमुखी, (*ūrmè me etaṃ stomaṃ parā dārbhyāya vaha-he rātri devi marudbhaḥ kṛtaṃ stotramahaṃ maṃtradṛt bhūtvā marutaḥ stutavānityevaṃ dārbhyāyābhimukhī,*)

श्यावाश्वय पराज्मुखी सती वह! (*śyāvāśvaya parājmukhī satī vaha!*) It was said earlier that the seer Śyāvāśva attained the rank of a seer by praising the Maruts. Earlier, in the conversation held at the time of the sacrifice between King Rathavīti and his father the seer Arcanānas for the sake of the marriage ⟨NOTE:586⟩, the king said in reply to Arcanānas's request: "You ask that my daughter be given to your son Śyāvāśva. But your son is not a seer who has seen a sūkta; in our line there is no custom of giving a maiden to one who is not a seer. Therefore it is not possible to give my daughter in marriage to Śyāvāśva." Śyāvāśva, who had been brooding in his mind over what was said, now that he had become a seer, prayed to the goddess Night that she should act as messenger and help his marriage, by making this known to King Rathavīti and telling him that the obstacles and hindrances he had mentioned earlier were now removed, so that he should give his daughter. When Night consented, saying she would fulfil his request, he sent a message to King Rathavīti through that goddess in these words: "I have now praised the Maruts with sūkta mantras and, by their grace, have become a seer who has seen mantras. The obstacle you raised, that a maiden cannot be given to one who is not a seer, has now been removed. Therefore give your daughter in marriage to me." Such was the errand he sent through the goddess Night. While sending it thus, it is described here that he said to Night, the messenger: "Set out facing Dārbhya Rathavīti and make my word known." The goddess Night, when leaving Śyāvāśva, was to go turned away from him, that is, leaving him behind with her back to him, and when going to Dārbhya, to go facing him (in front of him); so Śyāvāśva has instructed.

गिरो देवि रथीरिव-हे रात्रि देवि मरुद्विषयाः स्तुतीः रथीरिव परा वह । (*giro devi rathīriva-he rātri devi marudviṣayāḥ stutīḥ rathīriva parā vaha |*) रथी यथाभिप्रेतं,वसु स्थापयित्वाभिमतं देशं प्रापयति तद्वत्। (*rathī yathābhipretaṃ,vasu sthāpayitvābhimataṃ deśaṃ prāpayati tadvat|*) O goddess Night, just as one who travels seated in a chariot loads the things he needs and goes to the place he wishes, so take the praises I have made concerning the Maruts to the king Dārbhya Rathavīti and make them known to him. Thus the seer has described the messenger Night as comparable to the chariot-rider, and the praises addressed to the Maruts as comparable to the goods carried in the chariot.
notes: ನಾಂ printed; read as ವಾಂ

en: "O Ūrmyā (Night), speak also on my behalf. What is said? Thus: in Rathavīti, who has performed the Soma sacrifice, my desire concerning his daughter does not depart, does not cease." Thus say.
- कामः (*kāmaḥ*)—the love that is in Rathavīti's daughter
- न अप वेति (*na apa veti*)—is not in the least tarnished
- सुतसोमे (*sutasome*)—who has performed the Soma sacrifice
O goddess Night, make known to Rathavīti, who has performed the Soma sacrifice, explaining to him that my love for his daughter is not in the least tarnished.
And say on my behalf to Rathaviti, when the libation is poured out
my love (for your daughter) does not depart.

Śyāvāśva, who seeks the daughter of King Rathavīti in marriage, asks that it be made known that the affection he formerly had for that maiden, with whom he was infatuated, has not diminished in the least, and that even now his love for her is exceedingly great.

Sāyaṇa cites a verse: Śyāvāśva, having given his daughter and so fulfilled his purpose, then went to the forest; seeing Rathavīti practising austerity, with the seer's eye, in the lovely back (ridge) of the Himavat, he said that he dwells here. He then explains the Ṛk: this Rathavīti is मघवा (*maghavā*), that is, wealthy; गोमतीरनु (*gomatīranu*) means following the rivers that have water, he dwells on the banks of the rivers; पर्वतेषु (*parvateṣu*) means on the border regions of the Himavat mountain, he has taken shelter, that is, rests.
- गोमतीरनु (*gomatīranu*)—on the bank of the river Gomatī
- पर्वतेषु (*parvateṣu*)—in the border region of the Himavat mountain
The wealthy Rathavīti is dwelling on the bank of the river Gomatī. He has taken refuge in the border region of the Himavat mountain.
This opulent Rathaviti dwells upon the (banks of the) Gomati (river) and has his home on (the skirts of) the (Himalaya) mountains.
The commentator has stated a verse here concerning this Ṛk. Its explanation is as follows.

कन्यां दत्वा कृतार्थं तं श्यानाश्वोऽथ वनं गतं । रथवीतिं तपस्यंतं संप्रेक्ष्यार्षण चक्षुषा ॥ (*kanyāṃ datvā kṛtārthaṃ taṃ śyānāśvo 'tha vanaṃ gataṃ | rathavītiṃ tapasyaṃtaṃ saṃprekṣyārṣaṇa cakṣuṣā ‖*) ⟨NOTE:587⟩

King Rathavīti, having given his daughter in marriage to the seer Śyāvāśva and thinking himself blessed, went to a penance-grove to practise austerity. That King Rathavīti had gone to the penance-grove and was practising austerity there, the seer Śyāvāśva knew by his austerity-vision, or by the far-seeing vision natural to a seer, which can know past, future and present; and he spoke the sentence stated in this Ṛk, that King Rathavīti dwells (practising austerity) on the skirts of the Himavat mountain, on the bank of the river named Gomatī.

गोमतीः-गोमतीरनूदकवतीर्नदीः । (*gomatīḥ-gomatīranūdakavatīrnadīḥ |*) Here the plural form गोमतीः (*gomatīḥ*) is used. It means a river with abundant water. Or else it is more fitting to say that it is a river by the name of Gomatī. Concerning this river the Western scholar Wilson has said this: "गोमतीः (*gomatīḥ*) according to the comment, means, having water, rivers, being in the plural; as the name of a river it would be the Gomati river in Oudh (Ayodhya) which rises in the skirts of the first range of the Himalayas; or it may be a river of the same appellation more to the north-west, rising in Kulu, a feeder of the Beyas or Vyasa (the Beas river)".
notes: ಪಿನ್ನಥಃ printed; read as ಪಿನ್ವಥಃ

en: The connection is: I have seen the true orb of the Sun, which is covered (hidden) by water and is everlasting. "Where you two have your abode" means the abode of Mitra and Varuṇa is in the orb of the Sun. This is well known from passages such as Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-115-1 ⟨NOTE:591⟩, Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-61-1 and Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-63-1, which speak of the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa. "Where they release the horses" means that the praisers release the horses that stand in that orb, that is, horses held back by Mandeha and others.

Or else the praisers urge the horses by praise to run swiftly. In which orb ten hundreds, that is, a thousand rays abide, of such an orb, the best and most praiseworthy among the gods who have bodies, that is, who are possessed of splendour, such as Agni and the others (the genitive is to be taken either in the sense of possession or as a genitive of different relation). Or: the best of the bodies of the gods; for the orb is, as it were, the body of the Sun; that orb I have seen. Or it is to be explained thus: between you two I have seen the orb of the Sun, since there is the Vedic statement मैत्रं वा अहः (*maitraṃ vā ahaḥ*) (Tai. Brā. 1-7-10-1): Mitra himself is the Sun, with the Āditya in view.
notes: abbreviation ಋಗ್ವೇ. printed

en: - यत्र (*yatra*)—in which orb of the sun (O Mitra and Varuṇa)
- अश्वान् (*aśvān*)—the horses (held back by Mandeha and others)
- दश शता (*daśa śatā*)—(in which orb) the rays numbering a thousand
- सह तस्थुः (*saha tasthuḥ*)—abide together, and such a one (and that which is)
- वपुषां (*vapuṣāṃ*)—of all the bodies of the form of splendour
- सूर्यस्य तत् (*sūryasya tat*)—the orb of the sun
notes: ಚಾಗಮರ್ನಾಥಂ unclear in the machine-read text

en: O Mitra and Varuṇa, I have seen the orb of the Sun in which your abode is, where the praisers release the horses held back by Mandeha and others, in which a thousand rays gather together, which is the most excellent of all the bodies of the form of splendour of the shining gods, the one support, of everlasting duration, of the nature of truth, and covered by water.

I Have beheld the permanent orb of the sun, your (dwelling place), concealed by water, where (the hymns of the pious) liberate ( his ) steeds ; where a thousand rays abide together ; the one most excellent of the (embodied) forms of the gods.

सूर्यस्य ऋतं ऋतेन अपिहितं ध्रुवं अपश्यं-सूर्यस्य (*sūryasya ṛtaṃ ṛtena apihitaṃ dhruvaṃ apaśyaṃ-sūryasya*) सत्यभूतमुदकेना च्छादितं शाश्वतं मंडलमपश्यं । (*satyabhūtamudakenā cchāditaṃ śāśvataṃ maṃḍalamapaśyaṃ |*) The seer describes here that he saw the orb of the Sun, of the nature of truth and everlasting, covered by water, that is, by the cloud-orb,

or enveloped. Why is the orb of the Sun described in this Ṛk addressed in praise to Mitra and Varuṇa? Because Mitra and Varuṇa have a relation to the orb of the Sun. The seer explains that in the following sentences. In this sentence the Sun is described by the epithets ऋतं सत्यं (*ṛtaṃ satyaṃ*), because the Sun (Āditya) is the Supreme Brahman. That this Supreme Brahman is of the nature of truth and everlasting, that is, imperishable, is described in many Vedic sentences. In the sentence असावादित्यो ब्रह्मेति (*asāvādityo brahmeti*) (Tai. Ā. 2-1-1) it is clearly stated that this very Āditya, visible to our eyes, is Brahman. On the point that the Supreme Brahman is of the nature of truth, the sentence ऋतग्ं सत्यं पररॆ ब्रह्म पुरुषं कृष्णपिंगळं (*ṛtagṃ satyaṃ pararè brahma puruṣaṃ kṛṣṇapiṃgaḷaṃ*) (Tai. U. 4-24 ⟨NOTE:593⟩) makes this clear. Therefore it is natural that the seer, regarding the Sun as of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, praised him with epithets that describe the qualities of Brahman. In the expression ऋतेन अपिहितं (*ṛtena apihitaṃ*), for the word ऋत (*ṛta*) Yāska has given the explanation ऋतमित्युदकनाम प्रत्यतं भवति (*ṛtamityudakanāma pratyataṃ bhavati*) (Ni. 2-25). That is, the word ऋत (*ṛta*) means water. By his rays the Sun draws up (in the form of vapour) the water that is in the sea and other reservoirs. The water drawn up in this way becomes cloud and, remaining in the sky, covers, that is, hides, the orb of the Sun. Therefore here the meaning is the orb of the Sun covered by water, that is, covered by the cloud-orb made of water. The word ऋत (*ṛta*) is read among the six names of truth beginning with बट् (*baṭ*) (Ni. 3-13), and सत्यं वा यज्ञं वा (*satyaṃ vā yajñaṃ vā*) (Ni. 4-19): the word ऋत (*ṛta*) also has the meaning truth or sacrifice.

यत्र वां (स्थितिः)—सूर्यमंडले मित्रावरुणयोः स्थितिः । (*yatra vāṃ (sthitiḥ)—sūryamaṃḍale mitrāvaruṇayoḥ sthitiḥ |*) In explaining what the nature of the orb of the Sun is, the seer has said यत्र वां (स्थितिः) (*yatra vāṃ (sthitiḥ)*): your dwelling, O Mitra and Varuṇa, is in the orb of the Sun. In this matter:
चित्रं देवानामुदगादनीकं चक्षुर्मित्रस्य वरुणस्याग्नेः (*citraṃ devānāmudagādanīkaṃ cakṣurmitrasya varuṇasyāgneḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-115-1)
उद्वां चक्षुर्वरुण सुप्रतीकं देवयोरेति सूर्यस्ततन्वान् । (*udvāṃ cakṣurvaruṇa supratīkaṃ devayoreti sūryastatanvān |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-61-1)
चक्षुर्मित्रस्य वरुणस्य देवश्चर्मेव यः समविव्यक् तमांसि । (*cakṣurmitrasya varuṇasya devaścarmeva yaḥ samavivyak tamāṃsi |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-63-1)
In these and many other Ṛks the fact that Mitra and Varuṇa are stationed in the orb of the Sun is made plain.

यत्र अश्वान् विमुचंति—यस्मिन्मंडले स्थितानश्वान् विमोचयंति स्तोतारः । मंदेहादिभिर्निरुद्धानित्यर्थः । अथवा शीघ्रधावनाय स्तुत्या प्रेरयंति । (*yatra aśvān vimucaṃti—yasminmaṃḍale sthitānaśvān vimocayaṃti stotāraḥ | maṃdehādibhirniruddhānityarthaḥ | athavā śīghradhāvanāya stutyā prerayaṃti |*)

Sāyaṇa has given two kinds of meaning for this sentence. One meaning is that the praisers pray with praises in order to urge the horses of the Sun to run swiftly; or else that certain asuras named Mandeha hold back the horses of the Sun and obstruct the Sun's course. Who are the asuras who dwell on the island of Mandeha, and what is the reason why they obstruct the Sun's course? These and other matters are told as follows in Tai. Ā. 2-2:

रक्षाग्ंसि ह वा पुरोऽनुवाके तपोऽग्रमतिष्ठंत तान्प्रजापतिर्वरेणोपामंत्रयत तानि वरमवृणीतादित्यो नो योद्धा इति तान्प्रजापतिरब्रवीद्योधयध्वमिति तस्मादुत्तिष्ठंतग्ं ह वा तानि रक्षाग्स्यादित्यं योधयंति (*rakṣāgṃsi ha vā puro 'nuvāke tapo 'gramatiṣṭhaṃta tānprajāpatirvareṇopāmaṃtrayata tāni varamavṛṇītādityo no yoddhā iti tānprajāpatirabravīdyodhayadhvamiti tasmāduttiṣṭhaṃtagṃ ha vā tāni rakṣāgsyādityaṃ yodhayaṃti*) यावदस्तमन्वगात्तानिह वा एतानि रक्षाग्ंसि गायत्रियाभिमंत्रितेनांभसा शाम्यंति तदु ह वा एते ब्रह्मवादिनः पूर्वाभिमुखास्संध्यायां गाय त्रियाभिमंत्रिता आप ऊर्ध्व० विक्षिपंति ता एता आपो वज्री भूत्वा तानि रक्षाग्ंसि मंदेहारुणे द्वीपे प्रक्षिपंति यत्पदक्षिणं प्रक्रमंति (*yāvadastamanvagāttāniha vā etāni rakṣāgṃsi gāyatriyābhimaṃtritenāṃbhasā śāmyaṃti tadu ha vā ete brahmavādinaḥ pūrvābhimukhāssaṃdhyāyāṃ gāya triyābhimaṃtritā āpa ūrdhva0 vikṣipaṃti tā etā āpo vajrī bhūtvā tāni rakṣāgṃsi maṃdehāruṇe dvīpe prakṣipaṃti yatpadakṣiṇaṃ prakramaṃti*) तेन पाप्स्नानमवधून्वंत्युद्यंतमस्तंयंतमादित्यमभिध्यायन्कुर्वन् ब्राह्मणो विद्वान्कलं भद्रमश्नुतेऽसावादित्यो ब्रह्मेति ब्रह्मैव सन् ब्रह्माप्येति य एवं वेद ॥ (*tena pāpsnānamavadhūnvaṃtyudyaṃtamastaṃyaṃtamādityamabhidhyāyankurvan brāhmaṇo vidvānkalaṃ bhadramaśnute 'sāvādityo brahmeti brahmaiva san brahmāpyeti ya evaṃ veda ‖*) (Tai. Ā. 2-2)

Formerly the rākṣasas practised fierce austerity. Then the god Prajāpati appeared before them and asked what boon they wished. They then prayed: "Grant us the power and the opportunity to fight with the Sun." Prajāpati consented, saying "So be it." For that reason, as soon as the Sun rises the rākṣasas begin to fight with him, and they go on fighting until the time of his setting. But they can be driven away by water purified by the recitation of the Gāyatrī. For that reason the Brahmavādins, at the morning twilight (and at the evening twilight too), recite the Gāyatrī and offer the arghya with water purified by it. These drops of water offered as arghya turn into thunderbolts and hurl the rākṣasas into the island named Mandehāruṇa. Thereafter the Brahmavādins, by worship accompanied by circumambulation and obeisance, remove their sin. The Brāhmaṇa (the knower of Brahman) who knows this principle, if at sunrise and also at sunset he recites the Gāyatrī, offers the arghya, and thereby worships and meditates on the Āditya, obtains every kind of good (welfare). The Āditya is the Supreme Brahman. The man who, knowing that the Āditya, to be worshipped through the Gāyatrī, is Brahman, performs the worship, attains union with Brahman and becomes of the form of Brahman: thus the recitation of the Gāyatrī is praised.

यत्र दश शता सह तस्थुः देवानां वपुषं श्रेष्ठं—यस्मिंश्च मंडले सहस्रसंख्याका रश्मयस्तिष्ठंति तादृशं देवानां वपुष्मतां तेजोवतामग्न्यादीनां प्रशस्यं । (*yatra daśa śatā saha tasthuḥ devānāṃ vapuṣaṃ śreṣṭhaṃ—yasmiṃśca maṃḍale sahasrasaṃkhyākā raśmayastiṣṭhaṃti tādṛśaṃ devānāṃ vapuṣmatāṃ tejovatāmagnyādīnāṃ praśasyaṃ |*) In that orb of the Sun thousands of rays dwell. And that orb of the Sun, being endowed with a mass of splendour, is of the nature of the bodies of the gods such as Agni. The bodies of the gods, unlike the bodies of men, are free of any earthly connection and are distinguished by splendour. The matter stated here is that the orb of the Sun itself is the dwelling place of the bodies of such gods. Or else the commentator has said that another kind of meaning of this sentence is also possible: मंडलं हि सूर्यस्य वपुःस्थानीयं । तन्मंडलमपश्यं । नां युवयोर्मध्यॆ सूर्यस्य मंडलमपश्यमिति व्याख्येयं । मैत्रं ना अहः । वारुणी रात्रिः (तै ब्रा. १-७-१०-१) इति श्रुतेर्मित्रसैव सूर्यत्वादित्याशयेन । (*maṃḍalaṃ hi sūryasya vapuḥsthānīyaṃ | tanmaṃḍalamapaśyaṃ | nāṃ yuvayormadhyè sūryasya maṃḍalamapaśyamiti vyākhyeyaṃ | maitraṃ nā ahaḥ | vāruṇī rātriḥ (tai brā. 1-7-10-1) iti śrutermitrasaiva sūryatvādityāśayena |*) That is, the orb of the Sun is like a body to the Sun. The seer says: "I have seen such an orb of the Sun." Or else the meaning may be given: "Between you, Mitra and Varuṇa, I have seen the orb of the Sun." How? Mitra is the presiding deity of the day and Varuṇa the presiding deity of the night. Therefore the meaning may be explained also thus: "In the midst of day and night I have seen the day, or the orb of the Sun."
notes: erectcd printed; read erected

en: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, that greatness of you two is excellent, that is, exceedingly praiseworthy." What is it? The Āditya, who is ever-moving or the impeller of all, through the days (the sentence continues in the next part). ⟨NOTE:594⟩

Through days connected with the rainy season he has milked the waters that stood still. Moreover, of the Sun who moves by himself (स्वसरस्य (*svasarasya*)) you two increase all the cows, that is, the lights that gladden the worlds. Of you two there is one unrivalled पविः (*paviḥ*). The word पविः (*paviḥ*) means the rim of a chariot wheel, by the statement of Yāska (Ni. 5-5). Even so, here by indirect meaning it stands for the chariot, since a wheel alone cannot revolve. The one chariot of you two goes round in succession, that is, revolves in order.
notes: ಸ್ಥಾಣಂ printed; the verse has ಸ್ಥೂಣಂ

en: - मित्रावरुणा (*mitrāvaruṇā*)—O Mitra and Varuṇa, (by which greatness of yours)
- अहभिः (*ahabhiḥ*)—through the days that help him
- स्वसरस्य (*svasarasya*)—of the Āditya who is of the nature of moving
- अनु आ ववर्त (*anu ā vavarta*)—goes about everywhere eternally
