en: O Mitra and Varuṇa, that greatness of yours, by which the ever-moving Āditya, through the days that help him, makes the waters that stood motionless pour down, is exceedingly praiseworthy. You nourish all the rays of the Āditya, whose nature is to move and which delight the world. The one chariot common to you both goes about everywhere eternally.
Exceeding is that your greatness, Mitra and Varuna, whereby the
evet-moving sun has, through (succeeding, days, milked forth the stationary
waters : you augment all the (world-illumining) rays of the self-resolving
(sun) : the one chariot of you two (perpetually) goes round.
In this Ṛk the greatness of Mitra and Varuṇa is described. The seer describes it in three different ways in three sentences.

ईर्मा अहभिः तस्थुषीः दुदुहे तत् वां महित्वं— ईर्मा सततगंता सर्वस्य प्रेरको वादित्योऽहभिरहोभिर्वर्षतुसंबंधिभिः स्थावरभूता अपो दुदुहे दुग्धे । (*īrmā ahabhiḥ tasthuṣīḥ duduhe tat vāṃ mahitvaṃ— īrmā satatagaṃtā sarvasya prerako vādityo 'habhirahobhirvarṣatusaṃbaṃdhibhiḥ sthāvarabhūtā apo duduhe dugdhe |*) Because he is of a nature to move at all times, ईर्मा (*īrmā*) means the Āditya. Or

Because he impels everything, ईर्मा (*īrmā*) means the Āditya. This Āditya, by the days, causes the motionless waters to rain. That is, the sun or Āditya spreads his sharp rays, draws up the waters that lie in motionless reservoirs such as the ocean, turns them into cloud, and through them makes rain fall on the earth in the days of the rainy season. In this way the seer describes the sun's act of raining as the very excess of greatness of you, Mitra and Varuṇa.

सु स्वसरस्य धेनाः विश्वाः पिन्नथ (*su svasarasya dhenāḥ viśvāḥ pinnatha*)—It is you who nourish the world-pleasing rays of the Āditya, whose nature is to move about. This is another greatness of yours.

नां एकः पविः अनु आ ववर्त (*nāṃ ekaḥ paviḥ anu ā vavarta*)⟨NOTE:597⟩—Yāska has given the explanation of the word पवि (*pavi*): पविरिति रथस्य नेमिः पवी रथनेमिर्भवति (*paviriti rathasya nemiḥ pavī rathanemirbhavati*) (Ni. 5-5). पवि (*pavi*) means the felly of a chariot. Here the word is used in order to denote the chariot itself. O Mitra and Varuṇa, the one chariot that is common to you both, that is the same for both, goes about everywhere at all times. That is to say, of you two, Mitra and Varuṇa, each does not have a separate chariot; there is one chariot from both. That chariot is of a nature to move in every place and at all times: thus the praise of the chariot of Mitra and Varuṇa is expressed here. This is the third greatness of Mitra and Varuṇa.

मित्रराजानौ (*mitrarājānau*) is explained thus: those from whose presence the praisers, who are friends, become kings, lords and masters. "O Varuṇa" is in the dual with reference to its counterpart. O two gods, by your energies, that is, by your own powers, you uphold the earth and also the heaven. O two gods, you make the plants grow by sending rain. You nourish the cows, that is, you make cattle, horses and the like thrive; for that purpose send down the rain, impel it downwards. O जीरदानू (*jīradānū*), quick givers.
- मित्रराजाना वरुणा (*mitrarājānā varuṇā*)—O Mitra and Varuṇa, radiant ones and lords

O Mitra and Varuṇa, radiant ones and lords, by your energies you have upheld the earth and the heaven. O excellent givers, make the plants (vegetation and the like) grow. Nourish the cows. Pour down rain.
Royal Mitra and Varuna, you uphold by your energies. earth and heaven: prompt benefactors cause the plant to grow, give nourishment to the cattle, send dowm⟨NOTE:598⟩ the rain.

मित्रराजाना-मित्रभूताः स्तोतारो राजानाः स्वामिनः ईश्वरा भवंति ययोः सकातात्तौ मित्रराजान् । (*mitrarājānā-mitrabhūtāḥ stotāro rājānāḥ svāminaḥ īśvarā bhavaṃti yayoḥ sakātāttau mitrarājān |*). Out of friendliness the worshippers who praise you become, by your grace, kings or lords over all. Thus he explained the meaning of this word: Mitra and Varuṇa, who possess such greatness.

महोभिः पृथिवीं उत द्यां आधारयतं (*mahobhiḥ pṛthivīṃ uta dyāṃ ādhārayataṃ*)—O Mitra and Varuṇa, you uphold the earth and the atmosphere or heaven by your own power. The meaning is that it is by your excess of greatness that the earth and the atmosphere perform their respective functions.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, let your horses, सुयुजः (*suyujaḥ*), well yoked to the chariot, bring you hither. With reins held fast by the charioteer let them come towards us. The form of the water (the verse's ghee) follows you. Further, प्रदिवि (*pradivi*) is a name meaning ancient; the ancient rivers come to us through your favour.
- आ वहंतु (*ā vahaṃtu*)—let them bring you here
- यतरश्मयः (*yataraśmayaḥ*)—having reins held by the charioteer
- उप यंतु (*upa yaṃtu*)—let them come near us
- उप क्षरंति (*upa kṣaraṃti*)—flow (through your favour alone)

O Mitra and Varuṇa, let your horses, yoked to the chariot, bring you here. With reins held by the charioteer, let them come near us. The form of the water follows you alone. The ancient rivers flow through your favour alone.
May your easily-harnessed horses bear you both (hither), and with well-guided reins come down; the embodied form of water follows you, the rivers flow as of old.

यतरश्मयः (*yataraśmayaḥ*)—सारथिनियतप्रग्रहाः (*sārathiniyatapragrahāḥ*). Here रश्मयः (*raśmayaḥ*) means ropes, or the reins that restrain horses. When a charioteer drives the horses of a chariot, he keeps their reins under his control and by their help urges the horses to go wherever he wishes. Therefore यतरश्मयः (*yataraśmayaḥ*) means horses whose reins are subject to the charioteer.

श्रुतां (*śrutāṃ*) means well known. अमतिं (*amatiṃ*) is a word for form; the meaning is the splendour of the body. Increasing that, बर्हिः (*barhiḥ*) is the sacrifice; just as it is guarded by the yajus, the mantra, so you two guard and protect the broad form, नमस्वंता (*namasvaṃtā*), possessing food, O धृतदक्षा (*dhṛtadakṣā*), possessed of strength, O Mitra, O Varuṇa, O Mitra and Varuṇa. Being such as described, you sit on the गर्ते (*garte*), the chariot, in the midst of the इळासु (*iḷāsu*), the sacrificial grounds. The chariot too is called garta, says Yāska (Ni. 3-5): आ रोहथो वरुण मित्र गर्तं (*ā rohatho varuṇa mitra gartaṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-62-8)⟨NOTE:600⟩.
- मित्र, वरुण (*mitra, varuṇa*)—O Mitra and Varuṇa
- अमतिं (*amatiṃ*)—the form (the splendour of the body)
- इळासु अंतः (*iḷāsu aṃtaḥ*)—in the midst of the sacrificial grounds

O Mitra and Varuṇa, possessing food and acquired strength, making your well-known form increase, like the sacrifice that is protected by the mantra, and protecting that same extensive form, sit on your chariots in the midst of the sacrificial grounds.

Augmenting the well-known and ample form (of man), in like manner as the sacred grass is preserved by prayer, do you, Mitra and Varuna, who are invigorated by (sacrificial) viands, and abound in food, ascend your car in the midst of the place of sacrifice.

बर्हिः (*barhiḥ*)—The word बर्हिः (*barhiḥ*) is read both among the names of the atmosphere (Ni. 2-10) and among the names of water (Ni. 2-24). Besides, Yāska says बर्हिः परिबर्हणात् (*barhiḥ paribarhaṇāt*) (Ni. 8-9). At sacrifices and the like, so that the gods may come and sit, seats are prepared that are soft with darbha grass. These seats are made of darbha grass cut to one and the same measure. Such evenly cut darbha grass, or a seat of darbha grass, is called बर्हिः (*barhiḥ*). In the present Ṛk this word is used in the sense of sacrifice.

गर्तॆ (*gartè*)—Regarding the meaning of this word Yāska has given the explanation: रथोऽपिगर्त उच्यते गृणातेः स्तुतिकर्मणः । स्तुततमं यानं । आरोहथो वरुण मित्र गर्त० इत्यपि निगमो भवति । (*ratho 'pigarta ucyate gṛṇāteḥ stutikarmaṇaḥ | stutatamaṃ yānaṃ | ārohatho varuṇa mitra garta0 ityapi nigamo bhavati |*) (Ni. 3-5). That is, the chariot too is called garta. For this word is formed from the root meaning to praise and indicates the meaning of an excellent vehicle. An example in this matter is the scriptural sentence आरोहथो वरुण मित्र गर्त० (*ārohatho varuṇa mitra garta0*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5.62-8).

अक्रविहस्ता (*akravihastā*) means those whose hands are not miserly, that is, heroes in giving. For whom? For the सुकृते (*sukṛte*), the good praiser. परस्पा (*paraspā*) means protectors from beyond, guardians. O Varuṇa, O Mitra and Varuṇa: the sacrificer whom you protect in the midst of the इळासु (*iḷāsu*), the sacrificial grounds, to that good-doer be liberal-handed and protectors; such is the construction. Further, you two, shining and not angry, both together bear क्षत्रं (*kṣatraṃ*), wealth, and a house of the palace kind furnished with a thousand pillars, with many supporting posts, for the sacrificer who does good. Or else, क्षत्रं (*kṣatraṃ*) is strength, and you two together bear a chariot furnished with countless pillars and चागमर्नाथं (*cāgamarnāthaṃ*)⟨NOTE:601⟩.
- इळासु अंतः (*iḷāsu aṃtaḥ*)—in the midst of the sacrificial grounds
- त्रासाथे (*trāsāthe*)—you protect, to such a one
- सुकृते (*sukṛte*)—to the sacrificer who does good deeds
- सहस्रस्थूणं (*sahasrasthūṇaṃ*)—furnished with a thousand pillars, of the nature of a house

O Mitra and Varuṇa, the sacrificer whom you protect in the midst of the sacrificial grounds, to such a doer of good deeds be generous-handed givers and bestowers of excellent protection. You two, lords and free from anger, together bear wealth of the nature of a house furnished with a thousand pillars.

Be open-handed and benignant to the performer of pious acts, whom you protect in the midst of the place of sacrifice ; for you two, who are sovereigns, and free from wrath, uphold together a mansion of a thousand columns.

सहस्रस्थूणं (*sahasrasthūṇaṃ*)—सहस्रस्थूणमनेकावष्टंभकस्तंभोपेतं सौधादिरूपं गृहं च बिभृतः । (*sahasrasthūṇamanekāvaṣṭaṃbhakastaṃbhopetaṃ saudhādirūpaṃ gṛhaṃ ca bibhṛtaḥ |*). The commentator has taken this word to mean a great palace or house with a thousand pillars. Here "thousand" may be taken to mean many. A fine house with many pillars means a palace or mansion of the highest class (Mansion or Palace with a number of pillars). Ordinary houses do not have many pillars. Only palaces and the like that are built large and in an excellent manner are constructed with many pillars. Therefore here सहस्रस्थूणं (*sahasrasthūṇaṃ*) means an excellent palace built in an excellent manner. Or it may also be understood that you sit, for going to the sacrifice, in your chariot, which is strong and furnished with many pillars.

The chariot of these two is हिरण्यनिर्णिक् (*hiraṇyanirṇik*), of golden form; निर्णिगिति रूपनाम (*nirṇigiti rūpanāma*): it is a word for form. Of this chariot the स्थूणा (*sthūṇā*), the pins and the like, are अयः (*ayaḥ*); this is a name for gold; the meaning is that they are products of iron, or made of iron. Such a chariot shines in the sky, in the atmosphere. Like what? Like अश्वाजनी (*aśvājanī*): the अश्वा (*aśvā*) are the clouds, whose nature is to pervade; she who drives them is the lightning; like her it shines in the sky. Further, in an auspicious, that is, a gracious or praiseworthy place, the divine sacrificial ground, or in the तिल्विले (*tilvile*) (he explains: the root तिल (*tila*) in the sense of being unctuous; तिलुः (*tiluḥ*) is that field whose earth is moist, which is तिल्विलं (*tilvilaṃ*), the divine sacrificial ground; a field made moist by ghee, soma and the like and auspicious), there is set up the स्फूणा (*sphūṇā*), the sacrificial post. मध्वः (*madhvaḥ*), filled with honey, गर्तस्य गर्तं रथं (*gartasya gartaṃ rathaṃ*), the chariot, we would obtain (the genitive stands for the accusative; अधि (*adhi*) is a filler). Or else, on the chariot we would place the honey, the soma juice; that is the meaning.
- हिरण्यनिर्णिक् (*hiraṇyanirṇik*)—made of gold (this chariot of Mitra and Varuṇa)
- भद्रे क्षेत्रे (*bhadre kṣetre*)—in an auspicious place, whether
- तिल्विले (*tilvile*)—in the place of divine sacrifice, or

The chariot of these Mitra and Varuṇa is made of gold. The pins of this chariot are made of iron. This chariot shines in the atmosphere like lightning. Whether in an auspicious place or in the place of divine sacrifice where the sacrificial post is set up, let us fill the chariot with sweet soma juice.

The substance (of their chariot) is of gold ; its pillars are of iron, and it shines in the firmament like lightning: may we load the vehicle with the libation in an auspicious place, or in the sacrificial hall, (where the columns) are erectcd⟨NOTE:602⟩.

In this Ṛk there is a description of the chariot of Mitra and Varuṇa. Their chariot is made of gold. In order that the pins may be firm, they are made of iron. Such a chariot shines in the atmosphere very brilliantly, like lightning.

तिल्विले (*tilvile*)—For this word Sāyaṇa says: तिलुः (तिल स्नेहने) स्निग्धा इला भूमिर्यस्य तत् क्षेत्रं तिल्विलं देवयजनं । धृतसोमादिना स्निग्धे भद्रे च क्षेत्रे । (*tiluḥ (tila snehane) snigdhā ilā bhūmiryasya tat kṣetraṃ tilvilaṃ devayajanaṃ | dhṛtasomādinā snigdhe bhadre ca kṣetre |*). तिलुः (*tiluḥ*) means unctuous, moistened, that is, soaked with liquid substances such as ghee and soma juice

is the meaning. इला (*ilā*) means the earth. Because ghee, soma and the like are used liberally at the sacrifice, it is natural that the ground there is drenched by those juices, which are spilled from time to time. Therefore he has explained the word तिल्विल (*tilvila*) as such a drenched place, that is, the sacrificial ground.

उषसो व्युष्टौ (*uṣaso vyuṣṭau*) means in the morning. सूर्यस्योदितोवितावुदये (*sūryasyoditovitāvudaye*): the sunrise; that very time is stated in another way. At that time, O Varuṇa, O Mitra, you two mount the chariot, हिरण्यरूपं (*hiraṇyarūpaṃ*), golden in form, with iron pillars, with iron pegs, which has arrived at the sacrifice. Therefore you two behold अदितिं (*aditiṃ*), the unbroken earth, and दितिं (*ditiṃ*), the broken, the creatures and the like.
- वरुण, मित्र (*varuṇa, mitra*)—O Mitra and Varuṇa
- उषसो व्युष्टौ (*uṣaso vyuṣṭau*)—at the time of the appearing of the dawn
- सूर्यस्य उदिता (*sūryasya uditā*)—and at the time of sunrise
- दितिं च (*ditiṃ ca*)—and the creatures that are in parts

O Mitra and Varuṇa, at the time of the appearing of the dawn and at the time of the rising of the sun, you mount your chariot, which is golden in form and has iron pillars. Thereafter you behold the unbroken earth and the creatures that are in parts.
At the break of dawn, at the rising of the sun, ascend, Mitra and Varuna, your golden-bodied, iron-pillared car, and thence behold theearth⟨NOTE:604⟩ and its inhabitants

उषसो व्युष्टौ सूर्यस्य उदिता (*uṣaso vyuṣṭau sūryasya uditā*)—At the time of the appearing of the dawn and when the sun rises: both these expressions convey one and the same meaning, in the morning. When the sacrificial rite is going on in the morning, as soon as the Hotṛ invokes you, you mount your golden chariot with iron pillars in order to come to the sacrificial ground: thus the seer describes the coming of Mitra and Varuṇa.

अदितिं दितिं च चक्षाथे (*aditiṃ ditiṃ ca cakṣāthe*)—अदितिमखंडनीयां भूमिं दितिं खंडितां प्रजादिकं च पश्यथः । (*aditimakhaṃḍanīyāṃ bhūmiṃ ditiṃ khaṃḍitāṃ prajādikaṃ ca paśyathaḥ |*). The commentator has explained the word अदिति (*aditi*) as the earth, which has no divisions, that is, which is not divided into separate parts but is a single great whole of one form; and the word दिति (*diti*) as: you will behold the people who are in parts, that is, who are separate. When Mitra and Varuṇa, seated in their golden chariot, come by the path of the atmosphere to the sacrificial ground on the earth, they see first the earth and afterwards the people on it; that is, the earth first and then the people there come within the sight of Mitra and Varuṇa, who sit in the chariot looking downwards: this is the meaning suggested.

Application: at the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice यद्वंहिष्ठं (*yadvaṃhiṣṭhaṃ*), the ninth verse, is the yājyā for the offering to Mitra and Varuṇa at the second new moon. It is also stated in the sūtra: आ नो मित्रावरुणा यद्वंहिष्ठं नातिविधे सुदानू (*ā no mitrāvaruṇā yadvaṃhiṣṭhaṃ nātividhe sudānū*) (Ā. 2.14). In the animal sacrifice of Mitra and Varuṇa it is the yājyā for the offering; it is stated in the sūtra: यद्वंहिष्ठं नातिविधे सुदानू हिरण्यगर्भः समवर्तताग्रे (*yadvaṃhiṣṭhaṃ nātividhe sudānū hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre*) (A. 3-8)⟨NOTE:605⟩. O सुदानू (*sudānū*), good givers, O protectors of the world, you two bear that बंहिष्ठं (*baṃhiṣṭhaṃ*), most abundant, unbroken शर्म (*śarma*), happiness or a house, which is नातिविधे (*nātividhe*), impossible to pierce through; this is a qualifier of शर्म (*śarma*). With that protection protect us, O Mitra and Varuṇa. May we, desiring to win riches, wishing to conquer the riches of our enemies, be so.
- सुदानू (*sudānū*)—O Mitra and Varuṇa, excellent givers
- नातिविधे (*nātividhe*)—that cannot be cut through by others
- यत् (*yat*)—whatever happiness and protection you possess
- सिषासंतः (*siṣāsaṃtaḥ*)—we who desire to obtain wealth
- जिगीवांसः (*jigīvāṃsaḥ*)—having the power to conquer enemies and obtain their riches
- स्याम (*syāma*)—bless us that we may become

O Mitra and Varuṇa, excellent givers, you who are protectors of the world, protect us by that most abundant, unbroken happiness and protection, which cannot be cut through by others, that you possess. O Mitra and Varuṇa, bless us who desire to obtain wealth that we may become possessed of the power to conquer our enemies and obtain their riches.

Munificent Mitra and Varuna, protectors of the universe, (it is yours to grant) exceeding and perfect felicity, such as it is impossible to disturb: bless us with that (felicity), and may we ever be (possessed) of the riches we desire, and be confident of victory (over our enemies.)

At the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice, the ninth Ṛk of this sūkta, यद्वंहिष्ठं (*yadvaṃhiṣṭhaṃ*), is to be used as the yājyā mantra in the offering made to Mitra and Varuṇa at the second new moon; this is set out in the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra by the sūtra आ नो मित्रावरुणा यद्वंहिष्ठं नातिविधे सुदानू (*ā no mitrāvaruṇā yadvaṃhiṣṭhaṃ nātividhe sudānū*) (Ā. 2-14). And likewise in the animal sacrifice connected with Mitra and Varuṇa, when the offering is made, this Ṛk is to be used as the yājyā mantra; this is set out in the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra by the sūtra यद्वंहिष्ठं नातिविधे सुदानू हिरण्यगर्भः समवर्तताग्रे (*yadvaṃhiṣṭhaṃ nātividhe sudānū hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre*) (3-8).
In this Ṛk, which forms the conclusion of the sūkta, the seer prays to Mitra and Varuṇa to give lasting happiness, a house, wealth and the like, and that we may conquer our enemies.
वेदार्थस्य प्रकाशेन तमो हार्दं निवारयन् । (*vedārthasya prakāśena tamo hārdaṃ nivārayan |*)

इति श्री मद्राजाधिराजपरमेश्वर वैदिकमार्गप्रवर्तक श्री वीरबुक्कभूपालसाम्राज्यधुरंधरेण सायणामात्येन विरचिते माधवीये वेदार्थप्रकाशे ऋक्संहिताभाष्ये चतुर्थाष्टके तृतीयोऽध्यायः समाप्तः ॥ (*iti śrī madrājādhirājaparameśvara vaidikamārgapravartaka śrī vīrabukkabhūpālasāmrājyadhuraṃdhareṇa sāyaṇāmātyena viracite mādhavīye vedārthaprakāśe ṛksaṃhitābhāṣye caturthāṣṭake tṛtīyo 'dhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ ‖*)
Here ends the third chapter in the fourth Aṣṭaka of the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā, accompanied by the commentary of the venerable Sāyaṇa and by a translation in the Kannada language.
यदक्षरपदभ्रष्टं मात्राहीनं तु यद्भवेत् । (*yadakṣarapadabhraṣṭaṃ mātrāhīnaṃ tu yadbhavet |*)
तत्सर्वं क्षम्यतां देव वागीश्वर नमोस्तु ते॥ (*tatsarvaṃ kṣamyatāṃ deva vāgīśvara namostu te‖*)
